Des lingots d'or. Photo d'illustration : Pexels
Raffinerie d'or : au Burkina, le Canadien Iamgold obtient une dérogation
08/11/2026    par    Francis Noude
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Le groupe canadien  Iamgold , qui exploite  Essakane , la plus grande mine d’or du Burkina Faso, a obtenu une dérogation temporaire à l’obligation de faire raffiner son or dans le pays. Elle figure dans ses résultats du troisième trimestre, publiés le 5 novembre, mais sa durée et ses motifs ne sont pas précisés. L’annonce survient peu après l’inauguration de   Raffinor-BF   à Ouagadougou, le 28 septembre, une usine pour  « raffiner tous nos métaux sur place »  selon le président.
Un arrêté, mais des discussions en cours
Pour rappel, le 12 octobre, le ministère des Mines a pourtant exigé que les détenteurs de permis industriels livrent tout leur doré à des raffineries agréées du pays, à compter du 1er novembre. Iamgold, qui détient 85 % d’Essakane, y échappe pour l’instant, le raffinage local devant respecter les «  normes internationales de l’industrie  ». En effet, son directeur général,  Renaud Adams , a indiqué aux analystes que l’exemption n’a pas de date et que l’activité continue normalement.
Mais l’enjeu est considérable pour la nouvelle usine, puisqu’Essakane a produit 94 000 onces attribuables à Iamgold au troisième trimestre. Tant que cet or est raffiné ailleurs, Raffinor-BF reste donc privée de son principal fournisseur potentiel.

items.title: Cameroun, Kenya, Namibie : Dangote lance trois projets pétroliers en cinq semaines

original_payload.original_title: Cameroun, Kenya, Namibie : Dangote lance trois projets pétroliers en cinq semaines
original_payload.original_body:
Ph : Ibrahim Mansur/The cable
Cameroun, Kenya, Namibie : Dangote lance trois projets pétroliers en cinq semaines
08/11/2026    par    Francis Noude
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Entre le 30 septembre et le 4 novembre 2026, le milliardaire nigérian  Aliko Dangote  a lancé trois projets pétroliers au  Kenya , au  Cameroun  et en  Namibie . L’homme le plus riche  d’Afrique  étend ainsi son activité au-delà de sa raffinerie du Nigeria, du raffinage jusqu’à la distribution et au stockage.
Une raffinerie au Kenya et un dépôt de carburant en Namibie
Le 30 septembre,  Dangote  et le président kényan  William Ruto  ont lancé les travaux de la raffinerie de Lamu, sur la côte du  Kenya , prévue pour traiter 700 000 barils par jour et estimée à 16 milliards de dollars. En effet, le groupe compte financer environ 70 % du coût par l’emprunt et offre aux gouvernements de la région d’en détenir 30 % au total. Et depuis l’arrêt de la  Kenya Petroleum Refineries Limited , le pays ne compte aucune raffinerie opérationnelle.
Puis, le 4 novembre, à Walvis Bay, Dangote a lancé en Namibie un  projet de 2,5 milliards de dollars  qui associe un dépôt de carburant et un pipeline, avec 18 à 20 mois de travaux annoncés. La présidente namibienne  Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah  a elle-même assisté au lancement même si l’opposant Venaani dénonçait déjà en novembre 2025 le manque de transparence du gouvernement.
Au Cameroun, une filiale créée après l’accord avec la Sonara
Le 28 octobre, Dangote a dévoilé la naissance de  Dangote Oil & Gas Cameroon , que dirigera Bertrand Mbouck, d’après  Investir au Cameroun . Son champ d’action va des stations-service au bitume, aux lubrifiants et au GPL, mais aussi au raffinage, à la pétrochimie et aux pipelines. Six jours plus tôt, le groupe avait signé avec la Société nationale de raffinage (Sonara) et MRS un contrat de 30 mois pour alimenter le pays en carburants. En juillet, le Premier ministre  Joseph Dion Ngute  avait reçu le vice-président du groupe, Devakumar Edwin, qui évoquait la création d’un site de stockage destiné à alimenter une réserve nationale.
Dangote avait aussi annoncé avec  Neptune Oil  l’exportation de 60 000 tonnes d’essence vers le Cameroun, ce qui a poussé son propriétaire,  Antoine Ndzengue , à déclarer :  « Ce partenariat avec Dangote Refinery marque un tournant pour le Cameroun » . Cette expansion était en effet attendue, car l’industriel avait promis en juin 2021, à la sortie d’une audience :  « Nous sommes établis au Cameroun, il y a quelques années, et nous allons continuer nos investissements non seulement dans le secteur du ciment, mais aussi dans le pétrole et le gaz et dans d’autres domaines » . Il devra toutefois composer avec la SCDP, qui développe à Kribi un terminal de 230 000 m³ pour les produits blancs.

Photo : Présidence Bénin
Bénin : 26 membres installés pour piloter les soins primaires et hospitaliers
08/11/2026    par    Armel TOGNON
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Le secteur de la santé se dote de nouvelles instances de pilotage. Le ministre de la Santé, le professeur  Benjamin Hounkpatin , a procédé, vendredi 6 novembre 2026 à Cotonou, à l’installation des membres de la deuxième mandature du Conseil national des soins de santé primaires (CNSSP) et du Conseil national de la médecine hospitalière (CNMH). Au total, 26 membres ont été désignés pour un mandat de quatre ans.
La cérémonie s’est déroulée en présence de  Toussaint Jean Léon Olory-Togbé , président de l’Autorité de régulation du secteur de la santé. À cette occasion, le ministre a rappelé les résultats obtenus par les deux instances au cours de leur première mandature. Il a notamment salué l’élaboration de documents de référence destinés à encadrer les pratiques et à améliorer la qualité des prestations sanitaires.
(📲 Rejoignez dès maintenant  👉     la communauté de La Nouvelle Tribune sur WhatsApp  !)
Institués par les décrets n° 2019-405 et n° 2019-406 du 25 septembre 2019, les deux conseils ont des attributions complémentaires. Le CNSSP intervient dans la définition des politiques et stratégies nationales relatives aux soins de santé primaires. Il contribue également à l’élaboration des normes et protocoles, à la répartition équitable des ressources et à l’évaluation des dispositifs mis en place.
Le CNMH exerce des responsabilités similaires dans le domaine de la médecine hospitalière. Ses compétences couvrent aussi la définition des conditions d’évacuation sanitaire, ainsi que le suivi et l’évaluation de leur application.
L’application des normes comme priorité
Pour cette nouvelle mandature, le ministre de la Santé attend des membres qu’ils franchissent une étape supplémentaire. Après la production de documents de référence, leur mise en œuvre effective constitue désormais un enjeu majeur. Benjamin Hounkpatin a insisté sur la nécessité de traduire le travail normatif en changements concrets dans la prise en charge des patients.
Au nom des membres installés,  Marcel Zannou , président du CNMH pour cette deuxième mandature, a exprimé sa reconnaissance au chef de l’État pour la confiance accordée. Il a présenté les quatre prochaines années comme une période de  « consolidation d’impact et de transformation systémique » , avec pour ambition de renforcer durablement le fonctionnement du système sanitaire béninois.

Liga: avec Mbappé, le Real Madrid met la pression sur le Barça
08/11/2026    par    Saturnin Bossa
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Le  Real Madrid  a battu Valence 3-0 à Mestalla, samedi 7 novembre 2026 en  Espagne , et revient à 30 points, à égalité avec le FC Barcelone en Liga, selon  la chronique de l’agence EFE . original_payload.original_body:
Un véhicule de la police républicaine
Bénin : Sa fuite après un vol violent se termine sous un véhicule à Bohicon
08/11/2026    par    Armel TOGNON
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Un individu soupçonné d’avoir agressé une gérante de cabine Mobile Money pour lui arracher son sac a été interpellé dans la soirée du jeudi 5 novembre 2026, au quartier  Zounzonmè, dans l’arrondissement d’Avogbanna, à Bohicon . L’intervention de la police a permis de récupérer 560 825 FCFA ainsi qu’une machette et plusieurs talismans.
Les faits se sont produits aux environs de 21 heures. En patrouille dans le secteur, des agents du commissariat d’arrondissement d’Avogbanna ont été alertés par des appels au secours. Ils ont alors aperçu un homme qui venait de s’emparer violemment du sac d’une gérante de point de transfert d’argent mobile.
(📲 Rejoignez dès maintenant  👉     la communauté de La Nouvelle Tribune sur WhatsApp  !)
Les policiers se sont immédiatement lancés à sa poursuite. Après environ 200 mètres de course, le suspect a trouvé refuge dans une maison. Le binôme de patrouille a encerclé les lieux avant de demander des renforts.
Une équipe de cinq agents, conduite par le chef d’unité, est rapidement arrivée sur place. À leur approche, le fuyard a quitté la maison par l’arrière et poursuivi sa course jusqu’à un garage automobile. Il s’est alors dissimulé sous un véhicule. Armé d’une machette, il a tenté de tenir les policiers à distance. Les agents ont finalement réussi à le maîtriser avant de le menotter et de l’embarquer.
Plus de 560 000 FCFA récupérés
La fouille effectuée après son arrestation a permis de retrouver sur lui 560 825 FCFA, présentés comme la somme emportée lors de l’agression. Une machette et plusieurs talismans ont également été découverts en sa possession. Ces différents objets ont été saisis et placés sous scellés pour les besoins de la procédure judiciaire.

original_payload.original_title: Nigeria : une cathédrale de 120 000 places inaugurée à Port Harcourt par l'Église Salvation Ministries
original_payload.original_body:
Photo Unsplash
Nigeria : une cathédrale de 120 000 places inaugurée à Port Harcourt par l'Église Salvation Ministries
08/11/2026    par    Saturnin Bossa
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Au  Nigeria , l’Église Salvation Ministries a inauguré le vendredi 6 novembre 2026 la Hand of God Cathedral, un édifice annoncé à 120 000 places, à Igwuruta, près de Port Harcourt. D’après le site nigérian   Legit.ng  , la cérémonie s’est déroulée au siège de l’Église, sur la route de l’aéroport, autour de son fondateur, le pasteur David Ibiyeomie. Le bishop  David Oyedepo , à la tête de l’Église Living Faith, était arrivé la veille en jet privé pour y assister.
Un bâtiment en forme de main ouverte
Il faut savoir que l’édifice s’étend sur environ 56 000 m² et compte huit étages et cinq ailes. En outre, son plan reproduit une main ouverte, une forme que l’Église associe à la protection et à la grâce divines. Salvation Ministries affirme que la salle dépasse  The Ark , l’auditorium d’Oyedepo, qui accueille environ 109 000 personnes, mais aucune source indépendante ne confirme ce classement.
Le chantier a duré plusieurs années, et des médias nigérians signalaient déjà un culte du dimanche sur le site en janvier 2022. Cette dédicace marque donc l’ouverture officielle plus que la première utilisation des lieux. Fondée en 1997 à Port Harcourt,  Salvation Ministries  fait désormais de cette cathédrale son siège mondial et y tient ses cultes dominicaux.
Le Nigeria vient de franchir un nouveau cap dans la construction des infrastructures religieuses avec l'inauguration de la « Hand of God Cathedral », dirigée par le pasteur David Ibiyeomie.

items.title: Mozambique: Chigamane golf project breaks ground as Inhambane swings into the global golf tourism market

original_payload.original_title: Mozambique: Chigamane golf project breaks ground as Inhambane swings into the global golf tourism market
original_payload.original_body:
Photo: AIM The Mozambican Government has announced plans to transform Chigamane, in Vilankulo district, into a new golf tourism destination through a project whose construction began on Saturday and which aims to strengthen the tourism offer, attract visitors and create local jobs.
The initiative was announced by the Presidency following a ceremony in Chigamane, a locality in the tourist district of Vilankulo, Inhambane province, where Mozambican President Daniel Chapo laid the foundation stone for the construction of the golf courses
In a statement, the Presidency said the development represents an investment in diversifying Vilankulo’s tourism offer, seeking to strengthen the district’s ability to attract visitors and consolidate its position as a leading destination in national and international tourism markets.
“The initiative aims to attract tourists from various regions of Mozambique and countries such as South Africa, Zimbabwe, Tanzania and Zambia, creating conditions to stimulate the local economy, encourage business development and expand the participation of national operators in the tourism value chain,” the statement said.
The project forms part of the broader strategy established by the Government to develop golf tourism in Inhambane province. In October, the Government approved the regulatory framework for the new Special Zone for Golf Tourism (ZETG), established to attract domestic and foreign investment and develop a high-value-added tourism segment.
Photo: Ministério da Economia

items.title: Secretária de Estado apela à organização dos moçambicanos residentes no Zimbabwe

original_payload.original_title: Secretária de Estado apela à organização dos moçambicanos residentes no Zimbabwe
original_payload.original_body:
A Secretária de Estado dos Negócios Estrangeiros e Comunidade Moçambicana no Exterior, Maria de Fátima Simão Manso, apelou aos cidadãos moçambicanos residentes na cidade de Rusape, no Zimbabwe, a reforçarem a união e a organização da comunidade.
“Queremos uma comunidade moçambicana organizada, forte e envolvida no desenvolvimento do país”, afirmou Maria de Fátima Simão Manso, durante um encontro realizado no sábado, 7 de Novembro, com membros da comunidade moçambicana naquela cidade.
Na ocasião, a governante incentivou os cidadãos a constituírem associações legalizadas e a cumprirem regularmente o pagamento das quotas. Defendeu que os valores angariados devem ser geridos pela própria comunidade e aplicados em projectos por ela definidos.
“O dinheiro que vão contribuir será gerido pela comunidade e deve ser usado para projectos definidos também pela comunidade. Temos que estar unidos, temos que ser solidários uns com os outros”, afirmou.
Maria de Fátima Simão Manso apelou ainda ao respeito pelas leis do país de acolhimento e à preservação do patriotismo. A Secretária de Estado garantiu igualmente que serão enviadas brigadas para tratar da documentação dos cidadãos moçambicanos e convidou a comunidade a aderir ao registo consular.
O encontro decorreu no âmbito de uma visita de quatro dias que a governante efectuou ao Zimbabwe, com término previsto para este domingo.

original_payload.original_body:
Subiu de 22 para 33 o número de mortos nos ataques sauditas registados no sábado, na região de Sana, no  Iémen. Os dados constam do novo balanço divulgado hoje pelas autoridades.
O número de vítimas mortais do ataque aéreo a leste de Sana subiu para 33 civis, na maioria crianças e mulheres.   Houve também 39 feridos, de acordo com o ministério da Saúde dos rebeldes huthis, citado pela imprensa internacional.
Os rebeldes huthis atribuem o ataque à coligação militar liderada pela Arábia Saudita em apoio ao Governo iemenita reconhecido internacionalmente.
O ministério dos rebeldes afirmou que estes números são preliminares e que entre os mortos estão 12 homens, oito mulheres e 13 crianças, enquanto entre os feridos há 16 homens, 10 mulheres e 13 crianças.
Recorde-se que na passada sexta-feira houve um outro ataque que causou a morte de 30 pessoas depois de um mercado no sudoeste do Iémen, ter sido também alvo de um bombardeamento.

items.title: How Ethiopia’s Military Modernization Is Emerging as Strategic Pillar of Regional Stability?

original_payload.original_title: How Ethiopia’s Military Modernization Is Emerging as Strategic Pillar of Regional Stability?
original_payload.original_body:
By Staff Writer
November 8 , 2026 (ENA)
Ethiopia’s growing military and technological capabilities are becoming increasingly significant, not only for safeguarding its national security but also for advancing peace, stability and economic integration in the Horn of Africa.
By modernising its defence institutions, strengthening its air force and investing in advanced military technology, the country has enhanced its capacity to address emerging security challenges while contributing to a more secure and stable regional environment.
The current acquisition of 12 fighter jets from Russia marks another step in Ethiopia’s efforts to modernise its military capabilities. Beyond strengthening national defence, such technological advancements can contribute to regional security by enhancing the country's capacity to deter threats, respond to security emergencies and support collective efforts to maintain peace.
Rather than viewing military modernisation exclusively through the lens of geopolitical competition, greater attention should be given to its broader contribution to regional stability, security cooperation and economic integration. In this regard, Ethiopia’s defence modernisation offers significant benefits that extend beyond safeguarding its national sovereignty and territorial integrity. Its advancing military technology and growing operational capabilities can strengthen regional security, enhance collective responses to shared security challenges, deter potential threats and contribute to a more stable environment.
Through responsible military development, Ethiopia can also help build trust among regional partners by demonstrating that strong defence institutions and peaceful cooperation are complementary objectives. In particular, advancements in air power can improve the country's capacity to protect its airspace, support regional security cooperation and respond to emerging threats.
These capabilities can further contribute to protecting strategic infrastructure, securing cross-border trade routes and creating favourable conditions for regional economic cooperation and integration. A technologically advanced and professionally organised defence force is an important component of both national and regional security. In a region facing terrorism, cross-border criminal activities, political instability and other transnational threats, the ability of states to protect their territories and respond effectively to emerging challenges is essential.
Ethiopia's investment in defence technology, particularly in air power, surveillance capabilities and operational readiness, therefore, can strengthen its ability to address security threats that extend beyond national borders. Modern military systems can improve situational awareness, enhance the protection of critical infrastructure and facilitate timely responses to security emergencies.
Stronger defence capabilities also contribute to deterrence, reducing the likelihood of potential adversaries resorting to military confrontation. When supported by responsible defence policies, transparency and diplomatic engagement, military preparedness can reinforce confidence in national security institutions and contribute to a more predictable regional security environment.
Hence, Ethiopia's military modernisation should be viewed as part of the broader effort to build the institutional and technological capacity required to safeguard peace and stability in the Horn of Africa.
The security challenges confronting the Horn of Africa are interconnected and cannot be effectively addressed by individual countries acting alone. They require coordinated responses and stronger regional security partnerships.
Ethiopia's growing military capabilities can enhance its contribution to these collective efforts by strengthening its capacity to participate in regional peace and security initiatives as advanced defence technology can improve operational preparedness, intelligence assessment, border protection and the ability to respond to emerging threats.
Ethiopia has a longstanding role in regional peace and security efforts, including its engagement in African and international peacekeeping initiatives. Its experience and institutional capabilities provide an important foundation for continued cooperation with neighbouring countries and regional organisations.
Peace and security are fundamental prerequisites for sustainable economic integration. Regional trade, cross-border investment, transport networks, energy cooperation and infrastructure development all depend on a stable and predictable security environment.
The Horn of Africa possesses considerable economic potential because of its strategic geographical position, natural resources, expanding markets and opportunities for regional connectivity. However, persistent insecurity can undermine investment, disrupt trade routes, damage infrastructure and discourage economic cooperation.
Ethiopia's strong  defence capabilities helps  address these challenges by improving the protection of strategic infrastructure, transportation corridors and economic assets. A capable defence institution can also help create the security conditions necessary for implementing regional development projects.
This is particularly important as countries in the region pursue greater economic connectivity through road networks, railway systems, energy interconnections, ports and trade corridors. Protecting these shared economic interests requires not only diplomatic cooperation but also adequate national and regional security capabilities.
Consequently, advances in military technology also have an economic dimension when they contribute to protecting the foundations of regional development and integration. The development of air power is another important element of modern defence systems, particularly in geographically extensive regions where security threats can emerge across difficult terrain and national borders.
Ethiopia's modernisation of its air force can strengthen its capacity to monitor its airspace, protect national infrastructure and respond to emergencies. Modern aircraft and associated technological systems can also improve operational coordination and support humanitarian and disaster-response activities where appropriate.
The broader regional value of these capabilities lies in their potential contribution to security cooperation. Through appropriate bilateral and multilateral arrangements, countries can strengthen information sharing, coordinate responses to common threats and establish mechanisms for preventing security incidents.
Such cooperation can help ensure that advances in military technology become instruments of collective security rather than sources of mistrust. It also highlights the importance of combining military preparedness with diplomatic engagement and confidence-building measures.
Ethiopia's defence development should therefore be understood within the context of its legitimate national security interests and its broader responsibility to contribute to a peaceful neighbourhood.
In this context, narratives portray Ethiopia's defence advancements, including some media coverage emerging from Egypt, as inherently threatening risk diverting attention from the broader importance of regional security cooperation. Such interpretations can deepen mistrust and complicate diplomatic relations.
Countries in the region would benefit more from constructive engagement, mutual respect and dialogue than from interpreting one another's national defence developments as grounds for confrontation.
The relationship between defence capabilities and economic development is particularly important in a region where insecurity can undermine major development ambitions. Strong institutions, secure borders and protected infrastructure provide an enabling environment for trade, investment and regional connectivity.
Ethiopia's military and technological development can also contribute to these objectives by strengthening national resilience and supporting the security requirements of regional cooperation.
In conclusion,         Ethiopia's advancing military technology represents an important development with implications extending beyond national defence. Its potential contribution to regional peace, stability and economic integration lies in strengthening the capacity to deter security threats, support collective security initiatives and protect the infrastructure and economic corridors upon which regional cooperation depends.
The Horn of Africa needs a security environment that enables countries to expand trade, connect markets, develop shared infrastructure and pursue common economic interests. Achieving this requires capable national institutions, stronger regional partnerships and a shared commitment to resolving differences peacefully.
Ethiopia's military modernisation should therefore be assessed within this broader regional context. The objective should not be to turn technological advancement into a source of rivalry, but to ensure that stronger defence capabilities contribute to a more secure neighbourhood and a more integrated region.

items.title: Digital Sovereignty Priority for Africa’s Future: Innovation & Technology State Minister

original_payload.original_title: Digital Sovereignty Priority for Africa’s Future: Innovation & Technology State Minister
original_payload.original_body:
Addis Ababa, November 8, 2026 (ENA)— Strengthening digital sovereignty and developing artificial intelligence infrastructure should be the priorities for Africa, Innovation and Technology State Minister Solomon Soka said.
According to him, sovereignty is no longer limited to geographical boundaries, but increasingly depends on algorithms, computing centers, and artificial intelligence technologies.
“Our sovereign spirit cannot be broken by external domination, but the arena of sovereignty has fundamentally changed. Today, it is defined by algorithms, computing capabilities, and artificial intelligence,” he noted.
Warning the danger AI-powered disinformation poses to economic and social stability by undermining public trust and affecting markets and investment, the State Minister stressed the need to establish independent African AI systems that ensure control over data, algorithms, and technological capabilities.
He revealed that Ethiopia is pursuing an approach of functional sovereignty, guided by the philosophy of “Medemer,” which emphasizes integration, strengthening national capabilities, protecting critical data, and maintaining independent decision-making.
The Digital Ethiopia 2030 Strategy translates this vision into action through the development of digital infrastructure and national capabilities, he added.
Solomon highlighted the launch of the national digital identity system (Fayda), the initiative to train five million Ethiopians in coding, and the establishment of the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute.
The institute is developing AI models in Ethiopia’s local languages to strengthen the presence of national identity and culture in the digital space.
The State Minister noted that Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed initiated the establishment of Medemer Artificial Intelligence University, which is envisioned as a continental hub for developing expertise and strengthening African countries’ capabilities in artificial intelligence.
Moreover, he noted that reliable energy, expanded telecommunications networks, data centers, and cloud computing infrastructure are essential requirements for achieving digital sovereignty.
“You cannot build a sovereign home on rented land,” the State Minister said, stressing the importance of African countries owning their data centers and cloud infrastructure and hosting their data within their territories.
He noted that Ethiopia aims to host its national data, projected to reach approximately 600    petabytes within its digital infrastructure by 2030.
Solomon also called for stronger African technological integration, noting that individual African countries cannot compete with the massive investments of global technology companies on their own.
In his remarks at a parallel session on the sidelines of the Second African Political Parties Summit in Addis Ababa, the State Minister warned against the use of deepfake technology and disinformation to influence voters, urging political parties to adopt ethical and responsible AI practices.
He underscored that exploiting these technologies for electoral gains would undermine public trust in institutions and threaten political and economic stability

items.title: Arlit : la société civile interpelle l’Union européenne et remet sur la table les conséquences de plus de 50 ans d’exploitation de l’uranium par Orano

original_payload.original_title: Arlit : la société civile interpelle l’Union européenne et remet sur la table les conséquences de plus de 50 ans d’exploitation de l’uranium par Orano
original_payload.original_body:
La Coordination de la société civile d’Arlit a vivement réagi, ce dimanche 8 novembre 2026, aux déclarations attribuées à l’Union européenne concernant la coopération militaire entre le Niger et l’Algérie. Dans un communiqué au ton particulièrement ferme, l’organisation dénonce ce qu’elle considère comme une ingérence dans les affaires de deux États souverains. Elle profite de cette prise de position pour interpeller les partenaires européens sur les conséquences environnementales, sanitaires, économiques et sociales de plus d’un demi-siècle d’exploitation de l’uranium nigérien par les sociétés liées au groupe français Orano, anciennement Areva.
Cette sortie intervient dans un contexte de recomposition des alliances diplomatiques et sécuritaires au Sahel, marqué notamment par le rapprochement entre Niamey et Alger.
Une réaction ferme aux interrogations européennes
À l’origine de cette prise de position figure la controverse suscitée par les déclarations du porte-parole de l’Union européenne chargé des affaires étrangères, Anouar El Anouni, au sujet de la présence de militaires algériens au Niger dans le cadre de la coopération bilatérale.
Des médias ont rapporté que Bruxelles souhaitait obtenir des précisions sur la portée, les objectifs et le fondement de ce déploiement.
Pour la Coordination de la société civile d’Arlit, ces interrogations sont difficilement compréhensibles dès lors qu’elles concernent un accord conclu entre deux pays africains voisins.
L’organisation estime que le Niger et l’Algérie disposent du droit souverain de définir les modalités de leur coopération militaire, conformément à leurs intérêts et à leurs engagements internationaux.
Elle réaffirme ainsi son soutien à ce partenariat, qu’elle considère comme une expression de solidarité et de coopération entre deux pays liés par l’histoire, la géographie et des défis sécuritaires communs.
L’exploitation de l’uranium au cœur des critiques
Au-delà de la question diplomatique, le communiqué soulève un dossier particulièrement sensible dans le nord du Niger : l’héritage de l’exploitation de l’uranium dans les zones d’Arlit et d’Akokan. La Coordination de la société civile reproche notamment à la France de ne pas avoir suffisamment pris en compte les conséquences de plusieurs décennies d’activités minières sur les populations locales et leur environnement.
Depuis le début des années 1970, les gisements d’uranium de la région ont été exploités principalement par la Société des mines de l’Aïr (SOMAÏR) et la Compagnie minière d’Akouta (COMINAK), deux entreprises historiquement liées à Areva, devenu Orano. Ces activités ont contribué à l’approvisionnement de l’industrie nucléaire française et internationale, tout en constituant une source de revenus, d’emplois et d’infrastructures pour le Niger. Mais elles ont également laissé un lourd passif environnemental et suscité des interrogations persistantes sur la répartition des retombées économiques.
Les préoccupations exprimées par la société civile trouvent un écho dans plusieurs travaux indépendants, notamment ceux de la Commission de recherche et d’information indépendantes sur la radioactivité (CRIIRAD), ainsi que dans les investigations engagées par les autorités nigériennes.
Des millions de tonnes de résidus radioactifs : un défi environnemental majeur
L’une des conséquences les plus préoccupantes de l’exploitation de l’uranium concerne l’accumulation des déchets miniers.
Dans un rapport publié le 10 juillet 2025, à partir d’investigations réalisées en collaboration avec l’organisation nigérienne AGHIRIN’MAN, la CRIIRAD alerte sur la présence d’environ 20 millions de tonnes de résidus radioactifs issus des activités de la COMINAK. Ces matériaux, entreposés sur le site minier, contiennent des substances radioactives à longue durée de vie et représentent des risques de contamination des sols, de dispersion de poussières et de pollution des eaux souterraines.
Un document officiel nigérien consacré au contentieux avec Orano évoque, pour sa part, environ 22 millions de tonnes de matériaux sur une superficie de 120 hectares. Ces estimations, qui reposent sur des périmètres et des méthodes de calcul différents, illustrent l’ampleur du défi de réhabilitation.
La fermeture de la mine souterraine de la COMINAK, intervenue en mars 2021, a ouvert une nouvelle phase consacrée au réaménagement du site et à la gestion de ses conséquences à long terme. Cependant, la suspension des travaux de réhabilitation annoncée début 2025 a renforcé les inquiétudes des organisations environnementales.
La CRIIRAD souligne notamment que le recouvrement des résidus radioactifs demeure insuffisant pour garantir leur confinement durable. Une situation qui soulève des questions sur les responsabilités des anciens exploitants, les garanties financières disponibles et la protection des générations futures.
L’eau, une ressource vitale fragilisée par l’activité minière
Dans une région saharienne où l’eau constitue une ressource particulièrement rare, les conséquences de l’exploitation minière sur les nappes souterraines représentent un enjeu majeur.
Selon les investigations publiées en juillet 2025 par la CRIIRAD, plus de cinquante années d’activités minières ont eu des répercussions importantes sur la quantité et la qualité des ressources hydriques disponibles à Arlit.
Les analyses réalisées en octobre 2024 au nouveau château d’eau d’Arlit ont révélé une concentration relativement faible d’uranium, de 1,5 microgramme par litre. Toutefois, les chercheurs alertent sur les risques futurs de contamination liés aux infiltrations provenant des installations minières et des résidus radioactifs.
Le rapport fait également état d’une concentration de 484,5 microgrammes d’uranium par litre dans un ancien puits situé au nord d’Arlit, soit plus de seize fois la valeur guide de l’Organisation mondiale de la santé.
Pour les populations, l’enjeu dépasse la seule question de la radioactivité. Il concerne également la disponibilité de l’eau potable, les activités maraîchères, l’élevage et les conditions de vie dans une zone déjà confrontée à de fortes contraintes climatiques.
Des risques sanitaires qui nécessitent une surveillance renforcée
La question sanitaire constitue un autre sujet de préoccupation pour les habitants d’Arlit et d’Akokan. L’exposition prolongée à certaines substances radioactives peut augmenter les risques de cancers, notamment en cas d’inhalation de poussières contenant des radionucléides. L’ingestion d’uranium peut également présenter une toxicité chimique, particulièrement pour les reins.
Dans son rapport de 2025, la CRIIRAD relève que les évaluations d’exposition réalisées pour des enfants résidant dans certains quartiers d’Akokan faisaient apparaître une augmentation préoccupante des doses supplémentaires de radiation entre 2016 et 2020.
Déversement des effluents radioactifs à Arlit
Des conséquences économiques et sociales durables
La fermeture de la COMINAK, en mars 2021, a notamment affecté un tissu économique qui reposait directement ou indirectement sur plus de 1 400 salariés et sous-traitants, selon les données publiées par Orano. Le groupe indique avoir prévu un programme de reconversion professionnelle, d’accompagnement social et de développement d’activités alternatives. Un programme qui n’est plus d’actualité.
Sur le plan national, les retombées de l’exploitation minière font également l’objet d’un contentieux entre les autorités nigériennes et Orano.
Dans un document officiel, l’État nigérien soutient que la commercialisation de la production historique de la SOMAÏR aurait été marquée par un déséquilibre au détriment des intérêts nationaux. Les autorités évoquent notamment une production cumulée de 80 517 tonnes d’uranium entre 1971 et 2024, dont 86,3 % auraient été commercialisés par Orano, contre 9,2 % par la partie nigérienne.
Un contentieux désormais porté au plus haut niveau de l’État
Les préoccupations environnementales et économiques soulevées par la société civile d’Arlit s’inscrivent désormais dans un dossier national.
Le 28 février 2026, le Président de la République, le Général d’Armée Abdourahamane Tiani, a reçu un comité d’experts nationaux chargé d’évaluer les conséquences de l’exploitation de l’uranium dans la région d’Arlit entre 1968 et 2025.
Conduite par le professeur Rabani Adamou, cette mission a examiné les dimensions environnementales, sanitaires et économiques des activités minières.
Dans son argumentaire, l’État nigérien souligne également que le coût du programme de réhabilitation de la COMINAK, initialement évalué à 95 milliards de FCFA, a été révisé à 125,3 milliards de FCFA.
De son côté, Orano affirme avoir engagé des actions de réaménagement et d’accompagnement des populations. Le groupe attribue les difficultés rencontrées depuis fin 2024 à la perte de son contrôle opérationnel sur ses activités nigériennes et indique avoir engagé des procédures d’arbitrage international.
Cette divergence souligne la complexité du dossier et l’importance d’établir clairement les responsabilités juridiques, financières et environnementales de chaque partie.
La société civile réclame le respect de la souveraineté des États africains
Dans son communiqué du 8 novembre, la Coordination de la société civile d’Arlit établit un parallèle entre les interrogations européennes sur la coopération militaire nigéro-algérienne et les conséquences historiques de l’exploitation des ressources africaines.
Elle interpelle également la France sur son passé colonial en Algérie, notamment les essais nucléaires effectués dans le Sahara algérien, ainsi que sur son ancienne présence militaire au Sahel.
L’organisation considère que les partenaires européens devraient accorder davantage d’attention aux préoccupations environnementales, sanitaires et économiques des populations concernées par l’exploitation des ressources naturelles.
Elle réaffirme, en conclusion, son soutien à la coopération militaire entre le Niger et l’Algérie, qu’elle présente comme un choix souverain de deux pays africains partageant des intérêts communs.
Au-delà de la polémique diplomatique, cette prise de position remet en lumière une question fondamentale pour les populations d’Arlit et d’Akokan : comment garantir que les richesses extraites du sous-sol nigérien s’accompagnent d’une protection effective de l’environnement, de la santé publique et des intérêts des communautés locales ?
Après plus d’un demi-siècle d’exploitation de l’uranium, la réhabilitation des sites, la sécurisation des ressources en eau, le suivi médical des populations et la diversification économique apparaissent comme des enjeux majeurs pour l’avenir de cette région du nord du Niger.

items.title: Dozens killed after migrant boat sinks off Senegal

original_payload.original_title: Dozens killed after migrant boat sinks off Senegal
original_payload.original_body:
Catastrophe   Senegal
Dozens killed after migrant boat sinks off Senegal
Saim Dušan Inayatullah   with AFP, Reuters
11/08/2026  November 8, 2026    The incident occurred near Kebemer off the coast of northwestern Senegal. Authorities on El Hierro in the Canary Islands have declared an emergency after a marked increase in migrant boat arrivals.
https://p.dw.com/p/5PDGd
Prefer DW on Google
Thousands of people attempt to reach Spain's Canary Islands from West Africa through the perilous Atlantic route every year Image: Jesus Cabrera/REUTERS       Advertisement
At least 34 people were killed after a small boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of northwestern  Senegal , Senegalese authorities said.
Thousands have died in recent years after  embarking on boats from the Senegalese coast in order to reach Spain's Canary Islands  through the perilous Atlantic route.
Initially, the Senegalese Ministry of the Interior stated that only one person had been rescued from the capsizing and that 21 bodies had been recovered.
The ministry added that the toll was "provisional" and that search operations were still ongoing.
The incident occurred near Kebemer, some 180 kilometers (around 112 miles) north of the capital, Dakar.
On Saturday, the ministry stressed the government's "determination to combat people smuggling networks, notably through strengthened cooperation with neighboring countries."
Senegalese authorities said they intercepted 142 migrants on a similar boat aimed at reaching  Spanish  territory on Friday. The boat included nationals of multiple West African countries.
Authorities on the island of El Hierro have declared an emergency due to increased migrant arrivals Image: Jesus Cabrera/REUTERS
El Hierro island declares emergency over migrant arrivals
Authorities on El Hierro Island in the Canary Islands declared an emergency on Saturday after a marked increase in migrant boat arrivals.
El Hierro officials say that over 3,300 people have arrived on around 30 boats since the start of the month.
"We are very concerned... by this sharp increase in arrivals," Alpidio Armas, head of the El Hierro regional council, told Spanish television.
"This is precisely what has led us to declare an emergency in order to ensure a framework of cooperation with higher-level institutions," he added.
Armas said that conditions at the island's hospital have become "undesirable."
El Hierro is home to about 11,400 residents.
Migrant  arrivals reached a record high of 46,000 in 2024. Afterwards, arrivals have fallen sharply due to increased surveillance and cooperation with African countries.

items.title: South Africa elections: ANC marks its worst-ever performance

original_payload.original_title: South Africa elections: ANC marks its worst-ever performance
original_payload.original_body:
Politics   South Africa
South Africa's ANC hit by worst-ever performance in local elections
Wesley Rahn   with AFP, dpa     |   Darko Janjevic
11/08/2026  November 8, 2026    The African National Congress, the party of late Nobel Prize winner Nelson Mandela, slumped to its worst-ever result in South Africa's municipal election. The voters blame the ANC for water and electricity shortages.
https://p.dw.com/p/5PCNm
Prefer DW on Google
Millions of South Africans headed to the polls across the country's municipalities to elect local councilors and mayors (Photo: November 4) Image: Leandre Steenberg/Matrix Images/picture alliance       Advertisement
South Africa's African National Congress (ANC) turned in a  historically poor election performance , with the the final tally published on Sunday giving them less than 31% of the vote in  Wednesday's municipal polls .
Their closes rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), won just under 25% of the vote.
The ANC also lost its majority in six of the eight metropolitan regions,  South Africa 's Electoral Commission said on Saturday. With no outright winner declared in several major cities, politicians are expected enter tough coalition talks to form municipal governments.
ANC secretary general says outcome 'catastrophic'
While the ANC remains the most popular party in the country, they have been struggling with growing backlash from voters. In 2026, many South Africans are frustrated by water and electricity shortages, with the  ANC taking the blame  for the poor state of municipalities.  High unemployment, crime, and widespread corruption are high on the public agenda.
ANC leader, and South African president,  Cyril Ramaphosa , has not yet addressed his party's poor performance. In his weekly presidential letter, however, he admitted that "municipal failures have contributed to declining public trust and confidence in democratic governance."
On Saturday, ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula told reporters that the ANC needs to work on winning back public confidence.
"We cannot ask the people to trust us merely because of our history," Mbalula said.
"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC ... as much as we are the largest party, it has been catastrophic for the movement," he added.
The ANC's steady decline with voters
The ANC had governed with an absolute majority for most of its history up until the  general election in 2024  saw it  lose an outright parliamentary majority  for the first time in South Africa's democratic era.
"This is the most severe result that the ANC would have feared," political analyst Daniel Silke told the AFP news agency.
"It's the ANC's worst result in history," Silke said, adding that the result will undermine the ANC's ability to exert authority on the local and national level. The results could also provide a bellwether of voter sentiment ahead of the 2029 general elections.
Once led by Nelson Mandela , the ANC was instrumental in ending apartheid, and took and power in 1994 after South Africa became a democracy.
But over the past decade, it has steadily performed worse in one election after another. In 2024, the ANC secured just over 40% in the 2024 national polls and 46% at the previous municipal elections in 2021.
After losing the absolute majority in 2024, the  ANC formed a cross-party national unity government  with all the parties represented in parliament, which is still in power.
The ANC's decline comes amid disillusionment over corruption, mismanagement and high unemployment.  Smaller parties have also emerged  across South Africa's political landscape, cutting into the ANC's voter base.
DA opposition holds large cities
The pro-business, center-right DA is set to keep control of Cape Town after winning an absolute majority. It also performed well in the capital, Pretoria, and economic hub of Johannesburg, and is expected to form coalitions that exclude the ANC.
"All of the cut and thrust that comes with the election is now over, and it is time now... to put together governments that can actually fix these towns and cities," DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis told reporters.
"We have already reached out to many parties over the last 24 hours and will continue to do so today," he said.
Wesley Rahn   Editor and reporter focusing on geopolitics and current affairs

items.title: Egypt train crash leaves several dead, over 100 injured

original_payload.original_title: Egypt train crash leaves several dead, over 100 injured
original_payload.original_body:
Catastrophe   Egypt
Egypt train crash leaves several dead, over 100 injured
Darko Janjevic   with AP, dpa, AFP
11/08/2026  November 8, 2026    A train derailed after colliding with another train south of Cairo, with authorities confirming several deaths and saying more than 100 passengers were injured. Over 50 ambulances were deployed to the scene.
https://p.dw.com/p/5PDnQ
Prefer DW on Google
Scores of people were reported injured in the train collision  Image: AFP       Advertisement
At least seven people were killed in the train collision in  Egypt  on Sunday, with authorities also confirming over 100 people were injured.
The collision involved one train hitting the rear end of another while traveling through the Giza province on the line between Cairo and the southern Nile city of Aswan. One of the trains then derailed and several cars flipped, according to the Egyptian authorities.
Authorities said rescue teams and cleanup crews were deployed to the site Image: AP Photo/picture alliance
Officials said 52 ambulances were deployed to the scene some 52 kilometers (32 miles) south of Cairo. Emergency crews and cranes were also working to clear the line and restore railway traffic through Giza's al-Ayyat district.
The cause of the accident was not immediately clear.
El-Sissi says incident being investigated
In a social media post,  Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi  said he ordered an investigation. He also urged the state agencies to "hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent."
State media reports indicated a large number of injuries Image: AP Photo/picture alliance
The crash tool place in the same area as the worst train disaster in Egypt's history, which saw over 370 people were killed in a train fire in 2002. Several crashes also claimed dozens of lives in the same region in 2009.
In recent years,  Egypt has invested billions of dollars into new highways and high-speed rail lines , but is still  facing safety issues  and repeated crashes while attempting to  revamp its aging rail network .

General News  Dangote supports small businesses, community at sustainability week
By  Ismail Abdulaziz   ·   16 hours ago   ·  2 min read
✓
✓
Dangote Cement Plc, Obajana Plant, has reinforced its commitment to community development, economic empowerment and environmental sustainability with a series of interventions benefiting host communities during its 2026 Sustainability Week.
A statement from the company said the annual event featured several initiatives aimed at improving livelihoods, supporting local enterprises and promoting access to sustainable energy, underscoring the Company’s commitment to creating shared value beyond its core cement manufacturing operations.
It said as part of its economic empowerment drive, the Plant supported a number of small and micro businesses, providing encouragement and opportunities to strengthen their operations, improve productivity and contribute to local economic growth.
The intervention reflects Dangote Cement’s recognition of small businesses as important drivers of employment, household income and community prosperity.
It added that in another significant intervention, the Company inaugurated a 3.6kW solar inverter system in Oyo Community, providing access to renewable electricity and supporting sustainable water supply for residents.
“The project is expected to improve the reliability of electricity for community water infrastructure, reduce dependence on conventional energy sources and enhance residents’ access to this essential resources.
‘‘The solar installation also demonstrates the Company’s commitment to promoting cleaner energy solutions and supporting Nigeria’s transition towards more sustainable and environmentally responsible development.”
Speaking on the initiatives, the company reiterated that sustainability remains central to its operations and community engagement strategy.
It noted that meaningful development goes beyond infrastructure provision to include empowering people, strengthening local businesses and improving access to essential services.
The 2026 Sustainability Week further provided an opportunity to deepen engagement with host communities, celebrate collaborative achievements and reinforce partnerships aimed at addressing local development priorities.
Through these interventions, Dangote Cement Obajana continues to demonstrate that responsible industrial operations must go hand in hand with inclusive growth, environmental stewardship and improved quality of life for surrounding communities.
The week-long event brought together employees, sustainability champions, host community members, and local entrepreneurs in a series of activities aimed at promoting environmental stewardship, social impact, and sustainable development.
A major highlight of the programme was the SME Empowerment and Business Development Capacity Building, which provided local entrepreneurs with training on business growth, financial management, customer service, and sustainable business practices.
In recognition of their commitment to entrepreneurship and continuous improvement, 15 SMEs were honoured with plaques of recognition.(NAN)

By Abdulrahman Yahaya
President of the Nigeria Wrestling Federation (NWF), Adewale Adeniyi, has congratulated Nigeria’s U-17 women’s national team, the Flamingos, on their historic triumph at the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup.
The Hakeem Busari-led team defeated their Japan counterparts 2-1 to secure a historic first FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup for Nigeria on Saturday night in Rabat, Morocco.
In a statement he personally signed, Adeniyi praised the young Nigerian players for their inspirational performance, describing the victory as “a moment of immense pride not only for Nigeria but also for the entire African continent.
“I want to congratulate the Flamingos for this historic success that has given millions of young Nigerians a reason to dream bigger. Their success proves that dedication, hard work and collective effort can turn great aspirations into reality.
“Their remarkable feat has placed Nigeria and Africa on the global football map and demonstrated the immense potential of our young female athletes.”
Adeniyi added that having five different players of the team winning the players of the match is an assurance that the future is bright for female football in Nigeria.
He said “what is more reassuring about the future of the team is that for the five matches, five different MVPs emerged from the Nigerian team.
“Having five different players do so shows the depth of the team and how bright the future is.”
The NWF president also commended members of the technical crew for their dedication, sacrifices and mentorship, noting that their guidance played significant role in nurturing the young players and preparing them for the historic achievement. (NAN)

items.title: Cleric tasks Nigerian politicians, electorate on unity

original_payload.original_title: Cleric tasks Nigerian politicians, electorate on unity
original_payload.original_body:
Religious  Cleric tasks Nigerian politicians, electorate on unity
By  Funmilayo Adeyemi   ·   16 hours ago   ·  3 min read
✓
✓
By Philomina Attah
The Founder of Unity Worship Centre, Abuja, Pastor Tayo Olutayo, has warned that election cycles have further divided Nigeria along religious and tribal lines instead of uniting the country.
Olutayo gave the warning on Sunday in Abuja at the grand finale of Maranatha 2026, the annual programme of the church with the theme, “Our God Reigns”.
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the event, which focuses on the second coming of Christ, attracted clerics and worshippers who prayed for national unity.
Speaking on Nigeria’s current political atmosphere ahead of 2027, Olutayo said since his involvement in elections from 1979, every election cycle has divided the country further on two platforms: religion and tribe.
He said instead of elections bringing development, they have fuelled suspicion, tribal wars and disunity, with political campaigns now framed as North versus South, East versus South-South.
“We do not hear that from other countries that grow. Everybody is first of all a Nigerian and must practise like that.
“What the country needs first is unity, not polls.
“I rather prefer that all the resources we are spending and deploying for voter cards and registration, with all the confusion, we deploy our energy first to unite.
“Unity and faith is what our fathers told us. Our old national anthem preached unity and faith.
“Soldiers came and added peace and progress, but there can be no peace and progress without unity and faith,” he said.
Olutayo said the call for unity had become urgent due to insecurity that had displaced entire communities.
He urged the Federal Government to sit down and find a solution to disunity before pushing for elections, saying it is the task of the current government to correct past wrongs.
Also speaking, the Chairman, Elders Council of the church, Jide Adeniji, said the body of Christ must be united and rise above denominational differences, tribalism and religious bigotry.
“Nigerians must understand that God is God of all flesh and not for Christians or Muslims alone, hence no one should carry cutlasses to fight for God,” he said.
Similarly, a pastor in the church, Pastor Casmir Igwe, said Nigerians were desperate for survival due to economic hardship and insecurity.
According to Igwe, desperation should not be a license to commit crime or sin.
“As long as there is God and life, there is hope. Nigerians should allow God to reign in their lives, polity and economy,” he said.
Chairman of the Organising Committee, Pastor Okey Udoh, said anything of God was about unity, noting that members willingly contributed to make Maranatha 2026 a success.
Udoh said the essence of the church was to make better communities for social good and to encourage people to be better citizens.(NAN)

original_payload.original_title: Foundation raises N45.18m to support children battling cancer
original_payload.original_body:
Health  Foundation raises N45.18m to support children battling cancer
By  Ndubisi Ijeoma   ·   18 hours ago   ·  4 min read
✓
✓
By Justina Auta
The Okapi Children Cancer Foundation (OkapiCCF) says it has raised N45.18 million to support children battling cancer during the 2026/2027 intervention year to increase access to life-saving treatment and care.
Dr Kemi Adekanye, Founder and Chief Volunteer of OkapiCCF, said this at the presentation of the foundation’s 2026 donations and awards ceremony in Abuja.
Adekanye said the foundation raised N45.17 million, surpassing the N39.56 million raised in 2024/2025.
She described the achievement as a testament to the generosity and commitment of donors, partners and volunteers.
She said that 70 per cent of the funds, amounting to N31.62 million, had been earmarked for direct childhood cancer treatment.
“30 per cent is earmarked for awareness campaigns, children’s programmes, school sensitisation, scholarships and other interventions.
“This fund represents hope for children fighting cancer and their families.
“Every donation brings us closer to ensuring that no child is denied treatment because of financial constraints,” she said.
She said that the treatment fund would be shared among the National Hospital Abuja and University of Abuja Teaching Hospital, Gwagwalada (UATH).
“Others include Federal Medical Centre (FMC), Abuja, while a portion will support children in Lagos, Owerri and Zaria,” she said.
Adekanye said the organisation had, so far, carried out 288 childhood cancer interventions, trained 10,378 students, reached seven communities, trained 54 schools and awarded five educational scholarships for survivors.
She said that during the 2025/2026 year, the foundation provided N17.94 million in treatment support.
“We funded 69 treatment requests for 34 children, with 30 completing treatment, while the remaining are still on treatment or achieving remission.
“Our vision is to ensure wider access to treatment, strengthen sustainable funding and expand our reach so that every child diagnosed with cancer has a fighting chance,” she said.
Mr Gbenro Oladoja, Head of Management at OkapiCCF, said too many children continued to die from cancer despite the fact that timely diagnosis, affordable treatment and accessible healthcare can significantly improve survival.
“Our mission is simple: to make sure that no child is left to fight cancer alone.
“Through your support, we walk with families, support treatment, raise awareness, and speak up for stronger healthcare policies for young patients,” he said.
Dr Shuaibu Belgore, Permanent Secretary, Federal Ministry of Housing and Urban Development, emphasised the need for sustained efforts towards improving lives of children with cancer.
Belgore, represented by the ministry’s Director of Public Building, Mr Pemi Temitope, urged stakeholderers to continue to support improvement of access to healthcare, adding that a healthy population is fundamental to social development.
Dr John Balogun, Paediatric Oncologist, UATH, said that every support given to patients gives hope and restores lives.
”When adults survive cancer, they may go on to live many more productive years.
”When you help a child survive cancer, you are adding decades to that child’s future by giving him the opportunity to contribute meaningfully to the development of our nation.
Dr Ifeoma Ezeukwu-Orogade, Consultant Paedetrician, and Head, Paedetric Hematology Unit, FMC, said the support of the organisation has given hope to the children with cancer and their families.
”Your support has been a source of hope for families, healthcare professionals, and, most importantly, children battling cancer who desperately need access to quality care,” she said.
Dr Juliet Okpala, Senior Register, Haemotoncology Unit, NHA, said that many parents became overwhelmed due to the cost of treatment and lack of funds.
”At those difficult moments, when we reach out to you, you step in and provide the support these families desperately need.
”We do not take your kindness, commitment and partnership for granted. Your support gives these children another chance at life and gives their families renewed hope.”
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN)
reports that the foundation also honoured donors, volunteers and partners including Mrs Justina Auta, Senior Editor, NAN for their contributions to improving childhood cancer care and creating awareness.
Tina Auta receiving her award   OkapiCCF is a non-profit organisation that provides financial, emotional and psychological support to children diagnosed with cancer, while promoting awareness and early detection across Nigeria. (NAN)
Edited by Kadiri Abdulrahman

items.title: Voluntary blood donation: Giving survivors a second chance at life

original_payload.original_title: Voluntary blood donation: Giving survivors a second chance at life
original_payload.original_body:
Features  Voluntary blood donation: Giving survivors a second chance at life
By  Ndubisi Ijeoma   ·   6 hours ago   ·  7 min read
✓
✓
By Justina Auta, News Agency of Nigeria (NAN)
Nigeria requires an estimated 1.8 million to two million units of blood annually to meet its healthcare needs, but available supplies remain significantly below demand.
The World Health Organisation (WHO) says Nigeria collected 371,827 units of blood in 2024, highlighting the gap between the quantity required and available supplies.
The shortage affects access to blood for emergencies, surgeries, childbirth complications and treatment of life-threatening illnesses.
Consequently, patients and their families often resort to emergency appeals to relatives, friends and strangers to secure blood for transfusions.
For two-year-old Destiny Emmanuel, a desperate search for blood became a race against time as her family struggled to find a compatible donor during a medical emergency.
As doctors battled to stabilise her, her mother, Gift Emmanuel, watched helplessly, uncertain whether her daughter, who was undergoing chemotherapy for leukaemia, would survive.
Just as hope began to fade, an unlikely hero emerged.
A hospital security guard, who had watched the woman make frantic calls near the duty post seeking blood donors, offered to donate after being certified eligible.
For the mother, the stranger’s action transformed a moment of fear into a story of survival.
“My daughter is alive today because someone I did not know chose to donate blood. That person gave my family another chance to smile,” she said.
Similarly, Malam Usman Ali, a subsistence farmer, recalled how a neighbour came to his family’s rescue when his wife required an urgent blood transfusion following childbirth complications.
Ali said he almost lost his wife after she experienced prolonged labour and severe bleeding while delivering their fifth child.
“I almost lost my wife because she had a prolonged labour and lost a lot of blood while trying to deliver our fifth child.
“I couldn’t donate blood because of some health reasons, so my neighbour, who is not even from my tribe or religion, was the one who donated freely,” he said.
Beyond these experiences, families of children battling cancer also face difficulties accessing blood during treatment.
Gift recalled the challenges associated with securing blood when cancer treatment affects patients’ blood levels, making transfusions necessary to support their recovery and enable them to continue treatment.
These experiences underscore the challenges patients and their families face during medical emergencies, when access to safe blood can make the difference between life and death.
Against this backdrop, Dr Kemi Adekanye, Founder and Chief Volunteer, Okapi Children Cancer Foundation, urged Nigerians to embrace voluntary blood donation, saying the decision to give blood could help children fighting cancer complete their treatment.
“Blood donation is a critical part of childhood cancer care.
“Many children undergoing treatment, especially chemotherapy, experience low blood levels and require safe blood transfusion to continue their treatment and recover.
“For these children, every unit of blood donated is more than a medical resource; it is a lifeline that gives them strength, hope and another chance at survival,” she said.
Beyond cancer care, blood transfusion remains essential in managing several medical conditions, including maternal haemorrhage, severe anaemia, road traffic injuries, sickle cell complications and patients undergoing major surgeries.
The importance of adequate blood supplies is also evident in maternal healthcare.
According to WHO, postpartum haemorrhage accounts for approximately 23 to 30 per cent of maternal deaths in Nigeria, underscoring the need for timely access to safe blood during childbirth emergencies.
More broadly, WHO identifies safe blood as essential for emergency care, surgical procedures, pregnancy-related complications, trauma cases and the treatment of several medical conditions.
To ensure sustainable supplies, the organisation recommends that countries rely mainly on voluntary, unpaid blood donors, who generally constitute the safest source of blood.
WHO also recommends that countries collect at least 10 units of blood per 1,000 people annually to meet basic transfusion needs.
For Nigeria, with a population exceeding 200 million, meeting this benchmark requires sustained public enlightenment, stronger blood collection systems and increased participation in voluntary donation.
Meanwhile, health authorities and stakeholders have continued to express concern over the gap between blood demand and availability.
Prof. Saleh Yuguda, Director-General, National Blood Service Agency (NBSA), said Nigeria required about 1.8 million to two million units of blood annually to meet its healthcare needs.
Yuguda, represented by Dr Aliyu Waziri, Head of NBSA Abuja Operations Centre, spoke at a recent media roundtable on voluntary blood donation and safe blood advocacy in Abuja.
He said the agency’s collection figures remained extremely low, with its centres recording only about 24,000 to 25,000 units in the preceding year.
“As of last year, if we only take the census in the National Blood Service, we will only be talking about 24,000 or 25,000 units of blood generally.
“But when having a population of more than 200 million people, we should be talking about at least two per cent of our population giving blood. So there is a huge gap that we need to fill,” he said.
The NBSA official called for increased regular voluntary blood donation to bridge the supply gap and reduce dependence on emergency appeals.
However, misconceptions, fear and misinformation remain major barriers to voluntary blood donation in the country.
Dr Kefas Jibir-Gurama, Head of the Department of Paediatrics, Federal Medical Centre (FMC), Abuja, said some people wrongly believed that donating blood made them weak or exposed them to illness.
“Some people wrongly believe that donating blood makes them weak or exposes them to illness, despite assurances from health professionals that safe blood donation is harmless when conducted in approved facilities,” he said.
Health professionals say eligible individuals can donate blood safely when proper screening, sterile equipment and established medical procedures are followed.
In addition to addressing these misconceptions, stakeholders say the media has an important role in encouraging Nigerians to make blood donation a regular humanitarian practice rather than an activity undertaken only during emergencies.
Mrs Moji Makanjuola, Executive Director, International Society of Media in Public Health (ISMPH), said the media remained critical in promoting safe blood donation through public education, awareness creation, advocacy and community mobilisation.
“The media plays a vital role in promoting safe blood and voluntary blood donation through public education, awareness creation, advocacy, and community mobilisation,” she said.
Makanjuola added that media advocacy would help correct misconceptions, reduce fear, encourage regular voluntary donation and build confidence in blood transfusion services.
“Effective collaboration between the media, healthcare professionals, government, and the general public is essential to ensure an adequate and safe blood supply, and ultimately save lives,” she said.
Similarly, Mrs Bassey Ita-Ikpang, Chairperson, Nigeria Association of Women Journalists (NAWOJ), FCT Chapter, called on journalists to use human-interest stories to promote a culture of voluntary blood donation.
“Beyond reporting events, we must tell human-interest stories, amplify accurate health information, challenge harmful misconceptions and encourage a culture of voluntary, regular and unpaid blood donation,” she said.
Mr Joseph Kadiri, President, Association of Nigeria Health Journalists (ANHeJ), also reaffirmed journalists’ commitment to providing accurate information on blood donation.
For families of survivors, however, blood donation is more than a medical procedure; it is a lifeline that transforms fear into hope and despair into a new beginning.
As Nigeria works to strengthen its blood transfusion system, health authorities and survivors continue to urge citizens to embrace voluntary blood donation.
They believe becoming a regular blood donor is not only a medical responsibility but also an act of humanity, capable of turning moments of tragedy into stories of hope.
For the security guard who donated blood to save Destiny, the act may have lasted only a few minutes, but its impact on the child and her family will last a lifetime.
Ultimately, every donation represents an opportunity to restore a life, reunite a family and give someone another chance. (NANFeatures)
Edited by Tosin Kolade

(NAN)

original_payload.original_title: South Sudan inter-party dialogue set to resume to finalise resolutions
original_payload.original_body:
SPLM Secretary-General Akol Paul Kordit met senior party officials and representatives of other political groups earlier this week to prepare for the resumption of the inter-party dialogue in Juba on Monday, November 9, 2026.
The meeting agreed that the plenary session would discuss and finalise proposed resolutions and a joint communiqué, the SPLM said in a statement. The date of the closing ceremony would be determined in consultation with President Salva Kiir after the resolutions had been adopted.
At the conclusion  of the two-week dialogue last month, Senior Presidential Envoy Adut Salva Kiir reiterated the government’s position that elections should proceed as scheduled, saying further extensions were not open to negotiation.
The dialogue, launched by Kiir on September 24, brought together Juba-based political parties and other stakeholders to discuss preparations for South Sudan’s first general elections since independence in 2011.
However, some parties criticised the process, arguing that it was controlled by the government and could not address broader political grievances while former First Vice-President Riek Machar remained in detention and on trial.
At the opening of the dialogue,  Kiir warned political parties  against using the discussions to renegotiate the electoral timetable.
“This inter-party dialogue is not a place for negotiations and disagreement. It is not a place to shift the direction of the path that we have taken. It is not a place to hold us back,” he said.
His remarks followed the dissolution of the transitional unity government on September 22 and the appointment of a caretaker administration.
Political analyst and government critic Abraham Awolich told Radio Tamazuj on Wednesday that  the two-week dialogue had failed to reach a consensus  last month because the government insisted on holding elections as scheduled, while other parties called for their postponement and negotiations on a new political arrangement.
Awolich, a former managing director of the Sudd Institute, said the government wanted political parties to endorse decisions already taken by Kiir rather than negotiate the country’s political future.
“We had characterised this inter-party dialogue as a banquet among people who had already agreed to violate the constitution,” he said.
He said some participants had proposed postponing the elections without extending the mandates of the Revitalised Transitional Government of National Unity (RTGoNU) and institutions established under the 2018 peace agreement. Instead, they called for negotiations on an alternative political arrangement.
Government representatives insisted that elections should proceed despite the political and security challenges, he said.
Attempts to prepare final resolutions without the agreement of all participating parties were abandoned after concerns that excluded groups would publicly reject the document, Awolich said.
The inter-party dialogue ended last month without publicly agreed resolutions, he added.

items.title: Lakes State trains election officials

original_payload.original_title: Lakes State trains election officials
original_payload.original_body:
The Lakes State High Elections Committee (SHEC), in collaboration with the National Elections Commission (NEC) and the state government, has trained 34 election officials.
The three-day training, which concluded on Sunday in Rumbek, brought together 16 county constituency returning officers and their assistants appointed by the NEC. It focused on voter registration procedures and preparations for the elections.
Abraham Gop Achien, a facilitator, said the returning officers and their assistants would train 1,890 voter registration centre staff across the state’s eight counties next week.
“Today, we are training 16 returning officers and their assistants, covering the eight counties of Lakes State. Next week, we will train 1,890 voter registration staff at different centres,” he said.
Achien said Lakes State has 270 voter registration centres, each expected to have seven staff members, bringing the total number of personnel to be trained to 1,890.
Daniel Laat Kon, the Community Empowerment for Progress Organization (CEPO) coordinator in Lakes State, urged the officials to uphold impartiality, transparency and professionalism, saying their conduct would influence public confidence in the electoral process.
“For us to have free, fair and credible elections in South Sudan, we must adhere to the principles of impartiality, transparency and professionalism,” he said.
He cautioned the officials against misconduct, saying they must perform their duties in accordance with their training and avoid actions that could undermine the NEC’s credibility.
Professor Kot Kuocnin Kuer, chairperson of the Lakes State High Elections Committee, urged the officials to prepare for their responsibilities, saying supervisors would visit the counties to monitor their work.
Drawing on his experience during the 2010 general elections, Kuer said preparations had been rushed and election officials had faced resistance while carrying out their duties.
“You have to equip yourself here so that everyone knows you are a person who is trained and qualified to do the work,” he said.
He urged the officials to perform their duties transparently and without fear or favour, warning against personal relationships that could compromise their independence or damage the reputation of the state election committee.
Kuer said the officials would also play a role in training personnel recruited to work at voter registration centres, describing their contribution as part of a historic effort to organise South Sudan’s first general elections since it gained independence in 2011.
