items.title: Choléra en RDC: Kinshasa lance une vaste campagne de vaccination en coopération avec le Congo-Brazzaville

original_payload.original_title: Choléra en RDC: Kinshasa lance une vaste campagne de vaccination en coopération avec le Congo-Brazzaville
original_payload.original_body:
Choléra en RDC: Kinshasa lance une vaste campagne de vaccination en coopération avec le Congo-Brazzaville
Depuis mardi 3 novembre, Kinshasa et Brazzaville mènent une vaste campagne de vaccination de part et d'autre du fleuve Congo pour tenter d'enrayer la flambée de l'épidémie de choléra qui touche la RDC. Alors que l'OMS recensait 60 000 cas de la maladie dans le pays à la fin du mois d'octobre, l'objectif est d'immuniser deux millions d'individus dans les prochaines semaines.
Publié le :  09/11/2026 - 05:03
2 min     Temps de lecture
La campagne de vaccination conjointe contre le choléra menée par Kinshasa et Brazzaville vise en premier lieu les populations des îlots dispersés du fleuve Congo.         © Hugh Kinsella Cunningham
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Face à la flambée de l'épidémie de choléra qui touche actuellement la   RDC   - l'Organisation mondiale de la santé (  OMS  ) y recensait 60 000 cas de la maladie à la fin octobre -, une vaste campagne de vaccination se déploie dans le pays. Objectif ? Immuniser deux millions de personnes dans l’ouest du territoire congolais en commençant par les habitants des îlots dispersés du fleuve Congo.
Pour y parvenir, les autorités congolaises misent sur une opération conjointe avec le   Congo-Brazzaville  , coopération que le professeur Didier Bompangué, référent choléra de l’OMS en RDC, juge indispensable. «  Quand on vaccine le long du fleuve, agir sur une seule rive ne suffit pas. Si une vaccination de l'ensemble du corridor fluvial a déjà été réalisée à une petite échelle autour du Mai-Ndombe, dans la zone de Bolobo-Yumbi, il s'agit cette fois-ci d'une première du fait de la portée et de la dimension transfrontalière de l'opération  », explique ce dernier.
Les conditions météo pourraient compliquer la donne
Si, pour atteindre les populations des campements dispersés sur les îlots, les équipes sanitaires comptent sur les pirogues, les petits bateaux motorisés et les relais communautaires locaux, les conditions météorologiques actuelles pourraient cependant compliquer la campagne.
«  On est entré dans la saison des pluies alors qu'on subit déjà les conséquences d’une année El Niño annoncée de longue date avec des pluies torrentielles et l’élévation du niveau des eaux,  reprend Didier Bompangué, qui poursuit :  Dans les campements ciblés, les opérations auraient dû commencer pendant la saison sèche, mais les pluies ont démarré avec beaucoup d'intensité... c’est le défi climatique  ».
Selon l’OMS, la campagne a commencé le 3 novembre dans la province de l'Équateur. Elle doit se poursuivre dans le Mai-Ndombe, mardi 10 novembre, avant Kinshasa le 24, en coordination avec Brazzaville.

items.title: Centrafrique: la guerre au Soudan menace de déstabiliser le nord du pays

original_payload.original_title: Centrafrique: la guerre au Soudan menace de déstabiliser le nord du pays
original_payload.original_body:
Centrafrique: la guerre au Soudan menace de déstabiliser le nord du pays
Trois ans et demi de conflit dévastateur au Soudan voisin risquent de transformer la région de la Vakaga, dans l'extrême nord de la Centrafrique, en un foyer de déstabilisation régionale, affirme le dernier rapport de l'International Crisis Group publié jeudi 29 octobre. Dans cette région minière mais pauvre, enclavée et délaissée, l'afflux de réfugiés, les incursions de combattants et la circulation des armes favorisent la reconstitution des groupes armés centrafricains.
Publié le :  09/11/2026 - 05:04
2 min     Temps de lecture
Un Casque bleu zambien de la Mission des Nations unies en Centrafrique (Minusca) assure la sécurité auprès d'habitants de Birao et de déplacés venus d'autres régions de la Vakaga, à Birao, en Centrafrique, le 12 décembre 2025 (image d'illustration).        AFP - MARIAM KONE
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Alors que la préfecture de la Vakaga, située aux confins du Tchad et du Soudan, avait déjà été le berceau de la rébellion   Seleka   il y a une douzaine d'années en   Centrafrique  , l'International Crisis Group (ICG) affirme que la région est aujourd'hui en passe de redevenir un terreau d'instabilité.
En cause ? La guerre au   Soudan  , qui y a provoqué un afflux de réfugiés - en trois ans, la population de Birao, chef-lieu de la Vakaga, a doublé - et une flambée du banditisme en raison des incursions de combattants liés aux Forces de soutien rapide (FSR).
Une aubaine pour les groupes armés
Phénomènes plus inquiétants encore, le développement du mercenariat, la circulation des armes et les pillages permettent à des groupes armés centrafricains comme le Front populaire pour la renaissance de la Centrafrique (FPRC) de Nourreddine Adam, le Parti du rassemblement de la nation centrafricaine (PRNC) de Nourd Gregaza et le Mouvement démocratique pour le rassemblement du peuple centrafricain (MDRPC) d'Arda Hakouma de s'enrichir et de reconstituer leurs forces.
L'attaque du 30 juin dernier contre la ville d'Am Dafock, qui a fait une trentaine de morts, en est une illustration. «  Le conflit au Soudan est une aubaine pour les groupes armés centrafricains  »,   écrivent les chercheurs d'ICG  .
Le rapport alerte également sur le déploiement de milices progouvernementales dans la zone et sur les risques géopolitiques liés à l'influence croissante des   Émirats arabes unis   dans la région. De multiples sources affirment en effet que ces derniers alimentent le conflit au Soudan.
Cette situation intervient alors que les relations entre Bangui et Ndjamena se dégradent et que les   Nations unies   sont contraintes de réduire leur présence dans la région, faute de budget.

items.title: Ghana: à Accra, les étudiants manifestent contre la hausse des loyers «qui ne cessent d'augmenter»

original_payload.original_title: Ghana: à Accra, les étudiants manifestent contre la hausse des loyers «qui ne cessent d'augmenter»
original_payload.original_body:
Reportage
Ghana: à Accra, les étudiants manifestent contre la hausse des loyers «qui ne cessent d'augmenter»
À l’université du Ghana, des étudiants entament, lundi 9 novembre, deux jours de mobilisation contre la hausse des frais de logement. Après des projets de hausse de près de 20 % selon les chambres, la contestation des loyers a poussé les autorités à intervenir. Les étudiants réclament une baisse des tarifs et de meilleures conditions dans les résidences.
Publié le :  09/11/2026 - 06:16
2 min     Temps de lecture
Écouter - 01:20
Vue de l'université du Ghana à Accra, 2012.        © Wikimedia Commons CC-BY-SA-3.0/Simon Ontoyin
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Avec notre correspondante à Accra,   Welly Diallo
Avec une chambre pour deux, une salle de bain pour quatre et une cuisine pour tout l’étage, Nasiba Abass habite dans l’une des résidences étudiantes du campus. Dans sa chambre, son espace personnel fait moins de deux mètres de large.
L'organisatrice de la manifestation du jour refuse de payer plus cher pour des logements mal entretenus : «  Hier, on a vu des rats s’introduire dans une cuisine… Ils ne cessent d’augmenter les prix de logements. Alors qu'en réalité, ça ne vaut pas ce prix. Le logement est dans le même état qu’à notre arrivée. Nous sommes donc tout simplement abasourdis par ces hausses de frais.  »
En un an, le loyer de Nasiba est passé de 6 000 à plus de 9 000 cedis par an, soit de 450 à près de 700 €. Des prix qui obligent les étudiants les plus précaires à habiter en dehors du campus, quitte à passer plus d’une heure dans les transports en commun.
Joshua Ayivor est l’un des organisateurs de la campagne « Sauvons nos universités » : «  Avec les problèmes de trafic tous les jours, c’est quand même difficile pour les étudiants comme moi de pouvoir se concentrer pour étudier ici sur le campus. C’est ça qui fait que c’est difficile de pouvoir accéder au cours du matin.  »
Le 2 novembre, les nouveaux tarifs ont été suspendus après l’intervention du service ghanéen de contrôle des loyers. Les trop-perçus devront être remboursés et les négociations sont toujours en cours avec l’université.
À lire aussi  Au Ghana, la grève des enseignants se poursuit après l'échec des négociations

items.title: Mali: après deux semaines de grève, les enseignants-chercheurs poursuivent le mouvement de manière illimitée

original_payload.original_title: Mali: après deux semaines de grève, les enseignants-chercheurs poursuivent le mouvement de manière illimitée
original_payload.original_body:
Mali: après deux semaines de grève, les enseignants-chercheurs poursuivent le mouvement de manière illimitée
Au Mali, les enseignants-chercheurs entament leur troisième semaine de grève, ce lundi 9 novembre. Commencé le 26 octobre à l'appel du Syndicat national de l'enseignement supérieur et de la recherche scientifique (Snesup) qui n'a toujours pas obtenu satisfaction de son unique revendication - le versement d'une prime de recherche prévue par la loi depuis près de dix ans mais dont les enseignants-chercheurs n'ont jamais vu la couleur -, le mouvement est cette fois reconduit de manière illimité.
Publié le :  09/11/2026 - 05:04
2 min     Temps de lecture
Le bâtiment qui abrite l’université de Bamako, au Mali.        © DR
Par :
David Baché
Publicité
Le mot d'ordre de grève est renouvelé «  jusqu'à la satisfaction de notre revendication légitime  », martèle le communiqué du Syndicat national de l'enseignement supérieur et de la recherche scientifique (Snesup). En clair : la grève est désormais illimitée.
Si la quasi totalité des universités et grandes écoles du   Mali   sont largement paralysées par le mouvement depuis deux semaines, les autorités de transition n'ont pour autant pas encore ouvert la porte aux négociations.
Interrogé par nos confrères de Joliba TV, Namamoudou Sidiki Keïta, le secrétaire administratif du comité exécutif national du Snesup, rappelle que les enseignants-chercheurs attendent depuis un décret de 2017 - soit presque dix ans - le versement d'une prime dont il n'ont jamais vu la couleur. «  Nous ne faisons que réclamer un droit, parce que c'est un décret présidentiel qui a stipulé que les enseignants chercheurs avaient droit à une prime,  explique ce dernier qui poursuit :  Il faut qu'on nous en donne le montant, quand est ce que on va commencer à la toucher et comment l'État compte régler les arriérés  ».
À lire aussi  Mali: l'enseignement supérieur paralysé par une grève
Dénonçant les pressions exercées sur les grévistes de la part de l'administration, le Snesup appelle au maintien de la mobilisation «  sans céder aux tentations, aux distractions ni aux manoeuvres de diversion  ».
Samedi 7 novembre, une délégation notamment composée de responsables religieux et de communicateurs traditionnels a rencontré le syndicat et proposé son aide pour trouver une solution «  dans un esprit de dialogue et d’apaisement social  » - une démarche appréciée mais qui n'a pas remis en cause l'appel à la grève... Sollicité par RFI, le ministère malien de l'Enseignement supérieur n'a, lui, pas donné suite.
À lire aussi  Plusieurs dizaines de milliers d'orpailleurs expulsés de Guinée pris en charge au Mali

items.title: Niger: quelles conséquences pour les personnes déchues de leur nationalité?

original_payload.original_title: Niger: quelles conséquences pour les personnes déchues de leur nationalité?
original_payload.original_body:
Niger: quelles conséquences pour les personnes déchues de leur nationalité?
Plus d'une vingtaine de personnes ont été déchues de leur nationalité nigériennes ces deux dernières années, sur décret du général Abdourahamane Tiani. Voix critiques des autorités militaires, proches de l'ancien pouvoir renversé, toutes se trouvent actuellement hors du territoire nigérien. Les dernières déchéances remontent au mois de septembre. Elles concernaient cinq personnes, dont l'ancien Premier ministre Ouhoumoudou Mahamadou. Quelles sont les conséquences pour elles ? RFI leur a posé la question.
Publié le :  09/11/2026 - 05:06
2 min     Temps de lecture
Vue aérienne du centre-ville de Niamey. (image d'illustration)        © AFP - (Capture d'écran)
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Les conséquences concrètes sont avant tout administratives, témoignent plusieurs personnes déchues de leur nationalité au   Niger  , à partir du moment où leur passeport nigérien expire. C'est ce qu'explique Mayra Djibrine, présidente de l'Alliance des démocrates du Sahel :
«  Justement, en rapport avec les documents de voyage, je ne pourrai pas renouveler mon passeport nigérien qui va expirer dans quelques mois. Il faut faire aussi toutes les démarches administratives comme renouveler un titre de séjour, renouveler un contrat de travail, voyager. Du coup, j'ai commencé des démarches pour avoir le statut d'apatride et puis, voir ce qui serait le mieux adapté à mon profil.  »
À lire aussi  Niger: ce que cache la déchéance de nationalité de proches de l'ex-président Bazoum
Une mesure révoltante, affirme Mayra Djibrine, qui n'a pas d'autre nationalité et est devenue apatride, comme Hamid Amadou Ngadé, déchu de sa nationalité, il y a deux ans. Ancien responsable de la communication à la présidence sous   Mohamed Bazoum  , Hamid Amadou a obtenu l'asile politique :
«  Au début, je pense qu'ils ont pensé que cela pouvait avoir une influence, que ça allait nous pousser à nous taire. Cela n'a pas du tout été le cas. La nationalité, pour moi, n'est pas liée à un papier ou à un décret. Je pense que c'est quelque chose de plus profond que cela. C'est quelque chose d'émotionnel, de plus sentimental. Ce n'est pas quelque chose de palpable. Ce n'est pas quelque chose de physique. Donc moi, je n'ai pas été personnellement touché . »
L'ONG Human Rights Watch rappelle que le Niger est un État partie à la convention de l'  ONU   sur la réduction des cas d'apatridie, qui interdit de priver des personnes de leur nationalité, lorsque cela les rend apatrides.
À lire aussi  Niger: cinq personnes déchues provisoirement de leur nationalité sur décret d'Abdourahamane Tiani

items.title: African exporters seek Chinese buyers as tariff-free access meets market realities.

original_payload.original_title: African exporters seek Chinese buyers as tariff-free access meets market realities.
original_payload.original_body:
African businesses exhibiting at China’s biggest import fair are seeking buyers and investment, but transport costs, export procedures and the difficulty of securing commercial partners remain obstacles despite Beijing’s expansion of tariff-free access for African goods.
Gemstone traders from Zambia, a Ghanaian chocolate producer and craft sellers from Sudan are among exhibitors at the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), hoping to turn the event into lasting business relationships.
China extended zero tariff treatment to 20 additional African countries from May 1, 2026, adding to an existing arrangement for 33 African least developed countries. The measures cover 53 of the 54 African countries that maintain diplomatic relations with Beijing.
The expansion is intended to encourage African exports to China, but the experiences of exhibitors at the Shanghai fair suggest that lower tariffs alone do not guarantee orders or access to customers.
For South Sudan, the arrangements could offer an opportunity to expand exports beyond its dependence on oil.
Chinese Ambassador to South Sudan Ma Qiang said in September that more South Sudanese products were expected to enter the Chinese market under the zero tariff policy.
“More and more South Sudanese products are expected to enter China’s vast market,” Ma said at a reception in Juba marking China’s National Day.
South Sudan was already among the 33 African least developed countries covered by China’s earlier zero tariff arrangement, before the latest expansion to 20 additional countries. Exporters must still meet rules of origin and other Chinese import requirements.
South Sudan has also called for stronger economic cooperation with China in trade, investment, agriculture and agro-processing. Senior Presidential Adviser Kuol Manyang Juuk said such cooperation could support value addition, create jobs and promote industrial development.
But for businesses already trying to reach Chinese consumers, practical challenges remain.
Teresa Stumbeko, chief executive of Zambian company Colourful Culture, is exhibiting malachite and amethyst sourced from her home country. Attending the expo for a third time, she said Chinese customers showed interest in the stones, but transporting larger quantities to China remained difficult.
“Maybe if the government helped us to transport more goods here, it would be better,” she said.
Stumbeko said she currently brings products by air in her luggage and leaves some stock in China between visits, gradually building up supplies.
Finding customers who understand the value of the products is also essential, she said.
“Perhaps if you find the right buyers who actually know the product and the worth of the product, they will definitely spend money on it,” she said.
Another Zambian exhibitor, businesswoman Grace Njapao, is seeking investors for mining ventures and wider cooperation. She said businesses needed to understand the Chinese market and build the right connections.
Njapao outlined export procedures in Zambia, including registering goods with the geological survey, declaring them to the revenue authority and obtaining an export licence from the Ministry of Mines.
She said four memorandums of understanding she had previously secured did not progress because of the Covid-19 pandemic.
In Ghana, Eric Agbozo, chief executive of Sekoko Enterprise, is seeking to introduce an African chocolate brand to Chinese and international consumers.
His products combine cocoa with ingredients including nuts, seeds, dates, banana, coconut and ginger.
“What we are seeking to do is combine all this into a healthier chocolate for Africa and for the world at large,” he said.
Thomas, an exhibitor from Sudan, is presenting handmade products including wooden carvings, leather goods and crafts made from cow horn. He said some Chinese visitors were interested in the items, but the distance between Africa and Asia made transporting goods difficult.
“Sudan is far away from Asia, so it is really hard to bring goods here,” he said.
A Chinese visitor who gave her name as Zainu said she had tried a product from Namibia and liked it.
“I use it; I feel it’s good. It’s really good,” she said, adding that she would recommend African products to others.
The difficulties of converting exhibition exposure into business are not limited to African companies.
Helen Song, who runs Canadian food business Savour North, said she had not secured new customers or business agreements through previous editions of the expo, despite exhibiting products including sea cucumber, ginseng and oats.
She said Chinese consumers were looking for a combination of quality and affordability.
“People are wishing to find both with a good price and high quality,” she said.
The tariff initiative comes as China faces scrutiny over its growing trade surplus. Its global trade surplus reached a record $1.2 trillion in 2025, highlighting the imbalance between its exports and imports.
The expo, which runs from November 5 to 10, is part of Beijing’s efforts to promote imports and present China as an open market for international businesses.
For African exporters, the challenge is to turn preferential access and exhibition exposure into regular orders, affordable shipping, and reliable commercial partnerships.

items.title: Legal opinion| The readiness of NEC to conduct elections within the time frame of law

original_payload.original_title: Legal opinion| The readiness of NEC to conduct elections within the time frame of law
original_payload.original_body:
Question: Can the National Elections Commission (NEC) conduct the general elections fixed for 22 December 2026 in compliance with the time frames that the National Elections Act, 2012, as amended by the 2023 and 2026 Amendment Acts, requires it to observe?
Answer:  No. In my considered legal opinion, the NEC is not in a position to conduct the 22 December elections in conformity with the time frames in the Act. The register, the nomination windows and the polling station notices on which a lawful election depends have either lapsed or cannot be completed within the Act’s own minimum periods in the 45 days that remain. The Act does give the Commission a narrow power to adapt its timetable, but that power must be used openly, with reasons and with notice to every party. It cannot be used by silence.
Basis of the opinion
The National Elections Act, 2012 (Amendment) Act, 2023, assented to on 25 September 2023 (the 2023 Act). Section numbers below follow its renumbered text.
The National Elections Act, 2012 (Amendment) Act, 2026 (the 2026 Act).
Public statements and media reports from June to early November 2026, used only to establish which steps the NEC has taken.
All periods are counted in calendar days backwards from 22nd of December, 2026. The opinion deals with law and procedure.
1. The legal framework
1.1 The Act binds the Commission that administers it
The NEC derives every power it has from the Act. It must regulate, conduct and supervise elections, maintain the voter register and register candidates (section 15(2)). The Act is drafted in mandatory terms: the NEC “shall” announce, publish, notify and open the register by fixed dates. The Commission may issue regulations only “for proper implementation” of the Act (section 139). Regulations cannot lawfully shorten, waive or replace a period fixed by the Act itself.
1.2 The Act sets standards of credibility, not only dates
The Act must be construed consistently with the principles of credible, open, transparent and impartial administration of elections (section 6(1) and (2)). It requires preparation and conduct of elections to be professional, credible, transparent and open, and obliges the NEC to inform the public about voter registers, polling stations and candidates (section 7). The register publication, inspection, objection and audit provisions (sections 36 to 38) are the mechanism through which those principles reach the voter.
1.3 The 2026 Act: what it changed and what it left
The 2026 Act refers expressly to the December 2026 elections (section 9(1)). It “delinks” the schedule of elections from completion of a permanent constitution and a census, so those are no longer legal preconditions. It shortened a number of periods, including the voter register publication period, register inspection, signature forms and the campaign. It did not touch the final-register rule in section 38, the nomination windows in sections 49, 71 and 72, the polling station notice in section 32(6), or the independent-candidate deadlines in section 57.
As I understand it, the Transitional Period ends in February 2027, so section 9(1) requires polling about 60 days earlier. This should be verified against the current Agreement and Constitution.
2. Findings
a. The election date was properly announced
The NEC announced 22 December 2026 in June 2026. Section 16(1) requires at least six months’ notice, which, on 22 December, means 22 June. On the record, this requirement was met, subject to confirming the exact date and form of publication.
b. The voter register deadlines have been missed
Section 36(e), as amended in 2026, required the register to be published at least three months before polling, which was 22nd of September, 2026. Under the 2023 text, it was 22 June. Section 38(1), which the 2026 Act left in place, requires the final register to be approved and published at least six months before polling, which was 22nd of June, 2026, and forbids further objections once it is published. In early November, the NEC itself said registration had not started, and no register existed. A register that does not exist cannot have been published, inspected (section 37(c)), audited (section 37A), or used for voter transfers (section 35(6) and (7)).
This is the central legal defect. Every later stage of the electoral process, from candidate seconders to polling station lists, depends on a verified register.
c. The nomination windows have closed on the statutory arithmetic
Section 49(2) fixes the seven-day nomination period for President and Governors to start between 90 and 60 days before polling, that is between 2 September and 23 October 2026, with at least 15 days’ public notice. Sections 71(2) and 72(2) fix legislative assembly nominations at 65 to 50 days before polling, that is between 18 October and 2 November. Independent candidates must file their name and symbol 90 days before and their nomination paper 60 days before polling (section 57), that is, by 23 September and 23 October. I found no public notice that any of these windows opened. Absent a lawful adjustment, they cannot be reopened by the NEC simply by announcing new dates.
d. Polling station notice is overdue
Section 32(6) requires the NEC to notify voters of their polling stations at least 60 days before an election, which was 23 October 2026. The 3,161 centres the NEC has identified are registration centres. They are not the polling station notice the Act requires.
e. The remaining period cannot accommodate the Act’s minimum steps
If nominations opened today, the Act’s own sequence would run roughly as follows: a seven-day window to about 13 November, (section 49(1)); publication of the nominee list within 14 days of close, to about 27 November (section 51(1)); challenges within seven days, to about 4th of December (section 52(1)); a Court decision within seven days, to about 11 December (section 52(2)); then publication of the final list (section 53), ballot printing and distribution in about ten days. The 45-day campaign ceiling in section 80(1) could not begin before today. This assumes a completed register and ready regulations, neither of which exists on the record.
f. The 2026 Act is internally inconsistent, and the inconsistencies are litigable
The copy of the 2026 amendment reads as a bill with “New:” text set beside the old text. It is headed “Bill”, the assent clause names a “National Elections Commission Act”, and the date entries in the assent block are irregular. Public reports state that the President signed on 21th of September, 2026. The gazetted, consolidated text must be published and checked.
Section 65(2). The amendment purports to change the Council of States nomination period (45 days under the 2023 Act) but uses the wording of section 49(2) (President and Governors, 90 to 60 days) with new figures of 60 to 30 days. It is unclear which provision was intended, and section 49(2) was not formally amended.
Register rules. Section 36(e) now says three months. Section 38(1) still says six months.
Campaign. Section 80(1) caps campaigns at 45 days. Section 75(3) fixes 30 to 50 days for legislative assemblies.
Signature forms. Section 70(4) now says 15 days. Sections 48(3) and 64(2) still say 30 days.
Diaspora. Section 35(3), as amended, limits out-of-country registration to Presidential elections and referenda. Section 35(4) of the 2023 Act still requires regulations for out-of-country voting generally.
National Legislative Assembly. Section 60(2) fixes 270 members under the 50, 35 and 15 percent formula and adds 66 appointees. The total, and the fate of the earlier provisions on 332 members, must be stated clearly.
Each of these gives a party or candidate an argument that the election was not conducted in compliance with written law (sections 112, 118 and 130).
3. Can the Commission Cure the Position?
3.1. Section 138: possible, but only openly and for real exigencies
Section 138 allows the NEC, where a mistake, miscalculation, emergency, or unusual or unforeseen circumstance means a provision of the Act or other election law cannot be followed, to extend time, add officers or polling stations, or adapt any provision other than the Constitution, to the extent necessary. It must inform all parties and independent candidates of any action taken (section 138(2)).
The power has real limits. It cannot touch the Constitution. It is designed for exceptional circumstances, and the Commission set the 22nd of December date itself, in June, knowing the register and nomination periods the Act prescribes. A party that challenges its use will say the shortfall was foreseeable and within the Commission’s own control, not “unforeseen”. The safest use of section 138 is one published, reasoned timetable that states each provision being adapted and why, not a series of unexplained date changes.
3.2 Section 60: not available for administrative unreadiness
The Commission may postpone Presidential, Gubernatorial and Chief Administrator elections only for proven imminent danger or a declared state of emergency, and must fix a new date within 60 days of the original. Unreadiness is not a listed ground. Any longer deferral would need an amending Act or a constitutional route, and would have to be reconciled with the end of the Transitional Period.
3.3 Legislative correction
The 2026 Act itself proves that the Transitional National Legislative Assembly treats the calendar as amendable. A short amending Act reconciling sections 32, 36, 37, 38, 49, 57, 71, 72, 75 and 80, and correcting section 65(2), is the cleanest way to give a compressed timetable a secure legal footing.
4. Consequences of proceeding without a lawful basis
petitions
Any voter, candidate or aspirant may petition on grounds including the validity of the conduct of the election and non-compliance with the Constitution and written law that substantially affected the result (sections 112 and 124).
Nullification.
An election may be declared void where non-compliance substantially affected the result (sections 118(b) and 130). A new election would then follow (sections 121 and 133).
Speed.
Presidential petitions must be filed within 28 days and decided within 14 days (section 111). Governor and Chief Administrator petitions must be decided within three months, and legislative petitions within 120 days (section 123(5)).
Practical effect.
A defect built into the calendar from the start is a ready-made ground of challenge. It shifts the dispute from the ballot box to the courtroom after results are announced, which is the worst moment for national stability.
5. Fairness to the Commission
The Commission has made real progress. On the public record, it has announced the date, trained State High Election Committee and Administrative Area staff on registration, approved the registration book, identified 3,161 registration centres, passed 14 regulations, and received funding assurances and offers of African Union technical help. It has itself identified resources, security and logistics as continuing challenges. These steps are important. But they are preparatory, and the Act measures readiness by the completed legal steps, not by effort. The register, the nomination process and the polling station and candidate lists are the legally decisive items, and they are outstanding.
6. Conclusion
The National Elections Act is not a set of aspirations. It prescribes, in mandatory language, when the register must be published, when nominations must open and close, when polling stations must be announced, and how long each challenge may take. Those periods exist so that every voter can check the register, every candidate can compete on known terms, and every result can be defended.
Measured against that calendar, my opinion is as follows:
1. The election date was lawfully announced. The NEC has missed the statutory deadlines for publishing the voter register and the final register, and the periods for inspection, audit and voter transfer cannot now run as the Act prescribes.
2. The statutory nomination windows for President, Governors and the legislative assemblies, and the deadlines for independent candidates and polling station notices, have passed on the statutory arithmetic.
3. The 45 days that remain cannot hold the minimum durations the Act itself sets for registration, nomination, challenge, ballot production, and campaign.
4. The 2026 Act did not cure these problems. It left the final-register, nomination, and polling station provisions untouched, and introduced contradictions of its own.
5. Postponement under section 60 is not available for administrative unreadiness. The only lawful routes to a 22nd of December poll are an open and reasoned use of section 138, or a corrective amendment by the Transitional National Legislative Assembly which has already been dissolved on the 22nd of September, 2026.
Accordingly, the NEC is not legally ready to conduct the 22 December 2026 elections within the time frames of the Act as it stands. An election held on that date without a published legal basis for each departure would rest on a foundation that any court could be asked to examine. The better course, and the one most likely to protect the credibility of the outcome, is for the NEC to publish a single gazetted electoral calendar stating which deadlines were met and the legal basis for each adjustment; for the Legislature to correct the inconsistencies in the Act and gazette a consolidated text; and for the Commission to consult all parties, independent candidates and observers before the adjusted timetable takes effect.
The Act asks for elections that are credible, open, transparent and fair. The date matters, but so does the law that gives the date its authority.
The writer is an advocate & commissioner for oaths and secretary of Legal Affairs and Human Rights National Secretariat of the United Sudan African Party (USAP). He can be contacted via  bullenkulang@gmail.com .

items.title: Hamdok’s group warns Egypt against attacking Sudanese gold miners

original_payload.original_title: Hamdok’s group warns Egypt against attacking Sudanese gold miners
original_payload.original_body:
The Sudanese Forces of the Declaration of Principles, a coalition of political and military groups opposed to the ongoing war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), has warned the Egyptian army against repeating attacks on Sudanese miners similar to the Jebel Al-Uqaidat attack in Northern Wadi, which reportedly resulted in the deaths of approximately 200 miners.
Among the group’s prominent members are the coalition led by Dr. Abdalla Hamdok and the Sudan Liberation Movement led by Abdel Wahid Al-Nur.
Mohammed Abdulrahman Al-Nayer, a leader within the Sudanese Forces of the Declaration of Principles, told Radio Tamazuj that they warned the Egyptian army against targeting Sudanese people.
“The Forces of the Declaration of Principles have followed with grave concern the statement by the spokesperson of the Egyptian Armed Forces, which announced the launch of a new fourth military campaign beginning on Saturday 7 November, targeting poor Sudanese people working in gold mines, in coordination with the Sudanese Armed Forces in areas under army control, under the pretext of pursuing looting and infiltration gangs,” he stated.
Al-Nayer described the Sudanese government authorities as weak and submissive when it comes to addressing the concerns of their own people, saying that the blood of the miners was a responsibility that rested on the conscience of the nation.
“Traditional miners are unarmed civilians who have gone out in search of an honest livelihood,” he said. “Describing them as gangs and criminal elements raises serious concerns about the fate of people whose only wrongdoing is facing poverty and war.”
The Forces of the Declaration of Principles also expressed reservations about the Egyptian statement issued on Friday, which said that operations would be carried out on Saturday, November 7, inside Egyptian territory without affecting any civilian targets.
They noted that previous airstrikes, according to reports and testimonies from survivors, had taken place inside Sudanese territory and had been carried out by Egyptian aircraft. They called for an independent and transparent international investigation into the incidents and for the identities of those responsible for crimes against unarmed civilians to be revealed.
The coalition expressed serious concerns that the issue of Sudanese miners could become a pretext for the Egyptian army to expand its presence inside Sudan, at a time when dozens of reports have emerged about the looting of Sudan’s natural resources since the outbreak of the war, particularly gold, through organized Sudanese-Egyptian cartels, while poor Sudanese miners are pursued with bullets and airstrikes.
Al-Nayer stressed that the targeted mining areas are an integral part of Sudanese territory and should not become operational zones for foreign forces under any pretext, whether combating smuggling or securing borders.
He further stated that Egypt was coordinating with authorities that lacked legitimacy, referring to the Port Sudan government. He held the Sudanese Armed Forces responsible for failing to protect Sudan’s borders, as well as for their responsibility to safeguard the country’s sovereignty.
At the end of his statement, he called on all Sudanese civilians, political, youth, and humanitarian forces to stand united in defending the country’s miners and to support efforts to protect Sudanese sovereignty and national dignity.

items.title: W. Equatoria elects new athletics federation leadership

original_payload.original_title: W. Equatoria elects new athletics federation leadership
original_payload.original_body:
The athletics federation in Western Equatoria State has elected a new leadership following the dissolution of the Yambio Local Athletics Association, in a move aimed at strengthening athletics development and creating opportunities for young talents across the state’s ten counties.
The election, held on Thursday, ushered in four new officials who will lead efforts to promote athletics and establish stronger sports structures across the state.
The newly elected officials are President Jackson Gaaniko, Deputy President Mbabazi Desire, Secretary-General Angel Tata and Finance Secretary Malesh Ramadan.
Speaking during the election, Col. Beatrice Safari, Women’s Representative of the National Athletics Federation, announced the dissolution of the Yambio Local Athletics Association and called on the new leadership to establish an inclusive athletics structure representing all ten counties.
“I am urging all of you to cooperate and work together, engaging all the bomas to take the name of Western Equatoria State forward in athletics across South Sudan,” she said.
She also encouraged the federation to prepare athletes for the upcoming Third Republican Athletics Championships in Juba, saying Western Equatoria should have a strong athletics structure by 2027 to identify, develop and motivate talented young people.
Safari further urged the new leadership to demonstrate unity, commitment and good management in building a strong athletics federation.
Meanwhile, Tomoyo David, representing the Western Equatoria State Ministry of Culture, Youth and Sports, congratulated the newly elected officials and commended delegates for participating in the democratic process.
He said the election demonstrated the confidence members had placed in the new leadership, adding that the elected officials now had a responsibility to serve those who entrusted them with the mandate.
He urged the leadership to work closely with athletes, young people and other stakeholders, listen to their concerns and ensure inclusive participation in athletics development across the state.
In his appreciation message following his election, the newly elected President, Jackson Gaaniko, thanked the youth, community representatives and delegates for their support and confidence.
Gaaniko pledged to work with athletes and sports stakeholders without discrimination or favoritism, emphasizing that all ten counties deserve equal attention and representation.
“My priorities will include identifying and nurturing local talent, organizing athletics competitions, strengthening county and state-level structures, and creating opportunities for athletes to represent Western Equatoria at national and international competitions,” he said.
The new president also pledged to establish an inclusive leadership structure involving coaches, technical teams, advisers and other stakeholders to promote teamwork, transparency, accountability and effective management.
He called on government institutions, development partners, sports associations, youth and well-wishers to support the federation, stressing that athletics development requires collective effort.
The four newly elected officials are expected to lead efforts to organize athletics activities, strengthen the federation’s structures, promote sports education and develop local talent across Western Equatoria State.
The election marks a new chapter for athletics in the state, with the new leadership expected to build a united and inclusive federation representing all ten counties.

items.title: Opinion| Arrests and fines won’t clean Juba: Why citizen participation matters

original_payload.original_title: Opinion| Arrests and fines won’t clean Juba: Why citizen participation matters
original_payload.original_body:
Just days after I published an article urging the Juba City Council to move beyond technology and focus on behavioural change, news emerged that 17 residents and shop owners had been arrested in Munuki for violating sanitation regulations. Three of them, including a pregnant woman and two nursing mothers, were released on humanitarian grounds.
The city announced that violators would face immediate arrest and prosecution, while urging block committees to encourage residents and traders to keep their surroundings clean.
These arrests did not surprise me. In fact, they reinforce the concern I raised in my previous article: when a city faces a serious sanitation crisis, the temptation is to enforce the law rather than address the deeper causes of the problem.
Arrests make headlines. Fines generate revenue. But neither answers the most important question: Why do people continue dumping garbage in open spaces, sometimes shortly after a collection truck has passed?
The answer lies not simply in the behaviour of residents, but also in the reliability of waste collection, the accessibility of disposal facilities and the extent to which communities are involved in managing their surroundings.
The problem with punishment
The City Council’s decision to enforce sanitation regulations is not without legal justification. The 2025 anti-waste bylaw grants the municipality authority to penalise illegal dumping, while the JICA-supported project is helping establish a fee-based waste collection system.
The problem is not enforcement itself. It is treating enforcement as the first response rather than the last resort.
Imagine a resident who steps outside at nine in the evening with a bag of garbage. The collection truck has already passed, or perhaps the resident does not know when it is coming. The nearest designated collection point may be two kilometres away.
What options does that resident have?
Leaving the garbage at home may create health and sanitation problems. Dumping it in an open space is unacceptable. Yet if the collection system is unreliable and alternatives are inaccessible, the resident is being asked to comply with rules that the city has not made practical to follow.
This does not excuse illegal dumping. It does, however, raise an important question about fairness and responsibility.
When the system fails to provide a reasonable means of disposing of waste, punishing residents without addressing that failure is unlikely to produce lasting results.
The release of the pregnant woman and two nursing mothers on humanitarian grounds also raises concerns about how enforcement affects vulnerable residents. The city must ensure that its approach is proportionate and that residents have adequate opportunities to comply with sanitation regulations.
More importantly, arrest cannot teach people how to dispose of waste properly. Fear may prevent someone from dumping garbage in the presence of a police officer, but it cannot communicate collection schedules, teach waste separation, or provide a rubbish bin outside a household.
Enforcement can stop visible violations. It cannot, on its own, build the habits and attitudes needed to keep a city clean.
Lessons from Rwanda: Culture before enforcement
Some people may point to Rwanda and argue that Kigali is clean because of strict enforcement, including plastic bag restrictions and heavy fines.
That is only part of the story.
Rwanda’s experience with cleanliness is also closely associated with Umuganda, the monthly community work programme in which citizens participate in activities such as cleaning streets, clearing drainage channels and maintaining public spaces.
The significance of Umuganda goes beyond removing garbage. It creates opportunities for people to work together, take responsibility for their surroundings and strengthen relationships within their communities.
Neighbours become partners in a shared responsibility. Community leaders become organisers of collective action rather than simply messengers between residents and government.
This is an important lesson for Juba.
When cleanliness becomes part of community life, people begin to see it not merely as a government instruction but as a responsibility they share with others.
Juba does not need to copy Rwanda’s laws or penalties. It can learn from the importance of community participation while developing an approach that reflects its own social and cultural realities.
Enforcement has a role, but it becomes more effective when citizens understand the rules, have the means to comply, and recognize the importance of protecting public spaces.
From reporting problems to solving them together
In my previous article, I raised concerns about the plan to distribute mobile phones to community Sheikhs.
I still believe the initiative could be useful. However, its success will depend on how the phones are used.
If their only purpose is to report garbage accumulation to the City Council, the initiative will reinforce an approach in which residents identify problems and wait for government to solve them.
A more effective approach would use these phones to mobilise communities and strengthen communication between residents and sanitation services.
Community groups could use them to announce changes in collection schedules, organise neighbourhood clean-up activities, share information about proper waste disposal and encourage friendly competition between neighbourhoods.
They could also help identify households that may need assistance, including those headed by elderly people, persons with disabilities and newly arrived families.
This would turn the phones into tools for community participation rather than simply instruments for reporting violations.
JICA’s solid waste management project in Juba has established a framework for community-based waste collection, with plans to introduce fixed-time, fixed-location collection and charge households approximately 430 South Sudanese pounds per month.
The success of this system will depend on whether residents understand and trust it.
If households are expected to pay for waste collection, they must know when the truck will arrive, where to leave their garbage, and whom to contact when the service fails.
The municipality must also be prepared to respond to complaints and explain service disruptions.
Mobile phones can help build this trust, but only if the collection system itself is reliable.
Three priorities for a cleaner Juba
I would like to offer three practical recommendations to Mayor Christopher Serafino Wani Swaka and the Juba City Council.
1. Establish a reliable waste collection timetable
The City Council should publish a clear collection timetable for every neighbourhood and demonstrate that it can be followed consistently.
Residents should know the day, time and designated location for waste collection.
The timetable should be displayed in markets, shops, community centres, places of worship and other accessible locations. Community Sheikhs and block committees should help communicate the information to residents.
For at least eight weeks, the city should focus on educating residents, providing guidance and issuing warnings rather than imposing fines for ordinary sanitation violations.
This period would give households a reasonable opportunity to understand and adapt to the system.
After eight weeks, the City Council could begin imposing penalties for persistent violations, provided that reliable collection services and accessible disposal facilities are in place.
The objective should be to make compliance practical before making non-compliance costly.
2. Introduce a monthly community clean-up pilot
The City Council should launch a community clean-up programme in three neighbourhoods.
There is no need to adopt Rwanda’s mandatory Umuganda model. Juba can develop an approach that reflects its own social, cultural and administrative realities.
The proposal is simple: one designated day each month, during which community Sheikhs, block committees, residents and traders work together to clean public spaces and clear drainage channels.
The City Council should provide basic tools, waste collection, and transport support.
The pilot should also assess community participation and whether the cleaned areas remain clean.
The purpose is not simply to remove garbage. It is to demonstrate that collective responsibility can produce visible results.
Once the pilot has demonstrated its effectiveness, the City Council can expand the programme to other neighbourhoods.
3. Reinvest part of sanitation fines in neighbourhood improvements
A portion of the revenue collected from sanitation fines should be reinvested in improving sanitation services in the affected neighbourhoods.
Residents should be able to see the results through the installation of rubbish bins, the clearing of drainage channels, and improved waste collection points.
The municipality should publish simple reports showing how much revenue has been collected and how much has been spent on sanitation improvements.
This would strengthen public confidence in the enforcement system and demonstrate that penalties are intended to improve public services rather than simply generate revenue.
Punishment without visible improvement risks creating resentment. Enforcement linked to better services can encourage cooperation and strengthen public accountability.
A clean Juba requires its people’s participation.
Mayor Christopher Serafino Wani Swaka has demonstrated his commitment to a cleaner Juba. The arrest of 17 residents is one expression of that commitment.
However, the city must now move beyond the immediate appearance of action and focus on the long-term results residents need.
A clean city cannot be built through arrests and fines alone. It requires reliable services, public education, community leadership, and a shared sense of responsibility.
Juba’s real sanitation transformation will begin when a mother knows where to dispose of her household waste, when a community Sheikh can inform residents that the collection truck will arrive in twenty minutes, and when neighbours come together to clean their streets and take pride in the results.
I remain a supporter of the Mayor’s commitment to a cleaner Juba. Precisely because I support that objective, I urge him and the City Council to give greater attention to the systems and community participation that will make it achievable.
Let us put the handcuffs aside long enough to establish a reliable collection timetable. Let us complement fines with community meetings, civic education and visible improvements in sanitation services.
The responsibility for keeping Juba clean must be shared between the City Council, community leaders, businesses and residents.
The writer is a researcher and policy analyst based in Juba. He can be reached via    sebiternest@gmail.com .

It will be achieved when the people of Juba have the means, the knowledge and the motivation to keep their city clean. items.title: Damazin residents fear worsening insecurity amid escalating military operations

original_payload.original_title: Damazin residents fear worsening insecurity amid escalating military operations
original_payload.original_body:
Residents of Damazin, the capital of Sudan’s Blue Nile Region, are increasingly anxious amid rapidly unfolding military and security developments, reports of advances by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and their ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement, under the Tasis alliance, and recent drone strikes on the city.
The developments have raised concerns about the security situation in Damazin and the possibility of fighting spreading to new areas, as residents grapple with uncertainty and conflicting reports about the military situation.
Speaking to Radio Tamazuj, Samer Ali said living conditions and access to essential services had deteriorated significantly, with electricity and water supplies disrupted and grain mills forced to shut down.
“The security situation is unstable, and some residents have fled the city while others remained,” he said. “Some families are torn between leaving Damazin and staying, given the lack of reliable information about what lies ahead.”
“The situation is unstable, and no one knows where events are heading,” Ali added.
However, another resident, Mohamed al-Tayyib, offered a contrasting assessment, describing the city as calm and secure and urging residents to disregard what he called rumours and misinformation.
“I am confident that the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) will regain control of areas it has lost and I would like to reassure residents of Blue Nile and Sudanese citizens more broadly that the situation in Damazin remains under control,” he said.
According to al-Tayyib, markets, schools and government institutions were operating normally, with no reason for residents to be afraid.
Another resident, Fathia al-Toum, however, painted a bleaker picture, describing the security situation as dire.
She said large numbers of residents had left the city, but those able to afford the journey were the ones who had managed to flee, leaving low-income families behind.
“May God see us through,” she said.
The growing anxiety comes amid continued military confrontations across several localities in Blue Nile Region, particularly Kurmuk, Geissan and Wad al-Mahi, alongside battlefield developments in Sali, Bakouri and, more recently, the Magja area of Bau locality.
Reports of military movements towards other areas have added to the uncertainty. Recent drone strikes on residential neighborhoods in Damazin, which caused deaths and injuries, have further heightened fears of an expanding conflict and growing risks to civilians.
Damage to the city’s electricity substation and the resulting power outages have compounded concerns about the impact of military operations on civilian areas.
In response to mounting public anxiety, the Blue Nile Regional Government issued a statement urging residents not to be swayed by rumors or information from unidentified sources.
The government said it was closely monitoring military and security developments in coordination with the relevant authorities.
Nevertheless, the official reassurances have raised questions about the availability of credible information, the extent to which residents are being kept informed of battlefield developments, and the measures being taken to protect civilians and maintain stability in the city.
Civil society activist Ayman Abdallah told this publication that residents were living in a state of apprehension, fearing that the fighting could reach Damazin.
He called on the relevant authorities to provide the public with accurate, reliable information about the security situation across the region and to take adequate measures to protect civilians.
Abdallah also stressed the need to enable residents to prepare for potential developments, including further waves of displacement.
Caught between intensifying military operations and official assurances, Damazin residents remain uncertain about the region’s security outlook, amid growing calls for reliable information, stronger civilian protection measures and efforts to prevent the population from being exposed to the dangers of armed conflict.
The concerns follow escalating military operations in Sali, north of Kurmuk, and Bakouri in Geissan locality, as well as developments in Wad al-Mahi and other parts of Blue Nile Region.

items.title: Moundou : la revue annuelle du PAI 2026 s’achève sur une série de recommandations

original_payload.original_title: Moundou : la revue annuelle du PAI 2026 s’achève sur une série de recommandations
original_payload.original_body:
L’atelier consacré à la revue annuelle du Programme annuel d’investissement (PAI) 2026 de la province du Logone Occidental a pris fin ce samedi 7 novembre 2026, dans la salle de réunion du Conseil provincial à Moundou. La cérémonie officielle de clôture a été présidée par la première secrétaire de séance du Conseil provincial, Denenodj Silla, représentant le président de l’institution, en présence des autorités administratives, des conseillers provinciaux, des responsables des services déconcentrés de l’État et des partenaires techniques et financiers.
Durant quatre jours, du 4 au 7 novembre, les participants ont évalué le niveau de mise en œuvre des activités inscrites dans le PAI 2026, examiné les résultats obtenus et identifié les difficultés rencontrées dans l’exécution des investissements.
Les échanges ont également porté sur les mécanismes de planification, la mobilisation des ressources, la coordination des interventions et le suivi des actions de développement dans la province.
Lire aussi :  Mise en œuvre du PND : les partenaires saluent les avancées enregistrées par le Tchad
Dans son discours de clôture, Denenodj Silla a remercié l’ensemble des participants pour leur mobilisation et leur contribution aux travaux. Elle a souligné que la pertinence des analyses et la qualité des recommandations témoignent de l’engagement collectif des différents acteurs en faveur du développement harmonieux et durable du Logone Occidental.
Selon elle, cet atelier a constitué un cadre privilégié de concertation, de dialogue et de transparence pour apprécier les résultats du programme, identifier les difficultés et dégager des pistes d’amélioration.
Elle a rappelé que la réussite des politiques publiques repose notamment sur une meilleure coordination entre les acteurs, l’implication effective des communautés bénéficiaires, la transparence dans la gestion des ressources et le suivi rigoureux des engagements.
Lire aussi :  Un comité sera mis en place pour la mise en œuvre des projets du PND ‘’TchadConnexion2030’’
La représentante du président du Conseil provincial a également insisté sur l’importance des recommandations issues de cette revue annuelle, appelées à constituer une feuille de route pour améliorer la programmation, l’exécution et le suivi des investissements au profit des populations.
Rappelant le rôle du PAI dans la mise en œuvre des priorités définies dans le Plan de développement provincial 2022-2026, elle a toutefois souligné que le véritable défi demeure la réalisation effective des investissements et leur impact réel sur les conditions de vie des populations.
Au terme des travaux, plusieurs recommandations ont été formulées à l’endroit du gouvernement, des autorités provinciales, du Conseil provincial et des partenaires techniques et financiers.
À l’endroit du gouvernement et du ministère des Finances, les participants recommandent de renforcer la mobilisation des ressources financières pour garantir l’exécution effective des activités programmées. Ils préconisent également une meilleure coordination entre les autorités provinciales, les services techniques déconcentrés, les collectivités autonomes et les partenaires au développement.
La transparence, la traçabilité et la redevabilité dans la gestion des ressources financières et matérielles figurent également parmi les priorités. Les participants demandent en outre l’intégration des dimensions liées au genre, à l’inclusion sociale, à la protection et à la résilience climatique dans la planification des investissements.
Ils insistent aussi sur le transfert dans les délais des ressources financières destinées aux collectivités territoriales autonomes, ainsi que sur une implication accrue des autorités dans la prévention et la résolution des conflits pour consolider la cohésion sociale.
Concernant le Conseil provincial, les recommandations portent notamment sur l’adéquation entre les activités planifiées, les ressources disponibles et les capacités opérationnelles des structures chargées de leur exécution.
Les participants préconisent l’institutionnalisation des revues trimestrielles du PAI afin d’assurer un suivi régulier des réalisations et l’adoption de mesures correctives en cas de difficultés.
Ils recommandent également une implication plus active des femmes, des jeunes et des personnes vulnérables dans l’identification des besoins et le suivi des investissements. L’harmonisation des outils de collecte et de suivi des indicateurs de performance ainsi que la mise en place d’un mécanisme de suivi-évaluation des recommandations figurent également parmi les mesures retenues.
Les partenaires techniques et financiers sont, pour leur part, appelés à renforcer les capacités techniques et institutionnelles des comités CPA et CDA en matière de planification, de gestion financière, de suivi et d’évaluation.
Ils sont également invités à respecter les engagements pris lors de l’élaboration du PAI et à assurer une remontée régulière des informations sur l’état d’avancement des activités et les difficultés rencontrées.
À travers ces recommandations, les participants entendent renforcer la gouvernance locale, améliorer la coordination des interventions et garantir une meilleure efficacité des investissements publics dans la province.

original_payload.original_title: Aboubakar Assidick Tchoroma nommé secrétaire exécutif par intérim de la CEN-SAD
original_payload.original_body:
Aboubakar Assidick Tchoroma a été nommé secrétaire exécutif par intérim de la Communauté des États sahélo-sahariens (CEN-SAD). La décision a été prise ce 9 novembre par Mahamat Idriss Deby Itno, président de la République du Tchad et président en exercice de la Conférence des chefs d’État et de gouvernement de l’institution.
Cet intérim prendra fin à la date d’installation du nouveau secrétaire exécutif qui sera élu lors de la 13e session ordinaire de la Conférence des chefs d’État et de gouvernement de la CEN-SAD.
Le Tchadien Aboubakar Assidick Tchoroma prend ses fonctions au siège statutaire de l’organisation, situé à Tripoli, en Libye. Au Tchad, il avait été nommé conseiller diplomatique à la présidence de la République le 29 septembre précédent, après avoir occupé le portefeuille de l’Éducation nationale.
Lire aussi :  CEN-SAD : les ministres donnent leur accord au retour du secrétariat à Tripoli, décision finale attendue à N’Djamena
Cette nomination intervient à la suite de la tenue en Libye de la 22e session ordinaire du Conseil exécutif de la CEN-SAD. Selon un compte rendu de la diplomatie tchadienne, elle s’est achevée sur une  »note de satisfaction » et d’ »unanimité » autour d’un objectif majeur : la relance de l’organisation.
Lire aussi :  CEN-SAD : la Libye prépare le retour du secrétariat de l’organisation à Tripoli
Lors de cette rencontre, il a notamment été recommandé le retour du siège de l’organisation à Tripoli et la nomination d’un secrétaire exécutif provisoire pour une période de transition. C’est donc fait.

items.title: FNE 2026 : N'Djamena accueille ses premières délégations étrangères

original_payload.original_title: FNE 2026 : N'Djamena accueille ses premières délégations étrangères
original_payload.original_body:
Tchad
FNE 2026 : N'Djamena accueille ses premières délégations étrangères
N'Djaména s'apprête à abriter la 2e édition du FNE et le Séminaire régional des SPE. Les premières délégations africaines sont arrivées ce dimanche en vue de l'ouverture officielle prévue mardi.
Alwihda Info
09 nov. 2026
© DR
Par Ahmad Youssouf Ali
Le président du comité d'organisation du Forum national sur l'emploi (FNE), Bichara Doudoua, accompagné de son adjoint et directeur général de l'ONAPE, Nassouradine Abakar Kessou, a accueilli ce dimanche 8 novembre 2026 dans la soirée les premières délégations étrangères. Celles-ci participent à la 2e édition du FNE ainsi qu'au séminaire régional des Directeurs généraux des services publics de l'emploi (SPE), organisé en marge de l'événement.
Provenant du Mali, du Niger, du Cameroun, de la République centrafricaine (RCA), de la Guinée, de la Côte d'Ivoire, du Burkina Faso, du Bénin et du Sénégal, ces délégations marquent le lancement de ce rendez-vous majeur dédié à la coopération africaine en matière d'emploi.
Parmi les personnalités de premier plan figure Ibrahim An Noc, président de l'Association africaine des services d'emploi publics (AASEP) et directeur général de l'ANPE du Mali. Sa présence souligne l'importance accordée par les instances régionales à cette édition.
D'autres arrivées sont programmées ce lundi 9 novembre 2026, à la veille de l'ouverture officielle. Pour rappel, les travaux s'ouvriront le mardi 10 novembre 2026 à l'hôtel Radisson Blu de N'Djaména, sous le haut patronage du chef de l'État.

original_payload.original_body:
Tchad
Tchad : au Mandoul, les communautés mobilisées pour l'éducation et la protection des enfants
Le projet ALAPAJ, porté par ACRA et ses partenaires, lance une vaste campagne de sensibilisation dans six localités pour promouvoir l'éducation des enfants et la protection des filles.
Alwihda Info
09 nov. 2026
Par Dominique Didéo
Dans le cadre de la mise en œuvre de la composante 2 du projet ALAPAJ, l'organisation ACRA et ses partenaires déploient une vaste campagne de sensibilisation de masse dans six localités : Goré Nord, Beboni, Bembaïtada, Bekondjo, Komé Ndolébé et Bengamia.
Placée sous le thème « Investir dans l’éducation des enfants et la protection des filles, c’est investir dans l’avenir de la Nation », cette initiative vise à mobiliser les populations autour des enjeux cruciaux de la scolarisation et des droits des jeunes filles.
À travers cette démarche, les organisateurs cherchent à éveiller les consciences et à stimuler l'engagement des parents, des leaders communautaires, des autorités locales et de l'ensemble des acteurs sociaux. L'objectif est de bâtir un environnement protecteur et propice à l'épanouissement de chaque enfant.
Cette mobilisation de terrain constitue une étape déterminante pour favoriser l'accès à l'éducation, lutter contre les pratiques néfastes visant les filles et bâtir une société plus inclusive et équitable.

items.title: Beyond the Lab: How Constraint-Driven Innovation Reshapes Global Healthcare and Technology

original_payload.original_title: Beyond the Lab: How Constraint-Driven Innovation Reshapes Global Healthcare and Technology
original_payload.original_body:
English News
Beyond the Lab: How Constraint-Driven Innovation Reshapes Global Healthcare and Technology
Discover how constraint-driven medical breakthroughs, such as ultrasound-guided cardiac procedures and mobile surgical units, are bridging the gap between high-tech advancements and global accessibility.
Alwihda Info
09 nov. 2026
An agricultural technician operates an autonomous combine harvester to harvest rice using BeiDou positioning and 5G technology in Liangping district, southwest China's Chongqing municipality, on Sept. 7, 2026. (Photo/Liu Hui)
Par Meng Fanzhe, People's Daily
Can serious illnesses be treated with minimally invasive procedures? Traditional cardiac interventions often rely on X-ray guidance and iodine-based contrast agents, which can pose significant risks to pregnant women and patients with compromised kidney function.
Addressing this clinical limitation, researchers in China have developed an ultrasound-guided percutaneous cardiac procedure. By navigating instruments through the skin using real-time ultrasound imaging, surgeons can perform complex heart treatments without open-chest surgery, radiation exposure, or contrast dyes.
Such advancements not only minimize physical trauma and accelerate patient recovery but also underscore a broader principle: persistent medical challenges frequently serve as catalysts for scientific breakthroughs.
This pattern of constraint-driven innovation extends well beyond healthcare. In densely populated urban areas, engineers have designed vertical-shaft tunnel-boring machines that excavate downward to create underground parking spaces, significantly reducing surface disruption.
Similarly, while seawater holds vast potential for clean hydrogen generation via electrolysis, dissolved salts and impurities typically degrade equipment. By integrating physical separation with electrochemical processes, scientists have engineered a selective membrane that filters out contaminants, enabling direct hydrogen extraction from seawater without prior desalination.
Tackling these multifaceted problems demands interdisciplinary collaboration. By moving beyond established approaches, questioning conventional assumptions, and drawing on knowledge from different disciplines, researchers can open up new paths to innovation.
Translating laboratory breakthroughs into widespread public benefit, however, requires deliberate efforts to ensure accessibility. To expand access to the ultrasound-guided cardiac procedure, developers have integrated the necessary equipment into mobile surgical units. These fully equipped vehicles allow medical teams to deploy advanced care directly to remote communities.
Likewise, precision agriculture in China has been transformed by equipping farm machinery with the BeiDou Navigation Satellite System. Coupled with government subsidies and on-site technical training, this integration ensures that cutting-edge positioning tools are not merely technologically advanced, but practically usable for farmers nationwide.
The gap between a functional prototype and a widely adopted solution is often bridged by cost, training, and service infrastructure. Yet high performance and broad accessibility need not be trade-offs. Designing technologies for usability and equitable distribution is, in itself, a critical form of innovation. When development strategies explicitly incorporate deployment logistics and support, emerging technologies can realize their full societal impact.
Currently, the percutaneous and non-fluoroscopic procedure is used in nearly 2,000 medical institutions across 72 countries, including the UK, France, and Kenya, and has helped treat more than 200,000 patients.
Recognizing its global value, the United Nations has initiated training programs to expand medical expertise and patient access. Addressing a shared global health need, this innovation is strengthening medical capabilities while giving other countries more treatment options, representing a concrete contribution to global health cooperation.
Advanced technologies can benefit people across national borders. In Rwanda, local technicians who learn to grow mushrooms using Juncao grass go on to share their knowledge with women's cooperatives and youth groups.
China's Fengyun meteorological satellites also provide early warnings and disaster prevention services to countries and regions around the world, including developing nations.
Protecting lives, preventing disasters, and alleviating poverty are shared aspirations of people around the world. By sharing data, technical standards, and training talent, international cooperation extends beyond technology transfer to helping countries build local capacity, giving innovations greater global significance.
The idea of treating serious illnesses with less invasive methods reminds us that technological progress should start with human needs. Innovation can better serve humanity when it dares to explore new approaches, works patiently to lower barriers to access, and seeks to benefit others.
Looking ahead, turning strengths in independent innovation into drivers of development and improvements in people's lives will continue to strengthen the foundations of modernization and create more opportunities for the world.
original_payload.original_summary: Discover how constraint-driven medical breakthroughs, such as ultrasound-guided cardiac procedures and mobile surgical units, are bridging the gap between high-tech advancements and global accessibility.
original_payload.author: Alwihda Info

items.title: Ousted PM Sheikh Hasina seeks passport in sign of Bangladesh return plan

original_payload.original_title: Ousted PM Sheikh Hasina seeks passport in sign of Bangladesh return plan
original_payload.original_body:
Bangladesh’s ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has requested a new passport and identity card to allow her to return from self-imposed exile in India.
The request is the clearest sign that Hasina, who has been living in India for two years, plans to make good on her promise that she would return to Bangladesh in December.
Recommended Stories

list 2 of 3  Ten killed in fire at beach resort in Bangladesh
list 3 of 3  ‘Going hungry’: Garment workers in Bangladesh say wages barely cover needs

Hasina told the news agency Reuters that she intended to surrender before a court in Bangladesh, and her aides said on Monday the date would be announced once various formalities were completed.
Bangladesh’s war crimes court sentenced Hasina to death in absentia last November for ordering a deadly crackdown on student protests that  swept the country in 2024 . As many as 1,400 people may have been killed in those protests, according to United Nations estimates.
Hasina’s letter to the Bangladeshi government, cited by Reuters, asked that her request be processed “expeditiously” on the basis of her Bangladeshi nationality.
original_payload.original_summary: Hasina, who has been living in India for two years, has promised that she would return to Bangladesh in December.

items.title: Who are the seafarers caught in the US-Israeli war on Iran?

original_payload.original_title: Who are the seafarers caught in the US-Israeli war on Iran?
original_payload.original_body:
Commercial vessels moving through the Strait of Hormuz and its surrounding waters have come under repeated attack since the United States and Israel launched their war on Iran nine months ago.
The conflict has transformed one of the world’s busiest shipping corridors into a dangerous passage for crews transporting oil, gas and other goods.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  Iran says US reply to Hormuz plan ‘unconvincing’; Trump confirms strikes
list 2 of 3  Iran says tankers struck in Hormuz amid fears of new US attack
list 3 of 3  Why is Iran exempting India, China, Qatar, Iraq from Hormuz restrictions?
end of list
On Sunday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said three “rogue oil tankers travelling an unauthorised route” in the strait were subject to “explosions and severe fires”.
The International Maritime Organization (IMO) has recorded the deaths of at least 25 seafarers since the war started on February 28. Many of those killed have been citizens of India, one of the world’s largest suppliers of merchant sailors.
“It is unacceptable that throughout this conflict seafarers have been placed in harm’s way,” the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), a shipping trade association and advocacy group, told Al Jazeera.
“It is incumbent on all parties to take all necessary steps to safeguard the safety of seafarers who are simply going about their job and have found themselves, through no fault of their own, in a highly volatile situation,” an ICS spokesperson added.
The latest incidents have raised questions about the safety of civilian crews, their ability to refuse dangerous assignments and the protections available under international law.
What is happening to ships in the Strait of Hormuz?
The Strait of Hormuz is a crucial passage for international shipping, Before the war, roughly one-fifth of global oil consumption passed through the waterway, which connects the Gulf to the Arabian Sea.

items.title: What is next for Israel?

original_payload.original_title: What is next for Israel?
original_payload.original_body:
There are two ways to read the results of the Israeli elections. One way would be to see them as a defeat for the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. From holding a solid majority in the 120-member Knesset, the Netanyahu bloc has been reduced to a minority of 53 members. Anti-Netanyahu lawmakers, by contrast, hold 67 seats.
Had Israel been a democracy, we would have seen scenes of celebration similar to the ones we saw this year in Hungary, Brazil and Serbia, where political forces with undemocratic tendencies were defeated. But Israel is not a democracy, and Netanyahu was not necessarily defeated.
original_payload.original_summary: The message of the vote is that the violent Israeli policies within occupied territory and the region will continue.
original_payload.author: Ilan Pappe

items.title: Smog blankets New Delhi as Diwali firecrackers worsen air quality

original_payload.original_title: Smog blankets New Delhi as Diwali firecrackers worsen air quality
original_payload.original_body:
Heavy smog has blanketed New Delhi after firecrackers lit up the Indian capital during  Diwali celebrations , worsening the seasonal pollution crisis.
Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, was celebrated across India on Sunday. Despite restrictions on fireworks, New Delhi residents celebrated the festival of lights with firecrackers throughout Sunday evening, releasing smoke and fine particulate matter into the atmosphere.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  Rent-a-grandchild: Businesses offering companions to elderly grow in India
list 2 of 3  UK jailing of Indian sailor over Russia sanctions sets off ‘perfect storm’
list 3 of 3  India beat New Zealand by four runs via DLS in rain-hit second ODI
end of list
On Monday morning, the Air Quality Index exceeded 350 in several parts of the capital, categorised as “severe” and posing significant health risks, according to the World Health Organization’s (WHO) recommended exposure thresholds.
Last month, India’s Supreme Court put in place restrictions to limit Diwali pollution, allowing only approved “green firecrackers” under specified conditions for three-hour windows on Saturday and Sunday. The approved crackers produce fewer emissions but are not pollution-free.
Girls hold lit sparklers during Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, in New Delhi, India, on November 8, 2026 [Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters]   Seasonal pollution
On Wednesday, days before Diwali, toxic air pollution in New Delhi surged to more than 30 times the WHO’s recommended daily limit, data from air monitors showed.
New Delhi, home to 30 million people, persistently ranks among the world’s most polluted capital cities.
The issue is exacerbated during the winter, when cooler temperatures, low wind speeds and stagnant atmospheric conditions prevent pollutants from dispersing.
