items.title: UK and UNU-WIDER sign MoU to support Mozambique’s efforts to mobilise and access climate finance

original_payload.original_title: UK and UNU-WIDER sign MoU to support Mozambique’s efforts to mobilise and access climate finance
original_payload.original_body:
Photo: X/ @UKinMozambique The British High Commission in Maputo and the United Nations University World Institute for Development Economics Research (UNU-WIDER) have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) in Maputo. It provides USD 1.63 million (about £1.2 million) to FORÇA – Strengthening Capacity to Access Climate Finance (Fortalecimento da Capacidade para Aceder ao Financiamento Climático). FORÇA is a two-year programme that will support Mozambique’s efforts to mobilise, access climate finance and manage it well.
FORÇA will be led by the Government of Mozambique and implemented in partnership with the Ministry of Planning and Development. It will support the ministry’s National Directorate for Climate Finance, which leads the Government’s work on climate finance. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) is funding the programme. UNU-WIDER will serve as the fund manager and implementation partner, providing financial and operational oversight, technical expertise, and quality assurance, while working closely with the National Directorate for Climate Finance to strengthen institutional capacity and progressively embed new skills and systems within the Directorate.
Mozambique is one of the countries most at risk from climate change. Cyclones, floods and droughts cost the country several percentage points of its gross domestic product (GDP) each year. Mozambique also has strong solar, wind and water resources and could attract green investment. To make the most of these opportunities, national institutions need the skills, data and systems to find climate finance, coordinate it and use it well.
As Mozambique seeks to access increasing volumes of climate finance to support its development and climate objectives, the programme will help strengthen the institutional systems, technical expertise, and evidence needed to identify financing opportunities, coordinate stakeholders, and improve climate finance planning and implementation.
Evidence and data are integral to this institutional strengthening. By strengthening climate finance data systems, analytical capacity, and knowledge production, FORÇA will support better-informed climate finance decision-making and investment planning.
The programme will also promote collaboration between government institutions, researchers, development partners, the private sector, and other stakeholders to support a more coordinated and strategic approach to climate finance in Mozambique. Drawing on its research and policy expertise and its long-standing partnerships in Mozambique, UNU-WIDER will support DNFC in connecting evidence and analysis with policy and investment planning, while facilitating knowledge exchange and bringing relevant national and international expertise into the programme.

items.title: COP31 summit leaders urge world to move faster on climate

original_payload.original_title: COP31 summit leaders urge world to move faster on climate
original_payload.original_body:
] President of COP31 Murat Kurum of Turkey delivers a speech during the opening ceremony of the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, November 9, 2026. [Photo: Reuters/Murad Sezer] Leaders of the COP31 climate summit urged the world to accelerate the fight against global warming amid rising temperatures and worsening climate-driven disasters, as the annual meeting began in Turkey on Monday.
The comments at the start of the two-week UN conference were an appeal to governments to focus on climate, even as other international crises from war to soaring inflation and the uncertainty of artificial intelligence compete for their attention.
“The urgency of this moment must drive us forward,” UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell said at the opening of the event on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast, adding that progress so far was “nowhere near fast enough.”
A report by the United Nations Environment Programme published in October said the world was already poised to overshoot 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming above pre-industrial times, the threshold set at the 2015 Paris climate summit to avoid the worst consequences of warming.
This year is on track to be one of the four hottest on record, driven by a powerful El Nino, a UN report showed on Monday.
It has also stood out with a series of extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a catastrophic flood killing more than 1,450 people, with thousands still missing.
Turkey’s COP31 presidency has focused this year’s summit on a goal to electrify more than a third of the global economy by 2035, up from around a fifth today. It is asking nations to sign onto a pledge supporting that target.
Theoretically, such a goal could help reduce planet-warming emissions by speeding the global shift away from fossil fuel-powered vehicles, furnaces, boilers, cooking stoves, and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment.
“We want people to feel the results of climate talks in daily life: in buildings that use less energy, in clean public transport, in energy they can afford and in new jobs,” Turkey’s COP31 President Murat Kurum said.
But climate advocates have criticised the pledge because it does not require the additional electricity to come from low-carbon sources, setting up an early fight over whether electrification alone should count as climate progress.
Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan said he hoped Turkey could deliver concrete results.
“Our goal is to make this summit a platform where concrete results are produced, where countries turn their pledges into action, because it is no longer time to make promises that remain on paper,” Erdogan told reporters on a return flight from Azerbaijan, according to a transcript of his comments shared by his office on Monday.
War and tech
The Iran war has underscored the world’s attachment to fossil fuels, as has Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, though some say the wars have also shown the benefits of moving to renewables.
Now in its ninth month, the Iran war has severely disrupted Middle East oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, lifting fuel prices around the globe and prompting a scramble for new supplies.
US President Donald Trump’s administration — which is shunning climate talks for the second year running — has encouraged policies maximising oil, gas, and coal production to address the disruptions.
South Korea, India, Thailand and other Asian nations, meanwhile, have also increased their reliance on coal or taken steps to boost coal-fired power generation.
“A lot of people who previously might have been embarrassed to argue for continuing very high use of fossil fuel are now feeling empowered to make that case,” said John Holdren of Harvard University, who was a science adviser to Barack Obama when he was US president.
At the same time, the deployment of renewable energy has also risen, driven by surging exports of cheap clean tech from China.
Stiell told the summit renewables were the clear answer to improving energy security.
“This year’s fossil fuel cost chaos has delivered a global shockwave, hitting households hard and spreading inflation like a cancer,” he said.
“But the solutions are clear,” he added, saying renewable energy installations had already saved the global economy hundreds of billions of dollars.
The rapid rollout of AI is also complicating talks, driving a surge in global power demand and contributing to rising greenhouse gas emissions.
Turkey will call on governments, businesses and other institutions at COP31 to sign a pledge outlining principles to ensure AI is developed and deployed sustainably.
Chris Bowen, Australia’s president of COP31 negotiations, said he hoped the conference would show the world that multilateralism works.
“Let’s show future generations that this generation was equal to the moment, equal to the challenge,” he said.
Source:  Reuters

items.title: Trump to meet Iran war mediator Qatar, no imminent deal seen to end the war

original_payload.original_title: Trump to meet Iran war mediator Qatar, no imminent deal seen to end the war
original_payload.original_body:
FILE – A billboard with an image of Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on a street in Tehran, Iran, October 26, 2026. Majid Asgaripour/WANA [File photo: West Asia News Agency via Reuters]
Qatar’s Sheikh Mohammed will meet Trump and Vance in Washington after Tehran visit last week
Rubio says diplomatic breakthrough is not imminent and rejects Iran’s truce terms as unrealistic
Iran plan pushes nuclear talks back to later stage
US ​President Donald Trump will meet the prime minister of key mediator Qatar on Monday as efforts to end the Iran war ramp up following last week’s ‌midterm elections, though senior US and Gulf officials cast doubt on the chances of an imminent deal.
More than eight months into the conflict he launched alongside Israel on February 28, Trump has played down the likelihood of major warfare restarting soon but remains unwilling to accept an existing Iranian truce plan.
Mutual attacks continue, with the US striking Iran’s Qeshm island overnight, according to Iranian state media, and Iran attacking tankers in the Gulf and ​Strait of Hormuz this month while its Yemeni Houthi allies have hit Saudi Arabia.
Diplomatic moves
Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, who is both prime minister and foreign minister of ​Qatar, will meet Trump and Vice President JD Vance in Washington later on Monday after having visited Tehran last week.
Iran’s proposal to end ⁠the war involves an end to the US blockade of its ports, the lifting of some sanctions and a halt to bombing in return for Tehran stopping its own blockade ​of the Strait of Hormuz, with talks on its nuclear programme and other sanctions to follow.
The US has repeatedly rejected that plan, which Iran has said could be condensed to a ​two-day timeframe, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio describing Tehran’s conditions on Sunday as “outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic”.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei defended the plan on Monday as the most reasonable offer on the table.
Senior US Republicans including Vance have blamed their party’s losses in last week’s elections on the Iran war, but despite growing domestic political pressure to end the conflict, Rubio said he did not believe ​a diplomatic breakthrough was imminent.
A senior United Arab Emirates official, Anwar Gargash, echoed that view on Monday, saying a comprehensive political settlement between the US and Iran appeared difficult.
“We should… ​prepare for a long period of uncertainty in which neither a decisive resolution nor stable regional order can be taken for granted,” he said.
Vance, who led the negotiations for a short-lived truce in June, ‌will also ⁠meet Al-Thani, whose country has been a prime mediator since early in the war, conveying messages between the sides and proposing ways to bridge their differences.
Anxiety over the war has pervaded the region for months and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan said on Monday he had told Trump that Ankara did not want to see a new escalation.
“We emphasise at every opportunity that it is possible to resolve these issues through dialogue and diplomacy. Unfortunately, we see a negative shift once again. We are doing our utmost to prevent this,” Erdogan told reporters.
Military action
Sunday ​night’s strikes on Qeshm island did not impact ​vital infrastructure or services, a provincial ⁠official told Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency on Monday. The US has not commented on the Iranian media reports.
A senior Iranian source told Reuters that US strikes were targeting Iranian radar systems serving both air defence and ship navigation, as well as bases for missile launchers ​and mine-laying systems.
Attacks on tankers in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz ramped up sharply in October and have continued at the ​highest rate since the ⁠start of the war, figures from international maritime agencies showed last week.
Iran, which typically does not acknowledge striking vessels that report being hit by projectiles, said on Sunday a tanker had hit a mine east of the Strait of Hormuz.
A state television reporter said on Monday that 11 tankers had been “disabled” over the past 10 days.
The war has triggered a global energy shortage, prompted Iranian ⁠strikes on Gulf ​Arab countries, spilled over into a major Israeli offensive in Lebanon during the spring and summer and reignited ​Yemen’s long-frozen civil war.
On Sunday Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthi group said it had struck an office building of Saudi state oil company Aramco in Riyadh. The attack blew out windows across several floors of a building in the city’s financial district. The ​Energy Ministry acknowledged damage from an attempted attack on the building without assigning responsibility.
Source:  Reuters

items.title: Nine foreigners caught allegedly trying to leave South Africa to fight in Ukraine

original_payload.original_title: Nine foreigners caught allegedly trying to leave South Africa to fight in Ukraine
original_payload.original_body:
FIle photo: X/ @SAPoliceService Nine foreigners have been arrested in South Africa after they were caught allegedly trying to leave the country to fight in the war between Russia and the Ukraine, police say.
The group, aged between 20 and 26, were arrested in and around Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team on Sunday evening.
They were caught as they were “preparing to board flights out of the country”, authorities added, but their final destination is unclear.
The group is accused of contravening South Africa’s laws, which outlaw mercenary activity without government permission.
Police said the group were arrested at South Africa’s biggest airport, OR Tambo, and a hotel in Bruma, east of Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team that involved Interpol.
The police statement added that the involvement of Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies indicated that the suspects had also allegedly violated laws in their respective home countries, prompting cooperation with South African authorities.
Authorities declined to disclose the group’s nationalities but confirmed that none of them resided in South Africa.
They have also not said whether the group allegedly intended to fight for Russia or Ukraine nor provided details of the organisations allegedly involved in facilitating their travel.
Citizens of several African countries, including Kenya, Ghana and South Africa, have gone to fight for Russia in Ukraine – some they had been duped and had not realised where they were going.
A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.
Kenya at the time estimated that 252 citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia. In March, Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue.
He said at the time that an agreement had been reached to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.
In February, Ghana said that 55 of its citizens had been killed in the conflict, with 272 believed to have been lured to fight since the war started in 2022.
The same month, South Africa secured the return of 17 South Africans who were allegedly tricked into joining the war.
In December last year, South African authorities arrested five people, including a journalist, for allegedly recruiting people to join the war.
Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.
The nine arrested are expected to appear in court either later on Monday or Tuesday.
#sapsHAWKS [NINE FOREIGN NATIONALS ARRESTED AT OR TAMBO INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT]
Nine foreign nationals are expected to appear before the Kempton Park Magistrates’ Court soon following their arrest at the airport and a hotel in Bruma in connection with an alleged attempt to travel from South Africa to participate in the Russia-Ukraine war.
The arrests follow an integrated multidisciplinary investigation involving INTERPOL, the Hawks’ Crimes Against the State and Serious Organised Crime Investigation based in Germiston, International Law Enforcement agencies, SAPS Crime Intelligence, the Modus Operandi Centre, the Gauteng Provincial Tracking Team and the various security companies.
Acting on intelligence gathered during the investigation, the multidisciplinary team operationalised an intervention that resulted in the arrest of the nine suspects, aged between 20 and 26, last night. The suspects were allegedly preparing to board flights out of the country when they were apprehended.
The suspects are expected to face charges relating to the contravention of the Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act 15 of 1998.
The Acting Provincial Head of the Gauteng Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation, Brigadier Paulina Sekgobela, commended the multidisciplinary team for its coordinated efforts and successful operation.
The #HAWKS reiterate their commitment to working with local and international law enforcement agencies to combat crime and ensure compliance with the laws of the Republic of South Africa.

items.title: British banks join Tanzania’s $1.2 billion railway financing as global insurers back new trade route connecting farms and mines with the DRC and Indian Ocean

original_payload.original_title: British banks join Tanzania’s $1.2 billion railway financing as global insurers back new trade route connecting farms and mines with the DRC and Indian Ocean
original_payload.original_body:
FILE – Tanzania has secured a $1.2 billion commercial financing facility for the 411-kilometre electrified railway between Tabora and Kigoma. [File photo: AfDB]
Tanzania signed a $1.2 billion commercial facility for a 411-kilometre railway.
HSBC, FirstBank UK and Bank of Africa UK joined the lending syndicate.
Lloyd’s syndicates will assume part of $405.5 million in insured exposure.
The line will connect western Tanzania with the DRC and Dar es Salaam port.
Tanzania has secured a $1.2 billion commercial financing facility for an electrified railway intended to connect the country’s western agricultural and mining regions with the Port of Dar es Salaam and neighbouring markets.
The financing will support the 411-kilometre Tabora–Kigoma section of Tanzania’s standard-gauge railway, known as Lot 6.
Once connected to the wider network, the line will provide producers in western Tanzania with a high-capacity route to the Indian Ocean while expanding trade with the Democratic Republic of Congo through the ports of Kigoma and Kalemie on Lake Tanganyika.
The transaction also brings British financial institutions directly into one of East Africa’s largest current infrastructure financings.
HSBC, FirstBank UK and Bank of Africa United Kingdom are among nine banks participating in the facility. International insurers, including Lloyd’s syndicates, will also absorb part of the project’s credit exposure.
The African Development Bank announced the signed facility⁠ on November 4, with Tanzania’s Finance and Transport ministries subsequently confirming the development to local media.
How the $1.2 billion financing works
The African Development Bank acted as the initial mandated lead arranger and structured a partial credit guarantee of up to $800 million—its largest guarantee of this type.
The commercial facility was co-arranged by Deutsche Bank and Société Générale. The remaining lenders are HSBC, Commerzbank, Nedbank, Stanbic Bank Tanzania, First Abu Dhabi Bank, FirstBank UK and Bank of Africa United Kingdom.
The banks collectively committed $720 million in guaranteed lending and another $480 million against Tanzania’s sovereign credit risk.
Individual commitments were not disclosed. It would therefore be inaccurate to attribute a specific portion of the $1.2 billion to HSBC or either of the two UK-based African banks.
The AfDB guarantee covers the principal of the protected tranche and two years of interest. London-based insurance broker Texel has distributed $405.5 million of the exposure among international insurers, including Lloyd’s syndicates.
At the conversion used in Tanzanian reporting, the signed facility is worth approximately TSh3.1 trillion ($1.2 billion).
The structure allows Tanzania to attract commercial lenders while reducing part of the repayment risk they would ordinarily assume on a project of this size.
It also means the financing should not be described as a $1.2 billion AfDB loan. The money is being provided by the nine-bank syndicate, supported by the development bank’s guarantee and international insurance capacity.
Railway could open a new route to the DRC
The Tabora–Kigoma line is designed to carry agricultural produce, minerals and other bulk goods from western Tanzania to domestic and international markets.
Kigoma sits on Lake Tanganyika opposite the Congolese port of Kalemie. Connecting the town to Tanzania’s wider railway network would give businesses trading with eastern DRC another route to the Port of Dar es Salaam.
The broader railway programme is also intended to improve Tanzania’s transport connection with Burundi.
Tanzania expects the project to lower freight costs, improve market access and attract investment into agriculture, mining and manufacturing along the Central Corridor. Construction and railway operations are also expected to create employment, although the government has not published a verified jobs estimate.
Transport Permanent Secretary Godius Kahyarara said the financing would enable the country to connect Tabora, Kigoma and Burundi through Lot 6.
Three financing figures that must not be combined
The signed $1.2 billion facility is part of a wider financing structure, but the larger numbers attached to the railway do not represent money already secured.
The overall package planned for the Tabora–Kigoma section is $2.3 billion. Besides the signed commercial facility, it is expected to include an export-credit-agency tranche and another component to be mobilised with a co-guarantor.
Separately, Tanzania mandated the AfDB to structure and mobilise up to $3.2 billion for its broader regional railway programme.
The $2.3 billion and $3.2 billion figures are therefore not additional completed investments that can be added to the $1.2 billion. They describe wider financing requirements and mobilisation mandates.
The immediate development is that Tanzania has signed the $1.2 billion commercial tranche, backed by the AfDB’s record guarantee and a group of international lenders and insurers.
The deal gives British financial institutions direct exposure to infrastructure designed to connect East African farms, mines and industrial centres with one of the region’s largest neighbouring consumer markets.
Source:  Business Insider Africa

items.title: Mozambique: FEWS NET warns heat and poor rainfall could put pressure on next agricultural season

original_payload.original_title: Mozambique: FEWS NET warns heat and poor rainfall could put pressure on next agricultural season
original_payload.original_body:
FILE – For illustration purposes only. [File photo: Ministério da Agricultura] In its latest monitoring report, FEWS NET writes that the combination of above-average temperatures and rainfall deficits forecast for much of southern Africa during the 2026/2027 agricultural season, already under the influence of the El Niño climate phenomenon, could increase pressure on Mozambique’s agriculture.
In this regional bulletin, seen by Lusa, the organisation states that “above-normal temperatures are forecast for much of the region between October 2026 and April 2027” and adds that, “combined with rainfall deficits, higher temperatures will increase evapotranspiration and crop water requirements”.
The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) is an international early warning network for food crises, funded by the United States and specialising in monitoring climate conditions, agricultural production, markets and food insecurity risks in dozens of vulnerable countries, including Mozambique.
This month alone, Mozambican authorities have already issued two public warnings about heatwaves in the south of the country, with temperatures exceeding 40 degrees Celsius.
According to FEWS NET, these conditions “increase the impact of a delayed onset of the rainy season and prolonged dry spells on vegetation and crops”, raising the risks to agricultural production in several parts of the region.
The analysis also warns that high temperatures during dry periods could affect crops, pastures and water resources, worsening the consequences of any rainfall failures during the agricultural season.
The report comes amid the strengthening of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomenon, which is expected to continue into the first months of 2027. According to FEWS NET, the probability of a strong episode persisting remains above 80%, in a scenario historically associated with below-average rainfall across much of southern Africa.
Despite the risks facing the next agricultural season, current vegetation conditions vary significantly between regions of Mozambique.
According to the document, “conditions well above average in the south, including southern Mozambique, are mainly attributed to above-average rainfall during the 2025-2026 season”.
The organisation adds that rainfall recorded in recent months has also helped sustain the good condition of vegetation cover in that region.
The centre and north of the country, however, present a less favourable picture, with FEWS NET identifying below-average vegetation conditions and warning that “a subsequent deterioration in vegetation conditions is likely” if forecasts of below-normal rainfall over the coming months materialise.
According to the analysis, the risks are particularly significant for areas covered by projections of below-average rainfall between December 2026 and February 2027, when the rainy season normally reaches its peak.
The report indicates that soil moisture remains above average in parts of central and southern Mozambique, reflecting the effects of the good 2025-2026 agricultural season, while some areas in the north-east are experiencing below-normal conditions.
The organisation also notes signs of recovery in strategic water infrastructure in the region following the effects of drought in recent years.
Among the examples cited is the Cahora Bassa reservoir, which recorded a significant increase in storage levels throughout 2026.
The new bulletin complements another report released by FEWS NET in October, which estimated that between 1.5 million and 1.99 million Mozambicans could require urgent food assistance in April 2027. It considered that good harvests recorded in 2026, household food stocks and stable prices should mitigate the effects of the difficulties expected during the next agricultural season.
Source:  Lusa

items.title: Cultura e Turismo discutem oportunidades de geração de rendimento em Moçambique

original_payload.original_title: Cultura e Turismo discutem oportunidades de geração de rendimento em Moçambique
original_payload.original_body:
O Ministério da Educação e Cultura destacou o potencial económico da cultura para o desenvolvimento do turismo, durante a sua participação no Mozambique Tourism Summit e na Feira Internacional de Turismo (FIKANI) 2026, realizados nos dias 5 e 6 de Novembro, em Vilankulo, província de Inhambane.
O sector da Cultura esteve representado pela Secretária de Estado das Artes e Cultura, Matilde Muocha, acompanhada por uma delegação de quadros do ministério.
No âmbito do Summit, foi realizado um painel dedicado ao tema “A Cultura como Activo Económico do Turismo”, que reuniu representantes dos sectores público e privado para discutir formas de valorizar o património cultural, as artes, as indústrias culturais e criativas e as manifestações culturais nacionais como factores de atracção turística, geração de rendimento e criação de emprego.
Na sua intervenção, Matilde Muocha apelou aos operadores turísticos, investidores e parceiros internacionais a integrarem experiências culturais nos pacotes turísticos de Vilankulo e Inhambane, estabelecerem parcerias com artistas e comunidades locais e apoiarem a restauração e musealização do património histórico da região.
A governante defendeu igualmente a inclusão de Moçambique em programas internacionais de turismo cultural sustentável e criativo.
A participação do sector da Cultura no evento procurou reforçar a articulação entre as áreas da Cultura e do Turismo, com destaque para o aproveitamento do património, da diversidade cultural e da criatividade na oferta turística nacional.
O Mozambique Tourism Summit e a FIKANI 2026 decorreram em Vilankulo, com a abertura oficial dirigida pelo Presidente da República, Daniel Chapo, que destacou o turismo como um dos motores do desenvolvimento nacional.

items.title: Aguiar-Branco defende diálogo e condena terrorismo

original_payload.original_title: Aguiar-Branco defende diálogo e condena terrorismo
original_payload.original_body:
O presidente da Assembleia da República Portuguesa, José Pedro Aguiar-Branco, considera que o terrorismo e a violência são inaceitáveis numa sociedade livre e com instituições democráticas funcionais. O dirigente defendeu, por isso, que os parlamentos devem assumir um papel activo na construção de pontes de diálogo e na superação das diferenças existentes na sociedade. Aguiar-Branco falava na Assembleia da República de Moçambique, onde foi recebido pelos deputados.
Na ocasião, o dirigente português manifestou a solidariedade de Portugal para com o povo moçambicano e as autoridades nacionais face à violência provocada pelo terrorismo em Cabo Delgado. Garantiu que a Assembleia da República Portuguesa continuará a chamar a atenção para a situação da província nos fóruns internacionais, com vista ao restabelecimento da paz e à defesa da soberania nacional.
“Manifesto, em nome de Portugal, a nossa total solidariedade com o povo moçambicano e com as autoridades deste país. Na nossa parte, na Assembleia da República Portuguesa, continuaremos a chamar a atenção para Cabo Delgado nos fóruns internacionais, para que a paz regresse à província e para que a soberania de Moçambique e a dignidade deste povo nunca mais sejam postos em causa”, afirmou.
Aguiar-Branco defendeu ainda que o terrorismo e a violência não devem merecer reacções diferentes em função do país ou continente onde ocorrem, sublinhando a necessidade de uma resposta internacional coerente perante estas ameaças.
Na sua intervenção, destacou igualmente o papel dos parlamentos na promoção do diálogo e da democracia, num contexto marcado pela fragmentação e polarização social. Para o presidente do Parlamento português, as diferenças existentes nas sociedades devem ser ultrapassadas através da negociação, da construção de consensos e da cooperação entre as diferentes forças políticas.
“A política, numa democracia, não serve para prolongar a guerra, serve para a evitar”, afirmou, acrescentando que a actividade política deve permitir gerir pacificamente as divergências e construir projectos comuns.
O dirigente considerou, por outro lado, que a experiência e as consequências dos conflitos armados demonstram a importância da paz e da existência de instituições sólidas, capazes de representar a vontade popular e de promover o desenvolvimento.

items.title: Ramaphosa apela a priorizarem comunidades nas coligações

original_payload.original_title: Ramaphosa apela a priorizarem comunidades nas coligações
original_payload.original_body:
O Presidente sul-africano, Cyril Ramaphosa, apelou aos partidos políticos para colocarem os interesses das comunidades em primeiro lugar nas negociações para a formação de coligações, na sequência dos resultados das eleições municipais. Ramaphosa advertiu que a prestação de serviços essenciais não deve ficar refém de divergências políticas.
Um dia depois do anúncio dos resultados eleitorais, o Chefe de Estado defendeu o respeito pela vontade popular e a necessidade de os partidos responderem às expectativas dos eleitores.
“O povo falou. O seu veredicto deve ser respeitado. As suas preocupações devem ser ouvidas e as suas expectativas devem agora ser atendidas”, afirmou Cyril Ramaphosa.
Os partidos têm um calendário apertado para negociar a formação dos novos executivos municipais, uma vez que a lei determina que os conselhos eleitos realizem as primeiras reuniões no prazo de 14 dias após a declaração formal dos resultados.
Das oito principais cidades sul-africanas, apenas a Cidade do Cabo ficou fora das negociações de coligação, depois de a Aliança Democrática (DA) ter conquistado a maioria absoluta.
O Congresso Nacional Africano (ANC), que domina a política sul-africana desde o fim do apartheid, obteve 30,76% dos votos, o seu pior resultado eleitoral de sempre, segundo dados divulgados pela Comissão Eleitoral no domingo.
A ausência de maiorias claras em vários municípios abre caminho a negociações complexas entre diferentes forças políticas para a definição dos governos locais.

items.title: Ethiopia Mobilizes Global Partnerships, Climate Finance Ahead of COP32

original_payload.original_title: Ethiopia Mobilizes Global Partnerships, Climate Finance Ahead of COP32
original_payload.original_body:
Addis Ababa, November 9, 2026 (ENA)— Ethiopia is intensifying efforts to build international confidence in its climate commitments, attract climate finance and forge strategic partnerships as it prepares to host the 32nd United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP32) in Addis Ababa in November 2027, Finance Minister and COP32 Chief Negotiator, Fitsum Assefa (PhD) said.
Speaking on the sidelines of the ongoing COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, Fitsum described the conference as a crucial opportunity for Ethiopia to demonstrate its readiness to host COP32.
She added the country is also strengthening its influence in global climate negotiations and advancing international cooperation.
As the final global climate summit before COP32, she said, COP31 offers Ethiopia an important platform to help shape negotiating texts, declarations and other official outcomes, laying the groundwork for more meaningful progress on global climate commitments.
She stressed that Ethiopia's preparations are driven by a broader responsibility to advance collective global interests, rather than focusing exclusively on its national priorities.
A major component of this effort is Ethiopia's national pavilion, which features around 60 programmes and events showcasing the country's climate initiatives, national identity and preparations for COP32.
Beyond presenting Ethiopia's achievements, the pavilion is serving as a strategic platform to attract investment, explore climate-financing opportunities, promote international partnerships and engage governments, institutions and other global stakeholders.
Fitsum noted that the pavilion also highlights Ethiopia's distinctive contributions to humanity, including its coffee heritage and status as the origin of humanity, offering international participants a broader perspective on the country's identity and potential.
On the diplomatic front, Ethiopia is strengthening engagement with key climate negotiating blocs and international partners, including the African Group of Negotiators, the Least Developed Countries Group, the G77 and China, and the European Union.
These engagements are aimed at building common ground, narrowing differences among negotiating parties and securing broader international participation in COP32.
However, Fitsum emphasized that Ethiopia's ambition goes beyond bringing a large number of delegates to Addis Ababa. The country also seeks to make COP32 a substantive platform for advancing climate negotiations, strengthening adaptation efforts, accelerating climate action and mobilizing the investment needed to address global climate challenges.
Pointing to Ethiopia's domestic efforts, she highlighted the Green Legacy Initiative, which has mobilized millions of citizens in planting billions of seedlings, as a flagship demonstration of the country's commitment to environmental protection and climate resilience.
She also underscored that more than 90 percent of Ethiopia's energy consumption comes from renewable sources, predominantly hydropower, while the country is expanding electric mobility and promoting climate-compatible approaches to agriculture and urban development.
Despite its vulnerability to climate change and the persistent gap between its climate-financing requirements and available international support, Ethiopia is pursuing these initiatives as part of its broader green development ambitions.
Fitsum said the country's domestic actions provide a strong foundation for strengthening international confidence, attracting climate investment and mobilizing greater support for climate-resilient development.
Ethiopia is scheduled to host COP32 in Addis Ababa in November 2027, following COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20, 2026. The summit will offer a major opportunity to elevate Africa's climate priorities and strengthen the continent's role in shaping the global climate agenda.

items.title: Ethiopia Leverages COP31 to Build Momentum for Successful COP32 Hosting: Foreign Minister

original_payload.original_title: Ethiopia Leverages COP31 to Build Momentum for Successful COP32 Hosting: Foreign Minister
original_payload.original_body:
Addis Ababa, November 9, 2026 (ENA)— Ethiopia is using its participation in the ongoing COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, to advance preparations for hosting COP32 in 2027, strengthen international partnerships and contribute to effective global climate negotiations, Foreign Minister Gedion Timotheos said.
Ethiopia is stepping up diplomatic engagement and practical preparations for COP32      .
Moreover, the East African nation is       seeking to translate its participation in the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) into a strong foundation for successfully hosting the landmark global climate summit in 2027.
Speaking at the inauguration of Ethiopia's national pavilion in Antalya, Foreign Minister, Gedion Timotheos said the country has set clear priorities for its engagement at COP31, with a particular focus on contributing to effective negotiations, exchanging experiences and building partnerships ahead of assuming the COP32 presidency.
He emphasized that Ethiopia's engagement goes beyond showcasing its climate initiatives, highlighting the country's commitment to helping advance international climate action and ensuring a successful transition toward the next global climate conference.
In this regard, Ethiopia will work closely with Türkiye and Australia to support constructive negotiations and strengthen the groundwork for COP32.
The Ethiopian pavilion, meanwhile, will serve as a strategic platform to showcase the country's climate initiatives, share its experiences and achievements, and engage international partners through a series of panel discussions.
It will also provide an opportunity to mobilize broader international participation in COP32, while reinforcing Ethiopia's ambition to make the 2027 summit a meaningful platform for advancing global climate commitments and cooperation.
Gedion further disclosed that practical preparations for COP32 are already underway, with the designated Ethiopian team using COP31 to gain firsthand experience, exchange institutional knowledge and build the organizational capacity required to host the high-level international gathering.
He also expressed appreciation to Brazil, which hosted COP30, for facilitating experience-sharing and knowledge transfer, describing the opportunity as valuable to Ethiopia's preparations.
The 32nd session of the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP32) is scheduled to take place in Ethiopia in 2027, marking a significant milestone for Africa's climate diplomacy and global engagement.
Ethiopia's hosting of COP32 will make it the first African country since Morocco hosted COP22 in 2016 to welcome the global climate summit, placing the country and the African continent at the center of international climate negotiations.
As preparations gather momentum, Ethiopia's participation in COP31 signals its determination to use the upcoming summit not only as a major diplomatic responsibility but also as an opportunity to amplify Africa's climate priorities and strengthen international cooperation.

items.title: Ethiopia Expands Scientific Education, Innovation to Build Skilled Workforce

original_payload.original_title: Ethiopia Expands Scientific Education, Innovation to Build Skilled Workforce
original_payload.original_body:
Addis Ababa, November 9, 2026 (ENA)— Ethiopia is accelerating its focus on science, technology, research, and innovation to drive national development and power Africa’s broader economic transformation, according to Solomon Abraha, State Minister for Higher Education Development.
Speaking at the opening of the 23rd Conference on Mathematics, Science and Technology Education in Africa (COMSTEDA 23) in Addis Ababa, State Minister Solomon highlighted the vital role of skilled human capital in securing the continent's future.
The five-day gathering, hosted by the Ministry of Education from November 9 to 13, brings together educators, policymakers, researchers, and development partners from across Africa.
Held under the theme “Empowering Africa through STEAM Education and Innovation for Sustainable Development and Global Competitiveness,” the conference focuses on advancing Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and Mathematics (STEAM) learning to foster innovation and prepare learners for a modern global economy.
Speaking at the opening ceremony, Solomon described investing in scientific and technological education as both a national responsibility and a continental priority.
“Embracing science, technology, engineering, arts, mathematics, artificial intelligence, and innovation is the patriotism of our time,” Solomon said. “Our ambition must go beyond consuming knowledge and technology to creating, innovating, solving problems, and competing globally.”
He underscored that education remains the bedrock of Africa's economic transformation, describing COMSTEDA 23 as a vital platform for continental collaboration, educational research, and innovative teaching methods.
Highlighting Ethiopia’s regional leadership as a founding member of Strengthening Mathematics and Science Education in Africa (SMASE-Africa), Solomon pointed to major national reforms, including the Smart Ethiopia initiative, the Mathematics Science Education Empowerment Center, and the Ministry’s dedicated STEM Directorate.
These efforts aim to modernize curricula, expand lab facilities, enhance teacher capacity, and promote digital learning.
Delivering a key address, SMASE-Africa President Professor Benson Banda urged African nations to move past fragmented, isolated efforts in favor of a unified continental approach.
“Our languages, our knowledge, and our priorities must be inside the technologies. Africa must not only realize the future; Africa must build it,” Banda stressed, calling for indigenous knowledge systems and local languages to be integrated into tech advancements.
Invoking the philosophy of Ubuntu, “I am because we are”, Banda emphasized that no single nation has all the answers, citing how countries can pool expertise ranging from robotics and digital learning to specialized pedagogy.
"In education, that means the progress of one African system must become the progress of all," he stated.
Meanwhile, Dr. Rita Bissoonauth, Director of the UNESCO Liaison Office in Addis Ababa and Representative to Ethiopia, emphasized that the continent's future depends on shifting focus toward intellectual capital.
“Africa’s future competitiveness will depend not only on its natural resources, but increasingly on the knowledge it generates and the scientific capacity it nurtures,” Bissoonauth said.
Reaffirming the UN agency's support, she pledged UNESCO’s continued partnership with the Ethiopian government, the African Union Commission, and regional stakeholders to turn shared educational goals into tangible outcomes.
Over the course of the five-day conference, participants will explore concrete strategies to modernize classrooms, expand digital learning, strengthen teacher training, improve science and math instruction, and align regional innovation with Africa’s broader development priorities.

items.title: Ethiopia Targets to Become Africa’s Leading AI Innovation Hub by 2030: EAII Director General

original_payload.original_title: Ethiopia Targets to Become Africa’s Leading AI Innovation Hub by 2030: EAII Director General
original_payload.original_body:
Addis Ababa, November 9, 2026 (ENA)—  Ethiopia is accelerating efforts to position itself as one of Africa’s leading hubs for artificial intelligence (AI) research and innovation by 2030 through strategic investments in digital infrastructure, human capital development and continental partnerships, Director General of the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute (EAII), Worku Gachena, said.
Speaking at the opening of the Pan-African AI Ventures Residency Program in Addis Ababa, Worku said Ethiopia aims to build strong AI capabilities that support national development priorities while contributing to technological advancement across Africa through research, innovation and entrepreneurship.
He noted that the ambition is aligned with Digital Ethiopia 2030, the country’s strategic roadmap for digital transformation, and supported by initiatives designed to strengthen research capacity and develop the next generation of AI professionals.
Among these initiatives is Medemer AI University, established as an autonomous public university following the Council of Ministers’ approval of its founding regulation.
The institution is expected to train AI scientists, engineers and entrepreneurs while expanding the country’s technological and research capabilities.
Worku also highlighted the AI UniPod, inaugurated on February 16, 2026, through a partnership between EAII, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and Addis Ababa University.
The facility is equipped with advanced laboratories, robotics facilities, high-performance computing resources, design studios and collaborative learning spaces. It is designed to connect research with entrepreneurship and the development of practical technological solutions.
He emphasized that realizing Ethiopia’s ambition to become a leading African AI research and development hub by 2030 requires sustained investment in digital infrastructure, computing capacity and skilled human resources.
In this regard, the Pan-African AI Ventures Residency Program brings together young innovators from 12 African countries to develop AI-driven solutions to challenges facing the continent.
The initiative provides participants with mentorship, knowledge exchange opportunities, professional networks and platforms for cross-border collaboration.
Worku further underscored the importance of stronger African cooperation, particularly in responsible data sharing and developing African-language datasets and AI models, to ensure that emerging technologies reflect the continent’s realities and development priorities.
He also acknowledged the contributions of the Japanese government, UNDP and Addis Ababa University, noting that international and regional partnerships are essential to strengthening Africa’s competitiveness in the global AI landscape.
Japanese Ambassador to Ethiopia Shibata Hironori highlighted Japan’s support for the AI UniPod initiative through its Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, which provides approximately 1 million USD in annual funding to advance African AI capacity and digital innovation.
He said the initiative also creates opportunities for Japanese companies to collaborate with African startups through joint development and pilot projects, reaffirming Japan’s commitment to supporting Ethiopia in partnership with EAII, Addis Ababa University and UNDP.
Meanwhile, Matthias Z. Naab, Director of UNDP’s Regional Service Centre for Africa, called on African countries to move beyond being passive consumers of foreign technologies and become active creators of solutions to their own development challenges.
He said Africa’s youthful population, expanding digital economy and growing innovation ecosystem provide a strong foundation for developing homegrown AI technologies and generating sustainable employment opportunities.
Naab also highlighted UNDP’s investments in digital infrastructure through its EDGE initiative, which provides essential resources, including high-performance graphics processing units (GPUs) at the AI UniPod, enabling innovators to develop AI-powered products.
However, he stressed that access to computing resources alone would not be sufficient, emphasizing the need for young innovators to acquire practical skills and connect their solutions to real-world markets.
He added that promising ventures emerging from the residency program could advance to UNDP’s broader Timbuktoo Initiative, gaining access to thematic innovation hubs, venture capital and market networks.
The 10-day residency brings together 51 AI startup founders from 12 African countries at the AI UniPod for intensive training, mentorship, product development and networking, marking another step toward strengthening Africa’s homegrown artificial intelligence ecosystem.

items.title: Navigating Global Complexity: Peace, Markets, Climate and Technology in Focus

original_payload.original_title: Navigating Global Complexity: Peace, Markets, Climate and Technology in Focus
original_payload.original_body:
By Staff Writer
November 9 , 2026 (ENA)
The first week of November 2026 was marked by geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty, prolonged conflicts and mounting humanitarian and environmental challenges. Developments in the Middle East and Eastern Europe, alongside strategic competition among major powers, continued to influence global security, trade and energy markets. Meanwhile, artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shaped economic competitiveness, national security and global governance.
Against this backdrop, international developments centred on seven major areas: peace and security, the economy, climate change, democracy and governance, public health, humanitarian affairs and technology.
Peace and Security
Tensions between Iran and the United States remained a major security concern, with military warnings and diplomatic signals raising fears of escalation. Particular attention focused on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy route through which disruptions to commercial shipping could threaten oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, increase transportation costs and destabilize energy markets.
The Russia-Ukraine conflict also continued to shape European security, raising concerns over military escalation and threats to critical infrastructure. European governments face the challenge of maintaining support for Ukraine while strengthening their defence capabilities and pursuing a lasting settlement. The conflict continues to affect energy security, military expenditure, agricultural supply chains and international relations.
Meanwhile, Israel's political uncertainty coincided with a worsening
Economy
Global financial markets experienced renewed turbulence as geopolitical tensions, elevated energy costs and concerns over economic growth heightened fears of stagflation. Technology stocks came under particular pressure, contributing to the Nasdaq's sharpest single-day decline since April 2025, while Taiwan's stock market recorded its worst weekly performance since 2001.
Much of the volatility reflected doubts over whether massive investments in AI infrastructure, including data centres and advanced semiconductors, would generate sufficient returns. Although the International Monetary Fund projects global growth of 3.1 percent in 2026, a sharp contraction in AI infrastructure spending could reduce global GDP growth by as much as 1.1 percentage points by 2028.
Energy markets added to the uncertainty. Crude oil prices fell approximately 15 percent during the week to slightly below 100 U.S. dollars per barrel amid prospects of diplomatic de-escalation in the Middle East. Nevertheless, prices remained about 64 percent above early-2026 levels, while natural gas prices were nearly three times higher. These costs continued to fuel inflation and affect transportation, industrial production and household spending.
Central banks consequently faced the challenge of controlling inflation without further weakening growth.
Geopolitical developments and the U.S. midterm elections also generated uncertainty over Washington's future trade, defence and energy policies, with potential consequences for international cooperation and investment. For developing countries, these developments reinforce the need to diversify trading partnerships, strengthen domestic production and expand manufacturing.
Climate
The 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), scheduled for November 9–20 in Antalya, Türkiye, placed climate action back at the centre of international discussions. The summit is expected to emphasize practical implementation of commitments on emissions reduction, adaptation financing, renewable energy and the transition away from fossil fuels.
Calling for action rather than prolonged negotiations, COP30 President André Corrêa do Lago told Reuters, "We don't need more negotiations. What we need is for governments to start taking action."
However, inadequate financing remains a major obstacle.
The financing gap threatens investment in climate-resilient infrastructure, agriculture, water management and disaster preparedness. It is particularly serious for Africa, which contributes relatively little to cumulative global greenhouse gas emissions but faces increasing droughts, floods, irregular rainfall and rising temperatures. Climate finance is therefore essential to the continent's food security, energy access and poverty reduction efforts. Developing countries are also demanding financing that does not add to their existing debt burdens.
Meanwhile, reducing methane emissions has emerged as an important climate priority. A Climate Analytics report indicates that cutting methane and other short-lived climate pollutants could slow global warming by approximately 12 percent by 2035. Combined with a faster transition away from fossil fuels, these measures could help limit temperature increases, although they cannot replace broader decarbonization.
Beyond climate negotiations, hazardous smog blanketed northern India and neighbouring Pakistan, prompting emergency restrictions in Lahore and New Delhi. Seasonal atmospheric inversions, vehicle emissions, industrial activities and agricultural residue burning trapped dangerous particulate matter near the ground, exposing millions to unhealthy air.
Democracy and Governance
Elections in the United States, Brazil and Israel highlighted changing political dynamics and their implications for domestic governance and international relations.
In the United States, the Democratic Party secured majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the midterm elections, significantly changing the political balance facing President Donald Trump's administration. Democratic candidates also gained ground in traditionally conservative states, including Kansas and South Carolina.
The change in congressional control is expected to strengthen Democratic influence over legislation, government oversight and scrutiny of executive policies. Internationally, governments are assessing possible implications for U.S. trade, climate policy, defence spending and multilateral partnerships.
In Brazil, incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won re-election in a presidential runoff against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. The result preserves the country's left-leaning administration but reflects continuing political divisions. As one of Latin America's largest economies, Brazil's political direction also matters for South-South cooperation, regional trade, environmental protection and relations with major powers.
Health
The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continued to face a major public health emergency as an Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus spread across several provinces.
The outbreak has placed significant pressure on healthcare facilities, particularly their capacity for early diagnosis, treatment and contact tracing.
Many deaths occurred within communities, including among young children, highlighting barriers to healthcare access and the difficulty of identifying infections at an early stage.
The outbreak also prompted neighbouring countries to strengthen surveillance. Kenya reported nine confirmed cases, including two deaths, while Nigeria identified one imported case. Although neither reported new confirmed cases during the reporting period, Kenya maintained screening at entry points and reinforced cross-border monitoring.
The WHO urged regional partners to strengthen laboratory capacity, infection prevention, contact tracing and emergency preparedness. It also advised against general travel and trade restrictions, emphasizing coordinated public health measures to contain the outbreak.
Technology
Artificial intelligence remained central to discussions on economic competitiveness, technological competition and financial stability. However, investor concerns over the enormous cost of AI infrastructure raised questions about whether investments in data centres, advanced computing systems and semiconductors would generate sufficient commercial returns.
Meanwhile, digital sovereignty is gaining importance as countries seek greater control over their data, digital infrastructure and technological development. Speaking at the 7th World Media Summit in Beijing, teleSUR President Patricia Villegas argued that information sovereignty is essential to narrowing the artificial intelligence divide between developed and developing countries.
Her remarks highlighted the concentration of advanced computing capacity, data resources and proprietary AI models in a limited number of wealthy economies.
Conclusion
The first week of November 2026 demonstrated how closely interconnected global challenges have become. Geopolitical rivalries, prolonged conflicts, economic uncertainty, climate risks and technological transformation continued to shape international affairs. From tensions in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine conflict to financial market volatility and the Ebola emergency in the DRC, developments showed how instability in one region can generate far-reaching consequences for global security, trade and development.
Meanwhile, widening climate financing gaps and the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence reinforced the need for inclusive international cooperation. For developing countries, particularly in Africa, the priorities remain strengthening economic resilience, expanding regional integration, building domestic technological capabilities and securing equitable climate finance.
Ultimately, addressing these challenges requires sustained diplomacy, effective multilateral institutions and collective action that balances security, economic prosperity, technological advancement and environmental sustainability. Translating international commitments into practical solutions will be decisive in building a more stable, inclusive and resilient global future.

items.title: Ethiopia’s Future Through Young Eyes and Teenagers’ Confidence in a Nation of Growing Possibilities

original_payload.original_title: Ethiopia’s Future Through Young Eyes and Teenagers’ Confidence in a Nation of Growing Possibilities
original_payload.original_body:
Addis Ababa, November 9, 2026 (ENA)—
From a rapidly transforming capital to renewed cultural pride and entrepreneurial ambition, young Ethiopians envision a stronger, more prosperous and globally respected country, believing their generation will play a defining role in shaping its future.
For a generation growing up amid visible changes in Ethiopia’s urban landscape, expanding development ambitions and evolving national aspirations, the future is increasingly seen not simply as something to anticipate, but as something to build.
Across Addis Ababa, teenagers are developing an increasingly confident outlook on their country's prospects, expressing optimism that sustained development efforts, cultural pride, innovation and greater opportunities for young people could propel Ethiopia toward a more prosperous future and a stronger position on the global stage.
In conversations with the Ethiopian News Agency (ENA), several teenagers painted an ambitious picture of the Ethiopia they hope to see over the next two decades and beyond — a country that combines modern development with its extraordinary cultural heritage, unlocks its economic potential and earns greater international recognition.
Their perspectives, while shaped by their individual experiences and aspirations, converge around a common conviction: Ethiopia's future holds enormous possibilities, and today's young generation has a responsibility to help realize them.
For 16-year-old Nathan Berhanemeskel, Ethiopia's ongoing transformation is an exciting journey, with visible changes creating a sense of momentum and possibility.
"It's an amazing ride," he said, describing a country that is becoming increasingly "modernized, futuristic, and beautiful."
Nathan pointed to the growing range of social and recreational activities, alongside improvements in the urban environment, as signs of a changing society offering young people more opportunities to explore, interact and enjoy their surroundings.
"There is a clear positive trajectory in our country right now," he observed.
Yet, for Nathan, Ethiopia's appeal extends well beyond its changing cities and modern infrastructure. Its people, natural attractions and rich cultural heritage remain central to what makes the country special.
Describing Ethiopia as "an amazing country with beautiful people and great places," he conveyed a sense of national pride rooted in both its identity and its potential.
That connection between national identity and future ambition was equally evident in the reflections of 16-year-old Amen Haimanot, who sees being Ethiopian as an essential part of who she is.
"Being Ethiopian brings me a lot of joy; it makes me who I am today," she said.
For Amen, national pride is not merely an attachment to the country's past. It is also confidence in what Ethiopia can become.
She believes that if the current momentum in social and economic development is sustained, Ethiopia could emerge as "one of the most well-known and respected countries in the world."
Amen cited improvements in the urban environment, including expanding green spaces, cleaner air and more vibrant public parks, as encouraging signs of change.
But she also emphasized that Ethiopia's greatest strengths lie in its people, cultural diversity, historical legacy and resilience — qualities she believes can help the country project a more dynamic and compelling image internationally.
Looking ahead, she placed particular confidence in the capacity of younger generations to accelerate the country's transformation.
"In 10 to 20 years, our generation and the next will place Ethiopia where it truly deserves to be," she said.
This confidence in Ethiopia's future is also reflected in the way 15-year-old Markan Yonas views the transformation of Addis Ababa, a city increasingly associated with the country's development ambitions.
For Markan, the capital's changing skyline and modern infrastructure demonstrate how far the country can go when development aspirations are translated into action.
She envisions an Ethiopia that will become even more remarkable over the coming decades, with stronger international trade, expanded economic opportunities and a more influential presence in global affairs.
"In 20 to 50 years, Ethiopia will be an extraordinary country," she predicted.
However, Markan believes that progress should not come at the expense of the country's identity. As Ethiopia modernizes and strengthens its international engagement, she urged young people to remain connected to the traditions and cultural values that distinguish the nation.
"We should love our country, treasure our culture, and truly appreciate everything we have," she said.
Her message captures an important dimension of the aspirations expressed by the teenagers: the Ethiopia of tomorrow should be modern and globally connected while remaining firmly grounded in its historical and cultural foundations.
For 16-year-old Eyoel Leul, however, optimism about the future is accompanied by a more immediate determination to contribute to the country's economic development.
Feeling fortunate to have been born in Ethiopia, Eyoel encouraged international visitors and investors to discover the country's opportunities and untapped potential.
More importantly, he sees entrepreneurship and the growth of local businesses as practical ways through which young people can participate in nation-building.
Rather than viewing the country's future as the responsibility of government alone, he hopes to contribute through his own family's enterprise.
"My plan is to take over my father's business and use it to help build the country," he said.
His ambition reflects a broader understanding of development in which individual initiative, business expansion and productive engagement can complement national economic priorities.
All in all       , the teenagers' reflections reveal more than youthful enthusiasm. They offer a glimpse into how a new generation perceives Ethiopia's evolving national identity and its place in an increasingly interconnected world.
Their optimism is expressed through different lenses: Nathan sees a country undergoing exciting modernization; Amen draws confidence from national identity, environmental improvements and cultural resilience; Markan envisions a future of expanded trade and global influence; while Eyoel sees entrepreneurship as a direct pathway to contributing to national development.
Despite their different perspectives, a common aspiration runs through their accounts — a desire to see Ethiopia become more prosperous, internationally respected and full of opportunities for future generations.
Their vision also points to the importance of ensuring that young people are not merely spectators of national transformation, but active participants in it.
As Ethiopia pursues its development ambitions, investments in education, innovation, entrepreneurship, infrastructure and a greener urban environment will be important in translating such aspirations into tangible opportunities.
Equally important is nurturing a generation that values its cultural heritage while embracing new ideas, technologies and global engagement.
For these teenagers, Ethiopia's story is far from finished. Its next chapter remains unwritten, offering their generation an opportunity to shape the country's economic, social and international trajectory.
Their message is both hopeful and purposeful: a prosperous Ethiopia will not emerge from aspirations alone, but from the determination, creativity and collective efforts of its people.
And for a generation already imagining what their country could become in 10, 20 or even 50 years, the future is not simply a distant horizon. It is a responsibility they are eager to embrace.

items.title: Kenya: Food Crisis Hits Ethiopians Fleeing Violence Into Kenya's Moyale

original_payload.original_title: Kenya: Food Crisis Hits Ethiopians Fleeing Violence Into Kenya's Moyale
original_payload.original_body:
Nairobi — Thousands of Ethiopian families who fled violent clashes in their country and sought refuge in Kenya's Moyale area are facing acute food shortages, with more than seven in ten households reporting insufficient food, a new humanitarian assessment has found.
An estimated 50,000 people had crossed into Kenya by October 29, according to an assessment conducted by the Government of Kenya and the Marsabit County Government, with support from the International Organization for Migration (IOM), United Nations agencies and humanitarian organisations.
The assessment found that 71 per cent of households surveyed did not have enough to eat, while 80 per cent identified food as their most urgent need, highlighting the growing humanitarian needs among displaced families and the communities hosting them.

items.title: Kenya: Water Rationing Looms in Nairobi As Ndakaini Dam Levels Decline

original_payload.original_title: Kenya: Water Rationing Looms in Nairobi As Ndakaini Dam Levels Decline
original_payload.original_body:
Nairobi — Water rationing is set to intensify in Nairobi and neighbouring counties after declining levels at Thika/Ndakaini Dam forced a 35 per cent reduction in water production at two major treatment plants supplying the capital.
Nairobi City Water and Sewerage Company said the reduction at Ngethu and Kigoro water treatment plants took effect immediately, warning that customers should brace for extended periods without water as the utility moves to preserve the dwindling reserves.
In a notice issued on Monday, November 9, the company attributed the production cuts to below-average rainfall in the dam's catchment area, which has affected water inflows into the reservoir.
"Thika Dam, the principal source of water for Nairobi and surrounding areas, has experienced a significant decline in storage levels due to below-average rainfall within its catchment area," the company said.

original_payload.original_title: Somalia: Somali Opposition Accuses President of Using Force to Seize Supreme Court
original_payload.original_body:
Mogadishu, Somalia — Somalia's opposition coalition, the Somali Future Council, has accused President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud of using security forces to take control of the country's Supreme Court, escalating a political confrontation over the independence of the judiciary and the president's mandate.
The council, led by former president Sheikh Sharif Sheikh Ahmed and comprising several former Somali leaders, issued a statement condemning what it described as an assault on the Federal Supreme Court and an attempt by Mohamud to seize control of the country's highest judicial institution.
The opposition group also accused security agencies of intimidating former Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed and judges who issued a ruling challenging the terms of the country's federal institutions.

items.title: Africa: African Development Bank Approves $200 Million Regional Trade Finance Line of Credit Facility for Tdb to Support Trade Across Africa

original_payload.original_title: Africa: African Development Bank Approves $200 Million Regional Trade Finance Line of Credit Facility for Tdb to Support Trade Across Africa
original_payload.original_body:
The Board of Directors of the African Development Bank Group has approved a $200 million Trade Finance Line of Credit facility between the African Development Bank and Trade and Development Bank (TDB).
The facility is expected to boost intra-Africa trade, promote regional integration, and contribute to the reduction of the trade finance gap in Africa, in line with implementation aspirations of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
Approved on 28 October, this facility will enable TDB to extend trade finance to clients across Africa. It is expected to catalyse more than $1 billion in trade transactions over its 3.5-year tenor due to the revolving nature of underlying transactions.
Beneficiaries include financial institutions, corporates and small and medium-sized enterprises engaged in import and export activities whose growth has been constrained by inadequate liquidity. The facility will also support the procurement of critical goods, including refined petroleum products, fertiliser, pharmaceuticals, and essential food commodities in TDB's eligible member states under the Bank Group's recently adopted  Global Energy and Fertilizer Crisis Response Framework .

items.title: Ethiopia: Ethiopia Advances COP32 Preparations As COP31 Opens Amid Climate Finance Disputes

original_payload.original_title: Ethiopia: Ethiopia Advances COP32 Preparations As COP31 Opens Amid Climate Finance Disputes
original_payload.original_body:
Addis Abeba — Ethiopia is using its participation in the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), which opened on Monday in Antalya, Türkiye, to advance preparations for hosting COP32 in Addis Abeba in November 2027, as developing countries push for stronger climate finance commitments amid widening disagreements over how to address the climate crisis.
Foreign Affairs Minister Gedion Timothewos, who is also president-designate of COP32, said Ethiopia's engagement at COP31 would help establish the groundwork for a successful summit next year. Speaking about Ethiopia's participation, the state-affiliated  ENA reported  that Gedion outlined plans to work closely with Türkiye and Australia, which are jointly overseeing COP31, to strengthen negotiations, expand partnerships and build international participation ahead of the Addis Abeba conference.

items.title: Africa: African Development Bank Group At COP31

original_payload.original_title: Africa: African Development Bank Group At COP31
original_payload.original_body:
What:    African Development Bank Group participation in UNFCCC COP31, featuring high-level events, partnership announcements, bilateral engagements, and strategic discussions on climate finance, adaptation, resilience, energy transition, nature, and sustainable development.
Who:    The African Development Bank Group, led by Senior Vice President Marie-Laure Akin-Olugbade, the UNFCCC, and partners.
When:    9 - 20 November 2026
Where:    Antalya, Türkiye and online
The African Development Bank Group will participate in the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), engaging with governments, development finance institutions, the private sector, civil society organisations, Indigenous Peoples, youth, and international partners to advance global climate action and sustainable development. As climate and biodiversity agendas become increasingly interconnected, COP31 will provide a platform to promote integrated solutions that address climate change, and nature loss, while advancing economic development.
As an accredited observer to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the African Development Bank Group actively contributes to international climate negotiations and supports Africa's priorities in global climate decision-making. The Bank provides technical support to African negotiators and policymakers, mobilises finance and partnerships for climate action, shares knowledge and lessons learned, and showcases innovative African solutions that strengthen resilience and sustainable development.
At COP31, the Bank's engagement will focus on five strategic priorities:
Supporting African negotiators and strengthening climate leadership.
Accelerating and scaling climate finance for Africa.
Showcasing transformative African climate solutions.
Advancing the nature-climate-development nexus.
Strengthening partnerships and amplifying Africa's voice on the global stage.
The   Africa Pavilion  (A240) , under the theme  "Turning Climate Commitments into Investments,"  will serve as Africa's flagship platform at COP31, showcasing the continent's priorities, experiences, innovations, and solutions while fostering dialogue on adaptation, renewable energy, climate-smart agriculture, biodiversity, early warning systems, and resilient development.
