items.title: Islam et bonnes œuvres: La FOFIN mobilise les femmes musulmanes

original_payload.original_title: Islam et bonnes œuvres: La FOFIN mobilise les femmes musulmanes
original_payload.original_body:
Accueil  ›  Société
Islam et bonnes œuvres: La FOFIN mobilise les femmes musulmanes
10 novembre 2026  · ONEP NE
Une vue des femmes et disciples mobilisées
Partager vers les réseaux
La Fédération des Organisations Féminines Islamiques du Niger (FOFIN) a organisé, le dimanche 8 novembre 2026, un prêche bimestriel dans l’enceinte de l’école Anouaroul Islam, au quartier Cité Député, sur le thème : « La mort ». Ce prêche a pour objectif de rappeler aux femmes l’importance de leur engagement dans les pratiques islamiques et de renforcer leur foi. Ce rendez-vous religieux a également été couplé à une opération de don de sang.
Elles étaient nombreuses, vêtues de hijabs conformes aux normes de leurs makarantas, à prendre part à cette rencontre religieuse dans l’enceinte de l’école Anouaroul Islam. Le thème retenu a suscité un intérêt particulier auprès des participantes. Plusieurs grandes ‘’malamas’’ ont animé des prêches sur le sujet du jour avec beaucoup de précision, et cela dans plusieurs langues locales afin de permettre à toutes les participantes de mieux comprendre les enseignements dispensés et de mettre en pratique les conseils islamiques adaptés à cette thématique.
Les malamas ont d’abord axé leurs interventions sur la mort, avant d’aborder d’autres sujets, dont la multiplication des actes de charité, le bon comportement, le repentir et le respect des prescriptions de l’Islam. L’objectif était d’amener les femmes à multiplier les bonnes actions afin que leurs âmes puissent reposer en paix lorsque l’heure de la mort aura sonné.
Des membres de la FOFIN ont donné du sang pour sauver des vies
Selon Mme Mamoudou Yayé Sakinatou, jeune élève de la makaranta Anouaroul Islam, l’organisation de ce prêche est partie d’un constat fait depuis un certain temps, notamment le manque d’éducation des enfants. Cette situation a poussé les femmes à créer une organisation comme la FOFIN, afin de contribuer à redresser l’éducation des enfants. « Aujourd’hui, nous avons choisi de prêcher sur la mort parce que la mort est un chemin inévitable. Au-delà de son caractère inévitable, elle est également imprévisible. Donc, chaque personne doit s’y préparer avant que ce jour n’arrive », a-t-elle expliqué.
Mme Mamoudou Yayé Sakinatou a également lancé un appel à chaque être humain à craindre Allah dans ses activités et dans ses actions quotidiennes, car la mort ne prévient pas. « Le rendez-vous de la mort est l’unique rendez-vous que personne ne peut manquer. Jeunes ou vieux, riches ou pauvres, tout le monde doit répondre à cet appel-là », a-t-elle déclaré.
Abordant la question du don de sang, Mme Mamoudou Yayé Sakinatou a souligné son importance en Islam, le considérant comme un acte de grande valeur, bénéfique pour la communauté et l’humanité. Elle a rappelé que de nombreuses personnes perdent la vie par manque de sang, parmi les Forces de défense et de sécurité engagées sur le terrain, ainsi que les femmes confrontées à des complications après l’accouchement. « Après la mort, la seule chose qui reste ce sont les bonnes actions que nous avons accomplies de notre vivant. Donner son sang est une bonne action qui va nous accompagner dans notre tombe. C’est pourquoi, la FOFIN a sensibilisé les femmes à ce geste salutaire, dans le but de contribuer à sauver des vies », a-t-elle conclu.
À l’issue de cette cérémonie, des douas ont été formulées pour implorer Allah afin que la paix et la tranquillité reviennent dans les trois États de l’Alliance des États du Sahel (AES).
Assad Hamadou   (ONEP)

items.title: La COP31 se penche sur la transition vers une mobilité durable, enjeu majeur pour l’Afrique

original_payload.original_title: La COP31 se penche sur la transition vers une mobilité durable, enjeu majeur pour l’Afrique
original_payload.original_body:
La COP31 se penche sur la transition vers une mobilité durable, enjeu majeur pour l’Afrique
La 31e Conférence des parties à la Convention cadre des Nations unies sur les changements climatiques est réunie à Antalya, en Turquie, du 9 au 20 novembre 2026. Cette deuxième journée du 10 novembre, est notamment consacrée aux transports de personnes et de biens qui représentent un quart des émissions de gaz à effet de serre dans le monde. Un enjeu majeur pour l’Afrique. Explications.
Publié le :  10/11/2026 - 12:06   Modifié le :  10/11/2026 - 12:08
2 min     Temps de lecture
Écouter - 01:08
Une vue de la gare de Train express régional (TER) à Dakar, en février 2025.        AFP - RICCI SHRYOCK
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Ce sont les grandes thématiques de cette deuxième journée à la   COP-31   climat à Antalya en Turquie, ce mardi : les transports de personnes et de biens qui représentent un quart des émissions de gaz à effet de serre dans le monde. Et c'est aussi le secteur dont les émissions continuent de croitre le plus rapidement.
Réussir la transition vers une mobilité durable est donc un enjeu de tout premier plan, notamment en Afrique. Le secteur des transports représente en effet 31% des émissions de CO2 du continent et plus de 70% de la demande en carburants raffinés dépendent des importations.
Dans ce contexte, les véhicules électriques ont le vent en poupe. En Éthiopie, l'électrification des transports en commun est par exemple une priorité nationale. Au Sénégal, une flotte de bus entièrement électriques circule sur des voies qui leur sont réservées pour relier Dakar à 14 communes. Et l'Égypte étend ses réseaux de métros, monorails, tramways, et trains.
«  Favoriser un transfert modal vers la marche, le vélo, les transports publics  »
«  Les choses se mettent en place petit à petit , souligne Mohamed Mezghani, secrétaire général de l'Union internationale des transports publics, au micro de  Stefanie Schüler .  Mais il faut avoir suffisamment d'électricité pour pouvoir approvisionner ce réseau-là. Quand on voit ce qui s'est passé par exemple, cette année, en Tunisie, avec les coupures d'électricité l'été, ça donne une idée du défi qu'on doit surmonter  ».
Tout comme celui du déploiement des bornes de recharge : pour réussir la transition vers la mobilité durable, il ne suffit pas de remplacer les moyens de transport existants par des modèles électriques. Le temps est venu d'une véritable transformation de la mobilité dans son ensemble, insiste Mohamed Mezghani : «  Ce qu'il faudrait, c'est favoriser un transfert modal vers la marche, le vélo, les transports publics.  »
Une transformation déjà engagée dans les grandes métropoles occidentales et qui profite non seulement au climat mais aussi à la qualité de l'air et donc à la santé publique.

items.title: Centrafrique: les avocats de cinq activistes détenus depuis mi-octobre alertent sur leur santé

original_payload.original_title: Centrafrique: les avocats de cinq activistes détenus depuis mi-octobre alertent sur leur santé
original_payload.original_body:
Centrafrique: les avocats de cinq activistes détenus depuis mi-octobre alertent sur leur santé
En Centrafrique, cinq acteurs de la société civile sont toujours détenus à la prison du camp de Roux, à Bangui, près d’un mois après leur arrestation. Interpellés le 15 octobre, dans le sillage de la journée « ville morte » contre la hausse des prix des carburants et la cherté de la vie, ils attendent désormais la suite de la procédure judiciaire. Leurs avocats s’inquiètent de la dégradation de l’état de santé de certains détenus. Leurs arrestations suscitent également de nombreuses réactions, y compris dans les rangs de l’opposition, de la société civile et de certains acteurs proches du pouvoir.
Publié le :  10/11/2026 - 10:17
2 min     Temps de lecture
Une vue de Bangui, capitale de la République centrafricaine.        © Rolf Steve Domia-leu/RFI
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Avec notre correspondant à Bangui,   Rolf Steve Domia-leu
Les cinq acteurs de la société civile arrêtés sont Quentin Ngouando, coordonnateur du mouvement I Gwé, Élysée Nguémalé, de l’Observatoire pour la gouvernance démocratique en   Centrafrique  , Steve Bendo, Barry Mardios et Igor Mokpem.
Leurs avocats alertent sur la dégradation de leur état de santé. Élysée Nguémalé souffrirait de fortes douleurs lombaires. Barry Mardios, atteint de tuberculose, aurait été placé à l’isolement depuis le 9 novembre.
Les conseils dénoncent également des conditions de détention difficiles, notamment le manque de lumière et d’hygiène dans les locaux de la Compagnie nationale de sécurité (CNS), avant leur placement sous mandat de dépôt à la prison militaire du camp de Roux.
Poursuivis pour troubles à l’ordre public et incitation à la désobéissance civile
Sur le plan judiciaire, les cinq hommes sont poursuivis notamment pour troubles à l’ordre public et incitation à la désobéissance civile.
Leur arrestation est vivement dénoncée par des organisations de défense des droits humains et des responsables de l’opposition, qui réclament leur libération.
De leur côté, les autorités évoquent des liens présumés avec des responsables politiques et des groupes armés, ainsi qu'un projet de renversement du pouvoir. Des accusations contestées par les mis en cause.
Un procès est donc nécessaire pour faire toute la lumière sur cette affaire. Mais aucune date n’a encore été officiellement annoncée.

items.title: RDC: en Ituri, les violences menacent les populations et la lutte contre Ebola

original_payload.original_title: RDC: en Ituri, les violences menacent les populations et la lutte contre Ebola
original_payload.original_body:
RDC: en Ituri, les violences menacent les populations et la lutte contre Ebola
En Ituri, dans le territoire de Djugu, les violences armées menacent à la fois les populations civiles et la lutte contre Ebola. Le coordonnateur humanitaire par intérim des Nations unies en RDC, Alain Akpadji, tire la sonnette d’alarme après de nouveaux affrontements signalés depuis dimanche 8 novembre dans la zone de santé de Fataki. L’insécurité perturbe également les opérations humanitaires et sanitaires. Une situation particulièrement préoccupante dans une province qui concentre près de 70 % des cas confirmés d’Ebola.
Publié le :  10/11/2026 - 08:47
1 min     Temps de lecture
Une vue de l'hôpital général de Fataki, dans le nord-est de la RDC.        © Coralie Pierret/RFI
Par :
RFI
Publicité
avec notre correspondant à Kinshasa ,  Pascal Mulegwa
La situation sécuritaire compromet désormais les opérations d'assistance dans cette partie de l'Ituri. Selon le Bureau de la coordination des Affaires humanitaires des Nations unies, une mission d'évaluation humanitaire, qui était en cours dans la zone, a dû être suspendue en raison de l'insécurité. Autre conséquence : les restrictions de mouvement imposées aux acteurs humanitaires depuis la fin du mois d'octobre compliquent davantage l'accès aux populations vulnérables.
Le site de Plaine Savo, situé près de Fataki, accueille à lui seul plus de 76 000 personnes déplacées. C'est à proximité de ce site que les affrontements du 8 novembre entre groupes armés ont fait au moins cinq blessés parmi les civils. Des tirs ont également été signalés dans la cité de Fataki, à environ 25 kilomètres de là.
Pour Alain Akpadji, coordonnateur humanitaire par intérim des Nations unies en RDC, il est urgent que toutes les parties respectent le droit international humanitaire, protègent les civils et garantissent la sécurité ainsi que la liberté de mouvement des personnels humanitaires et sanitaires. L'enjeu est aussi sanitaire.
L'Ituri, qui compte plus d'un million de déplacés, représente environ 70 % des cas confirmés d'Ebola en   RDC  . L'accès rapide et sans entrave des équipes de riposte est donc essentiel pour protéger les populations et sauver des vies.
À lire aussi  Ebola: deux nouveaux vaccins contre la souche Bundibugyo vont être prochainement testés en RDC

items.title: Madagascar: le chef de l'État fait le point sur la concertation nationale et le calendrier électoral

original_payload.original_title: Madagascar: le chef de l'État fait le point sur la concertation nationale et le calendrier électoral
original_payload.original_body:
Madagascar: le chef de l'État fait le point sur la concertation nationale et le calendrier électoral
Après la chute du président Andry Rajoelina en octobre 2025, les nouvelles autorités ont promis une grande concertation nationale pour réformer les institutions, puis des élections en 2027. Mais cette concertation n’a pas encore vraiment commencé. Ce 9 novembre 2026, le chef de l’État a présenté la restitution des premières discussions préparatoires, consacrées aux élections. Une étape pourtant préliminaire : le pays est encore loin d’un calendrier électoral.
Publié le :  10/11/2026 - 09:48
2 min     Temps de lecture
Écouter - 01:19
[Image d'archives] Le colonel Michael Randrianirina à Antananarivo, Madagascar, le 17 octobre 2025.        © AP/Brian Inganga
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Avec notre correspondante à Antananarivo,   Aurélie Kouman
En ouvrant les travaux, le colonel Michaël Randrianirina a défendu la démarche : «  Elle traduit notre ferme volonté de privilégier le dialogue, l’écoute et l’échange avec l’ensemble des forces politiques du pays afin d’accélérer le processus électoral.  » Il a aussi rappelé que le calendrier électoral devait être respecté.
Première question sur la table : l’ordre des scrutins. Le 4 novembre, la Haute Cour constitutionnelle (HCC) s’est prononcée en faveur d’un référendum constitutionnel avant la présidentielle. Le projet de loi de finances 2027 prévoit des crédits pour les deux scrutins. En mai, la commission électorale avait proposé un référendum en juin 2027 et une présidentielle en octobre. Rien n’a été officialisé depuis.
À lire aussi  À Madagascar, le processus de concertation nationale accumule les retards
Le programme de transition remis à la Communauté de développement de l’Afrique australe (SADC) prévoit une présidentielle avant fin 2027. En juin, cette organisation régionale avait exhorté   Madagascar   à respecter un calendrier «  précis  » et «  transparent  ».
Dans la salle, certains acteurs de la société civile s’inquiètent d’un référendum précipité. «  On ne peut pas faire un référendum si les électeurs qui vont voter ne connaissent même pas la Constitution qu’ils vont voter  », estime Jacques Randrianirina, président de l’organisation Servir Mada. Il plaide pour une éducation citoyenne «  depuis le fokontany  », l’échelon administratif de base dans le pays.
Parmi les participants figurent aussi des jeunes qui ont manifesté en septembre 2025. Miangola Razafindrakoto appelle sa génération à s’impliquer : «  Si moi je ne prends pas position et toi non plus, qui va prendre position pour nous les jeunes ?  »
«  Nous n’avons toujours pas d’agenda clair  »
D’autres participants se montrent plus sceptiques face à une réunion annoncée comme une restitution, mais qui s’est transformée en nouvelle séance de questions, avec des décisions prises à main levée. «  Le régime est censé être la tête de proue, mais nous n’avons toujours pas d’agenda clair  », confie l’un d’eux, sous couvert d’anonymat.
En parallèle, la concertation nationale menée par les Églises, censée poser les bases de la refondation des institutions, prévoit sa phase finale entre mars et mai 2027. La veille de la réunion, le chef de l’État a lui-même reconnu qu’elle accusait du retard. Les débats d’Ivato se poursuivent ce mardi.

items.title: Génocide des Tutsis en 1994: un Rwandais expulsé des États-Unis

original_payload.original_title: Génocide des Tutsis en 1994: un Rwandais expulsé des États-Unis
original_payload.original_body:
Génocide des Tutsis en 1994: un Rwandais expulsé des États-Unis
Emprisonné aux États-Unis puis renvoyé au Rwanda : l'auteur présumé de plusieurs crimes durant le génocide des Tutsis au Rwanda en 1994 est arrivé le 9 novembre 2026 à Kigali après son expulsion par les autorités états-uniennes. Jean Léonard Teganya avait été arrêté par la police en 2014 alors qu'il était en fuite. Condamné pour avoir menti aux services d'immigration et pour parjure, il a purgé sa peine avant d'être renvoyé au Rwanda où il devrait en principe être poursuivi pour son rôle durant le génocide.
Publié le :  10/11/2026 - 09:56
2 min     Temps de lecture
Vue de Kigali, au Rwanda, le 13 octobre 2026.        © Yuhi Irakiza / AP
Par :
RFI
Publicité
C'est la  National Public Prosecution Authority  (NPPA), l'autorité judiciaire rwandaise, qui annonce le retour de Jean Léonard Teganya, inculpé par la justice de son pays depuis 2014 pour crimes contre l'humanité durant le   génocide des Tutsis en 1994  .
Au moment des faits, cet homme de 55 ans était interne à l'hôpital universitaire de Butare, dans le sud du   Rwanda  .
Congo, Kenya, Inde, Canada puis États-Unis
Il était parvenu à fuir le pays après le génocide, passant par le Congo, le Kenya et l'Inde, avant d'atterrir au Canada cinq ans plus tard, où il s’est présenté comme un survivant et non comme un bourreau.
Mais une longue enquête a dévoilé le passé de Jean Léonard Teganya et l’a poussé de nouveau à fuir dans le nord-est des États-Unis cette fois, où il a été interpellé - dans l'État du Maine - en 2014.
Son procès détaille son appartenance à la milice hutue des Interahamwe et la manière dont il se servait de l'hôpital où il était interne pour piéger des Tutsis. Les preuves montrent que Teganya a participé au meurtre de sept personnes et au viol répété de deux femmes, tous cachés dans l'établissement.
Condamné pour fraude à l'immigration et parjure
Malgré tout, la justice américaine l’a condamné uniquement pour avoir menti sur son passé aux services de l'immigration.
Après plus de sept ans de prison aux États-Unis, il devrait désormais être poursuivi au Rwanda.
À écouter aussi  L'art de raconter le monde - «Kwibuka, se souvenir», le génocide rwandais en héritage

items.title: DR Congo: 66 soldiers sentenced to death for cowardice in conflict with FRN rebels

original_payload.original_title: DR Congo: 66 soldiers sentenced to death for cowardice in conflict with FRN rebels
original_payload.original_body:
Conflicts   Democratic Republic of Congo
DR Congo: 66 soldiers sentenced to death for cowardice
Elizabeth Schumacher   with local media
11/10/2026  November 10, 2026    Dozens of defendants were put on trial over accusations that they abandoned their posts and refused to follow direct orders.
https://p.dw.com/p/5PHPG
Prefer DW on Google
This is not the first time Congolese troops have been sentenced to death for abandoning their posts Image: Alain Uaykani/Xinhua/IMAGO       Advertisement
Some 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death in  DR Congo  on charged of cowardice, mutiny, and failure to obey orders. The sentence was handed down by the Goma Garrison Military Court.
At least 71 members of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) were arrested in several separate incidents related to the fierce fighting between the military and rebel groups near the country's borders with Uganda, Rwanda, and Burundi.
They were arrested on allegations of abandoning their posts or running away from clashes with FRN rebels. Prosecutors had sought capital punishment for 70 of the defendants, while asking for a 10-year jail term for an intelligence officer. The court, however, acquitted four defendants,
Major Dieudonne Kasereka, head of communications for FARDC in the affected region, said that the charges were necessary to reinforce discipline in the country's embattled North Kivu and South Kivu regions.
What is the FRN?
The Front for the Refoundation of the Nation is an umbrella group of rebels that also includes the  March 23 Movement (M23)  and Alliance River Congo (AFC).
The group's origins can be traced back to the Rwandan genocide in 1994 and the ensuing ethnic conflict, as it emerged from the Congolese Tutsi militias of the time.
It is led by  former DR Congo President Joseph Kabila . When current President Felix Tshisekedi came into power in 2019, Kabila found himself increasingly ostracized politically and went into self-imposed exile in an area occupied my what was then M23. Further complicating the conflict is the involvement of the FDLR rebel group, an ethnic Rwandan Hutu militia also active in South Kivu.
Although Rwanda's strongman president Paul Kagame denied involvement in the conflict, both DR Congo and many in the international community held that evidence of Rwandan involvement was clear. Indeed, Rwanda was involved in  the 2025 US-brokered peace deal  — which was seen as mostly serving US economic interests and doing little to resolve the long-running conflict.
Earlier this year, the United Nations condemned FRN and Rwandan soldiers for "murder, torture and other ill-treatment, corporal punishment, forced unlawful recruitment and abusive labor, and use of child soldiers."
M23 rebels continue push into DRC despite Trump peace deal

items.title: Africa's fight against fake news: Who decides what's true?

original_payload.original_title: Africa's fight against fake news: Who decides what's true?
original_payload.original_body:
Education    Africa
Africa's fight against fake news: Who decides what's true?
Antonio Cascais
11/09/2026  November 9, 2026    From Ghana to Mozambique, the fight against fake news keeps gaining momentum. But combating disinformation also requires safeguards for free speech, leaving some governments in an inconvenient position.
https://p.dw.com/p/5P8sx
Prefer DW on Google
In junta-run countries like Burkina Faso, fact-checking initiatives like Fasocheck are under increased government scrutiny Image: Boureima Salouka/DW       Advertisement
Misinformation threatens democracy worldwide: An exaggerated  WhatsApp  message, a manipulated  TikTok  video or an apparent breaking news alert on Facebook can mislead people in Africa and beyond — particularly in the run-up to elections.
As  artificial intelligence  is making it increasingly easy to manipulate images, voices and videos, more and more countries are trying to equip their populations with skills to identify and counter  fake news .
But are these efforts really about raising awareness, or are certain governments using this fight to control public opinion, silence dissident voices and misguide the populace — from both within and outside of these respective nations?
Civil society groups fill gaps left by governments
Journalism lecturer Dani Madrid-Morales at the University of Sheffield believes that African governments must significantly step up their efforts to combat sources of disinformation and misinformation.
He told DW that "there are very few countries — if any — that are actually doing a good job" of beating the influence of fake news.
Dani Madrid-Morales believes that civil society has an important role to play in fighting disinformation Image: Privat
Meanwhile, he points out that there also are civil society initiatives in various African nations, which help inform people about the dangers of such false narratives.
For instance, in South Africa, organizations like Africa Check and Media Monitoring Africa work together to highlight the impact of fake news on elections. Similar coalitions also exist in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Senegal.
However, these initiatives mostly focus on fighting disinformation during election periods; the rest of the time, they typically lack funding and sustained engagement with civil society to continue to make a change.
When African governments become part of the problem
There are also deliberate efforts by certain governments not to battle fake news; some let it happen while others engage in deliberately spreading this kind of disinformation.
Madrid-Morales distinguishes between three types of disinformation in this context: There are scams and similar schemes, which some governments, he says, fail to sufficiently fight, leaving people susceptible to financial losses and other problems.
Secondly, he adds that there also are certain foreign influence operations trying to impact public opinion from outside a country and, in many instances, outside of the continent.
Finally, there are political disinformation campaigns which originate from within a country that are intended to deliberately derail impartial views, he explains.
"Governments are particularly interested in the third category," says Madrid-Morales, adding that this is especially prevalent in the Sahel region.
He highlights how in nations like Burkina Faso and Mali, military governments have shut down media outlets, prosecuted journalists and expelled foreign correspondents to silence  free speech .
In his view, these junta governments are primarily concerned with preventing negative or false information about themselves from circulating rather than actively recruiting followers.
Why we need fact-checking more than ever
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that  supports HTML5 video
Do outside forces shape public opinion in Africa?
Foreign powers meanwhile also appear to play a considerable role in shaping public opinion across the continent.
Afrobarometer, a pan-African research network, examined the influence of international actors in terms of their influence across Africa — including those suspected of sharing fake news.
The study found that over 60% of respondents viewed China's political and economic influence positively; this was followed by 52% for the United States.
Both countries have no past colonial history in Africa, although they are now competing for economic gains while focusing otherwise on furthering infrastructure projects — partly to maintain this largely benevolent perception towards them.
However, perceptions of other former colonial powers vary notably in some cases, depending mainly on factors such as the impact of past injustices: For example, in French-speaking countries, only 34% of respondents viewed France's ongoing influence positively.
Komi Amewonou from  Afrobarometer      told DW that such attitudes are not necessarily the outcome of targeted propaganda campaigns for or against certain nations outside the continent but rather the result of African governments letting negative perceptions simply run their course.
Komi Amewonou stresses the dangers of foreign powers also influencing public opinion across Africa Image: Africa-Fact Summit 2026
The mixed role of media literacy initiatives
In some countries, there are media development projects trying to educate people and animate them to think for themselves and thus fight sources of fake news and disinformation.
In Ghana, the NGO Penplusbytes runs the " Caravan of Hope " initiative — a project supported by the German development agency GIZ and by DW Akademie.
This mobile campaign brings media literacy training to rural communities through theater, role-playing exercises, public discussions and videos in local languages. The initiative has managed to reach 3,000 people in five districts to date.
The campaign also involves trusted community figures, as studies show that locals most trust people they know personally — particularly traditional village leaders and community representatives.
Rebecca Avusu from Penplusbytes, who helped develop the project, told DW that "information must be verified before people believe it or pass it on. This is particularly important for those without smartphones or with limited formal education."
This event in the village of Odomase is part of the "Caravan of Hope" media literacy project in Ghana Image: Penplusbytes
Initiatives in South Africa take a similar approach: The country is home to Africa Check — one of the continent's best-known  fact-checking  initiatives.
The organization visits schools and teaches classes how to identify manipulated images, verify sources, and deal with misinformation circulating on WhatsApp groups.
However, Madrid-Morales says that there can be a downside to such media literacy programs as well; pointing to research conducted in South Africa, he highlights that while some young people do become more discerning consumers of information, others eventually lose trust in almost every source, resulting in a complete lack of knowledge about important developments.
Limited powers elsewhere in Africa
In countries elsewhere in Africa, there's greater resistance against such media literacy initiatives — chiefly by their own governments.
In 2026, the International Media and Information Literacy Institute (IMILI) was opened in the Nigerian capital Abuja under the auspices of UNESCO, with a mission to promote research, training and international cooperation across media literacy initiatives.
This came after the Nigerian government announced that it aimed to play a leading international role in Africa in the fight against fake news; however, civil rights groups say the state often blurs the line between genuinely battling disinformation and silencing public dissent in the country.
Rebecca Avusu, project coordinator of "Caravan of Hope," incorporates local leaders in media literacy projects Image: privat
In Kenya, there are similar concerns: T  he Media Council of Kenya has been tasked with supporting journalists and boosting fact-checking initiatives.
However, its scope of operations is limited, as the  organization abides by the country's laws to remain in operation — in particular legislation supposedly designed to target the spreading of  false information .
Conversely, these laws have come under increased scrutiny, as they can also be abused to silence views against the government.
Madrid-Morales says that in such contexts, there need to be independent oversight bodies to ensure that people do not refrain from expressing themselves publicly for fear of reprisal.
Mozambique: Fighting disinformation as a tool of control
Meanwhile in Mozambique,  the media institute MISA     has also launched a series of media initiatives such as MISACheck. The program is designed to train young journalists and social activists in fact-checking techniques.
Olivia Massango, the vice-president of MISA, says that the efforts of such civil society groups may seem like a drop in the ocean; Massango is particularly critical of how state authorities deal with misinformation.
"When something becomes inconvenient, the government ... invokes public interest, but ultimately often ends up protecting only what suits it," she told DW.
"Combating disinformation must not mean criminalizing opinions, criticism or journalistic work," she warns.
Olivia Massango highlights that governments can abuse fake news initiatives to suppress press freedom Image: Privat
Guidance from Europe — with limited safeguards
More and more African nations meanwhile are turning to Europe in hopes of adopting useful mechanisms to fight fake news.
Morocco and Senegal are among the examples where proposed disinformation legislation is widely inspired by EU standards. Madrid-Morales, however, stresses that while following strong EU legislation in the battle against disinformation can be a success, there also need to be independent oversight and enforcement mechanisms to make them work.
In the cases of Senegal and Morocco, these are yet to be established, he explains, stressing that both nations have repeatedly had to deal with various forms of political instability influenced by fake news.
Rebecca Avusu says she is also concerned about such efforts maintaining loopholes to suit governments if and as needed: "We do not want laws designed to combat disinformation to become instruments for silencing people who question government decisions or express legitimate opinions," Avusu warns.
A journalist's guide to spotting fake news

original_payload.original_title: Tompolo ​‌⁠‍‌‍‍⁠⁠‍‍​‍​⁠⁠⁠‍‌​donates 50 vehicles for Tinubu’s re-election in Enugu, C’River
original_payload.original_body:
Community  Tompolo ​‌⁠‍‌‍‍⁠⁠‍‍​‍​⁠⁠⁠‍‌​donates 50 vehicles for Tinubu’s re-election in Enugu, C’River
By  Dorcas Jonah   ·   4 hours ago   ·  5 min read
✓
✓
Tompolo ​‌⁠‍‌‍‍⁠⁠‍‍​‍​⁠⁠⁠‍‌​donates 50 vehicles for Tinubu’s re-election in Enugu, C’River
By Anita Uzoagba
The Grand Patron of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement, Chief Government Ekpemupolo, has donated 50 vehicles for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election campaign in Enugu and Cross River States.
Ekpemupolo, popularly known as Tompolo, disclosed this in a statement made available to newsmen on Monday in Abuja.
He said the vehicles were donated at separate campaign rallies in the two states on Monday, during the inauguration of the state chapters of the movement and distribution of campaign materials to the state coordinators.
According to him, the two states got 25 vehicles each.
He called on the people of Cross River to come out en masse and vote for Tinubu and all other APC candidates in the 2027 election.
Tompolo, who was represented by Kestin Pondi, Managing Director of Tantita Security Services, said the ongoing reforms were like the planting and harvest season and human gestation period.
He said that it would take some time but it was sure to yield positive results, provided the right steps were taken.
“Today, we no longer have fuel queues.
“We like to compare Nigeria with Asian countries that are doing well, like Malaysia and Indonesia, but one thing we forget to remember is that in those countries, reforms took over 25 or 35 years in some cases.
“Given the same conditions as we have in Nigeria, under which President Tinubu is operating, they may not have achieved what he has achieved in four years.
“If you want reforms like NELFUND, which is guaranteeing tertiary education for your children, more federal allocation to your state for projects and so on, you must re-elect Tinubu to continue,” he said.
Tompolo said it was wrong to start development and truncate it, “that is why we want you to vote APC candidates in all elections.”
Tompolo, who emphasised that the donation of vehicles was to support the states in their campaigns, said: “We will stand by you in this campaign. If the plan was to deliver 80 per cent, this should help you take it to 99 per cent.”
He described President Tinubu as a courageous leader who has taken difficult decisions from the beginning of his administration to reposition the Nigerian economy.
He expressed confidence that the ongoing reforms would deliver a brighter future for the country.
Tompolo said the campaign would cover wards, polling units, churches, mosques, markets and other public places, ensuring that the achievements and policies of the present administration are properly communicated to people across the country.
He also commended Gov. Mbah for projects and initiatives in the state, including road infrastructure, bus terminals, the command and control centre, international conference centre, smart schools, airport and Enugu Air.
In Cross River, the government pledged to mobilise voters in the state to deliver no less than 1.5 million votes for President Tinubu’s re-election in 2027.
According to latest data from the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Cross River State has 1,928,978 registered voters.
The statement quoted Gov. Bassey Otu as saying that Cross River was for Tinubu as a mark of appreciation for the developments he had brought to the state.
Otu listed the developments to include the Lagos-Calabar Super Highway, increased federal allocation which had ensured prompt salary payment and infrastructure development, among others.
Otu, represented by the Deputy Governor, Peter Odey, said it was also important to re-elect the president so that the state could regain its status as an oil-producing state.
He said President Tinubu would also ensure the actualisation of the Bakassi Deep Sea Port which the president will inaugurate on Nov. 13.
“If we don’t support Tinubu to be re-elected, we will miss a lot, so support for Tinubu is support for ourselves.
“If we were to give the president one million votes, the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement has made it 1.5 million because of the logistics support which will enable us to go deep into the corners of the state to campaign at every door,” the governor stated.
In Enugu, Gov. Peter Mbah, represented by his deputy, Ifeanyi Ossai, commended the movement for its investment in grassroots mobilisation, particularly its recruitment of members across electoral wards.
He said the Tinubu administration was working to address the challenges facing Nigerians, adding that the achievements recorded in the last three and a half years provided a basis for continuity.
Earlier, the National Coordinator of the Movement, Sunday Asuku, called on the people to get ready to make a loud statement with their PVCs in the 2027 election.
He pointed out that “Rome was not built in a day and here in Nigeria too, President Tinubu is doing it one step at a time and doing it well.”
He said what Nigeria needs now was continuity and consolidation of ongoing reforms, and so people should tell the opposition that there was no vacancy in Aso Rock.
Asuku urged Nigerians to consider the antecedents of the presidential candidates, insisting that Tinubu remains the best choice for the country. ( NAN )

items.title: Tinubu’s exception performance ’ll make it difficult to unseat him – Wike

original_payload.original_title: Tinubu’s exception performance ’ll make it difficult to unseat him – Wike
original_payload.original_body:
Politics  Tinubu’s exception performance ’ll make it difficult to unseat him – Wike
By  Philip Daniel Yatai   ·   11 minutes ago   ·  2 min read
✓
✓
By Philip Yatai
The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Mr Nyesom Wike, says it will be immensely difficult for opposition parties to unseat President Bola Tinubu in the upcoming 2027 general elections.
Wike said this in Abuja on Tuesday, after inspecting some ongoing projects within the federal capital territory.
He cited what he described as Tinubu’s undeniable and rich report card of infrastructure development across the country.
The minister said that the volume and pace of visible achievements delivered under Tinubu’s administration left very little room for political detractors to challenge the ruling party’s record.
“You can see clearly that it will be difficult to unseat the president today because the report card is obvious in terms of what he has done.
“Like I told you, this is our campaign. People ask what we are going to campaign with, but we have so many visible achievements all around us.
“There is no way residents of Abuja will see the kind of infrastructure we have provided and say they are not happy with the achievements of Mr President. It is second to none,” he said.
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the minister inspected the ongoing construction of Innet Southern Expressway, from  Area 1 roundabout to Games Village bridges; Southern Parkway, linking Oladipo Diya Road with Ring Road II.
He also inspected the ongoing construction of Arterial Road S1 project in Abuja to connect Ring Road II to the FCT Fire Service Station in the Kaura and Gaduwa district corridors.
Highlighting the rapid speed of execution on several key projects in the territory, Wike referenced the rapid transformation of the Southern Parkway project, which was flagged during the celebration of Tinubu’s third year in office.
“Within six to seven months, you can see what has been achieved. It is unimaginable and that is why we are very happy,” Wike said.
He pledged that the FCT administration remained on track to inaugurate at least 10 high-impact projects before the general elections scheduled for Jan. 16, 2027.(NAN)
Edited by Deborah Coker

items.title: Wike defends N10m incentive to councillors, slams critics over ‘bribery’ claims

original_payload.original_title: Wike defends N10m incentive to councillors, slams critics over ‘bribery’ claims
original_payload.original_body:
Politics  Wike defends N10m incentive to councillors, slams critics over ‘bribery’ claims
By  Philip Daniel Yatai   ·   5 minutes ago   ·  3 min read
✓
✓
By Philip Yatai
The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Mr Nyesom Wike, has defended his offer of a N10 million cash reward to councillors who successfully deliver their respective electoral wards to President Bola Tinubu in the 2027 election.
Speaking to newsmen in Abuja on Tuesday after he inspected some ongoing projects, Wike dismissed criticisms that the incentive amounts to vote-buying or bribery.
Wike insisted that critics and media analysts were confusing legitimate reward systems designed to drive hard work with corrupt practices.
Addressing the controversy sparked by his announcement during a town hall meeting in Kwali, Wike clarified that the monetary pledge was strictly a reward for political commitment and mobilisation, rather than funds earmarked to compromise voters.
“It is only trained journalists or reasonable persons who understand the difference between a reward and a bribe.
“You tell your son, ‘I want a first class from you. Get a first class, and you get a house or a brand new car.’ Just go and work hard.
“That is what we are bringing. I didn’t say take this money and go and buy voters; I said go and work and show commitment,” he explained.
Drawing a comparison to international political practices, Wike cited high-profile political incentives abroad, including recent public mobilisation initiatives in the U.S. by billionaire Elon Musk, to argue that rewarding performance is standard global practice.
The minister also turned his sights on media coverage, specifically criticising television anchors for framing political campaign incentives as illegal inducements while profiting heavily from political campaign advertisements.
“Votes buying is giving someone money to go and vote for a specific candidate.
“Media houses collect millions for prime-time advertisement slots to let voters know what candidates offer, but when you tell your constituents or party workers you will reward their hard work, critics call it bribery,” he said.
Wike highlighted the economic impact of the ongoing projects, noting that thousands of residents were currently gainfully employed and feeding their families through the administration’s infrastructure drive.
He maintained that the performance of  President Bola Tinubu speaks for itself and serves as the primary tool to win over voters.
“Look at the residences here now; look at the number of people that are employed, earning salaries and feeding their families. Our focus is to sell our program to the people,” he added.
Wike also dismissed allegations from opposition parties claiming that political opponents were given a level playing field to canvas for votes, possible denial of access to campaign facilities or restricted from holding rallies ahead of upcoming polls.
The minister insisted that democratic space remains open to all qualified participants.
“Who is not allowing the opposition to campaign? I know they held a rally the other day in a state stadium. In Rivers, I don’t think anybody has complained to you that we are not allowing them to campaign.
“Let them go to the main stadiums, mobilise, and talk to the people,” he said.
He reiterated that his current priority remains national development rather than partisan squabbles, calling on well-meaning Nigerians to support the President’s vision.
“What I am concerned about is the development of the country. You don’t need to play partisan politics before you contribute your quota to national development.
“Everybody who wishes this country well will naturally support what the President is doing,” Wike said. (NAN)
Edited by Sadiya Hamza

items.title: FG, ILO seek stronger coordination to tackle child rights violations ​‌⁠⁠⁠‍‍⁠⁠‍‍​‌‍

original_payload.original_title: FG, ILO seek stronger coordination to tackle child rights violations ​‌⁠⁠⁠‍‍⁠⁠‍‍​‌‍
original_payload.original_body:
General News  FG, ILO seek stronger coordination to tackle child rights violations  ​‌⁠⁠⁠‍‍⁠⁠‍‍​‌‍
By  Ndubisi Ijeoma   ·   1 hour ago   ·  4 min read
✓
✓
By Joan Nwagwu
The Federal Government and International Labour Organisation (ILO) have called for stronger coordination, accountability and grassroots engagement to tackle child rights violations across Nigeria’s communities.
The Federal Ministry of Women Affairs and Social Development and ILO made the call in Abuja on Monday at a National Technical Workshop, themed “Strengthening Child Protection Systems.”
The five-day workshop was organised by the National Child Rights Implementation Committee (NCRIC) in collaboration with the ILO, ECOWAS Commission and FMM West Africa II Project funded by the European Union.
Mrs Esuabana Asanye, Permanent Secretary of the ministry, said children continued facing sexual abuse, trafficking, child labour, child marriage, violence, neglect and online exploitation despite government interventions nationwide
Asanye was represented by Mr Andrew Ali, Director, Child Development Department.
She said: “child protection is a shared national responsibility and a fundamental obligation of all stakeholders. Every Nigerian child deserves to grow up in a safe and supportive environment.
“We must strengthen institutional capacity, technical competence and coordination mechanisms required to guarantee the protection, survival, development and well-being of every Nigerian child.
“The effectiveness of Nigeria’s child protection system depends significantly on institutions working together, coordinating interventions, sharing information and ensuring accountability for agreed commitments.
“These include institutional accountability among agencies.”
Asanye expressed concern over violence against children within families, citing a television report involving a woman who allegedly poisoned her co-wife’s two children, leaving one child dead, according to reports.
She identified the National Child Rights Implementation Committee (NCRIC) as the principal coordinating structure for implementing the Child Rights Act 2003 and related policies, currently undergoing review at national level.
She urged stakeholders to extend the workshop’s outcomes to State Child Rights Implementation Committees and Local Government Implementation Committees to strengthen child protection mechanisms nationwide, particularly within local communities.
“What we are doing here today must not end at the national level. The impact will be greater when extended to state and local government levels,” Asanye said.
Dr Vanessa Phala, ILO Country Director for Nigeria, said stronger institutional collaboration was essential to addressing child labour, trafficking, violence, exploitation and other violations affecting children nationwide.
Phala, represented by Dr Agatha Kolawole, National Project Coordinator, Support Free Movement of Persons and Migration(FMM), West Africa, called for coordinated action across sectors at every level nationally.
“Protecting children is not the responsibility of one institution alone. It is a collective responsibility requiring coordinated action across sectors and levels of governance,” Phala said.
Phala described child labour as both a child protection and labour rights issue, requiring collaboration among government institutions, schools, social welfare services, law enforcement agencies, social partners and workers’ organisations.
“Child labour remains both a child protection concern and a labour rights issue. Its elimination requires strong collaboration among relevant institutions, organisations, communities and families,” Phala said.
She commended Nigeria’s domestication of the Child Rights Act across several states and implementation of the National Action Plan for the Elimination of Child Labour, describing these as notable gains.
She also cited the Durban Call for Action and Marrakech Framework Principles as important frameworks supporting national efforts to protect children and eliminate exploitative labour practices across the country today.
Phala said the ILO remained committed to supporting Nigeria through the EU-funded Free Movement of Persons and Migration in West Africa Project and Netherlands-funded ACCEL Africa Project initiatives as well.
“Our success will not be measured by the number of meetings held or reports produced, but by the number of children protected from exploitation,” Phala said.
Also speaking, Co-Chair of NCRIC, MacJohn Nwaobiala, called for improved data collection, effective reporting systems and grassroots engagement, saying children remained exposed to neglect, exploitation and hazardous labour in communities nationwide today.
“Development starts at the grassroots, where many of the issues affecting children occur. We must understand their circumstances at local government and ward levels,” Nwaobiala said during the workshop today.
Nwaobiala acknowledged development partners’ support amid funding constraints and urged stakeholders to meet Nigeria’s reporting obligations to the United Nations, African Union and ECOWAS, improving accountability and compliance consistently nationwide.
He urged participants to translate workshop recommendations into practical interventions, strengthen advocacy and sustain coordination across national, state and local government levels to protect every child in communities nationwide effectively.(NAN) www.nannews.ng

items.title: Cleric urges Christians to embrace praise, thanksgiving to God

original_payload.original_title: Cleric urges Christians to embrace praise, thanksgiving to God
original_payload.original_body:
Religious  Cleric urges Christians to embrace praise, thanksgiving to God
By  Nefisetu Yakubu   ·   19 minutes ago   ·  4 min read
✓
✓
By Chidi Opara
Christians have been urged to cultivate the habit of praising and thanking God for His numerous blessings, protection and gift of life.
Rev. Chinedu Egere, Pastor-in-Charge of The Redeemed Evangelical Mission (TREM), Apapa Branch, Lagos, gave the advice at the 60th birthday celebration and 31 years of impactful ministry of Rev. Nathaniel Anwumabelem, Pastor of TREM Lifecamp Branch, Abuja.
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the celebration was held on Sunday in Abuja.
Egere said God deserved continuous praise and thanksgiving, noting that many people were quick to forget His goodness and mercy in their lives.
Taking his text from Psalms 103:1-4, the cleric said God had not only preserved Anwumabelem for 60 years but had also strengthened him in his pastoral ministry.
In a sermon entitled, “60 Reasons to Thank God”, Egere identified salvation, forgiveness of sins, healing, deliverance from destruction, good health, tender love, kindness and compassion as some of God’s benefits to humanity.
He thanked God for enabling the celebrant to live beyond Nigeria’s estimated life expectancy of 55 years and prayed for more fruitful years for him, his family and ministry.
Also speaking, Pastor Remi Olagunju, Vice-Chairman, Pentecostal Fellowship of Nigeria (PFN), described Anwumabelem as a man of impact.
Olagunju commended him for his contributions to the PFN and the positive impact of his service in the Christian community.
Similarly, Rev. Maxwell Gbinije, Pastor-in-Charge of TREM Utako and Coordinator of TREM Northern Zone 2, congratulated the celebrant.
He described Anwumabelem as a dedicated and exemplary leader who rose from being a youth coordinator at the church’s Apapa Branch to becoming a pastor.
Gbinije said the celebrant had remained committed and steadfast in his service to God.
Another TREM pastor, Rev. Emmanuel Awo of the Nyanya Branch, described Anwumabelem as a leader, mentor and team player whose life had positively influenced many people.
“I have known Anwumabelem for close to 30 years. He is always focused and dedicated in his service to God,” he said.
Pastor James Dagunduro of the Redeemed Christian Church of God (RCCG), Abuja, and brother-in-law to the celebrant, thanked God for his 60th birthday and 31 years of successful ministry.
Dagunduro said Anwumabelem had known God from an early age and remained committed to his faith without compromise.
He said the celebrant joined the pastoral ministry when there was little to show for it, adding that his priority had always been to please God.
“My prayer is that God will continue to bless him in the ministry,” he said.
Responding, Anwumabelem, who is also the Pastor-in-Charge of TREM Northern Zone 1, expressed gratitude to God for 60 years of mercy, grace and goodness.
He said God had sustained him through the challenges of life and ministry, adding that he had continued to depend on divine promises.
The celebrant also appreciated the Presiding Bishop of TREM, Dr Mike Okonkwo, for believing in him as a young man and entrusting him with the responsibility of pastoring a church branch in Northern Nigeria.
“God has been faithful all the way. All He said He would do, He has done. He is a good God; He is ever faithful,” he said.
Anwumabelem thanked the visiting pastors, church members, family and other guests for their support towards the success of the celebration.
Some church members also testified to the celebrant’s positive influence on their lives, saying his teachings, counsel and spiritual guidance had helped them grow in faith.
They described the celebration as a demonstration of God’s grace, a legacy of impact and a journey of faith.
They prayed for God’s continued protection, blessings and rewards for his integrity and commitment to ministry.
The highlight of the occasion was the cutting of the birthday cake and presentation of a special gift to the celebrant.(NAN)

items.title: BPP D-G tasks procurement officers on value for money, transparency

original_payload.original_title: BPP D-G tasks procurement officers on value for money, transparency
original_payload.original_body:
Business  BPP D-G tasks procurement officers on value for money, transparency
By  Abdulrahman Kadiri   ·   26 minutes ago   ·  3 min read
✓
✓
By Precious Akutamadu
Dr Adebowale Adedokun, the Director-General, Bureau of Public Procurement (BPP), has urged procurement officers to prioritise value for money, transparency and accountability to improve service delivery.
Adedokun made the call at the opening of the second batch of the Mandatory Continuous Public Procurement Capacity Development Training Programme on Monday in Port Harcourt.
Represented by Mr Nasir Bello, the Director, Civil Infrastructure Department, Adedokun said that the programme would boost the performance of procurement officers
He said that the training was organised to equip officers with procurement principles, processes, regulations and ethics in line with the Public Procurement Act 2007.
The D-G described public procurement as a strategic instrument for national development, economic growth and effective implementation of government policies.
Adedokun said that sound procurement decisions would ensure that funds allocated to hospitals, schools, roads, agriculture and security translated into quality services.
He urged the participants to distinguish between the lowest bid and the best evaluated offer, correct wrong practices, and pursue further professional development beyond obtaining training certificates.
He said that the bureau would monitor their performance after the training to ensure that lessons learnt translated into improved workplace practices.
Mr Nelson Ojougboh, the Coordinator, Training and Programmes, said that participants were selected through an advertised and rigorous process.
“This was done considering their professional levels, years of service, and schemes of service,” he said.
Ojougboh stated that the programme gave priority to junior officers in order to establish sound procurement practices early in their careers, and strengthen professional capacity within government institutions.
The coordinator described the participants as cooperative and compliant, adding that certification would depend on assessment performance rather than attendance alone.
Ojougboh said that the resource persons were screened by the bureau for competence and experience, and that participants could continue to seek professional guidance after completing the programme.
Mr Hamza Abdullahi, the Procurement Officer, Consumer Protection Tribunal, Abuja, said that the training would deepen his understanding of procurement processes and improve his competence in handling contract awards.
Abdhullahi commended the Federal Government for creating opportunities for procurement officers to network, exchange ideas and promote effective management of public funds.
Also another participant, Mr Chima Kingsley Awuruonu of Imo State University, Owerri, described the training as timely, saying that it will strengthen procurement practices, and promote value for money in public expenditure.
Awuruonu said that procurement officers’ decisions directly influenced the quality of hospitals, roads and other infrastructure delivered to citizens.
Shekina Lamb, a Procurement Officer with Alex Ekwueme University, Enugu, said that the training would strengthen accountability, integrity, confidence and value-for-money practices in her professional responsibilities.(NAN)

By  Ndubisi Ijeoma   ·   22 minutes ago   ·  2 min read
✓
✓
By Ginika Okoye
The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) says the corporation has zero tolerance for diversion of funds realised from sale or recovery of failed banks’ assets.
Mr Oluyinka Ogungbemi, Director, Asset Management Department, NDIC, said this at the Stakeholders Seminar and Public Relations Workshop organised by the Asset Management Department (AMD) in Abuja on Monday.
Ogungbemi said that staff of the corporation do not have access to the assets funds.
The director added that asset realisation was the hardest part of banks’ liquidation, and that loan recovery was the most difficult of asset recovery.
”A loan that is not paid when the bank was in existence will not be easy when the bank is closed.
”We are are expected to recover assets  timely as delay erodes value because a loan not pursued becomes difficult to recover,” he said.
He said the workshop was aimed at ensuring higher loan and assets recovery thereby strengthening public confidence.
Ogungbemi urged the stakeholders to uphold their professional conduct in the discharge of their duties, stressing that the corporation had zero tolerance for funds diversion in banks’ assets recovery.
”This seminar is not a routine gathering, it is a deliberate one.
”It is part of the strategic initiative of the asset management department to improve asset realisation, and the first thing we aim to do is strengthen our relationship with you (stakeholders),” he said.(NAN)

items.title: FG moves to save $1.5bn through local milk production

original_payload.original_title: FG moves to save $1.5bn through local milk production
original_payload.original_body:
General News  FG moves to save $1.5bn through local milk production
By  Nefisetu Yakubu   ·   21 minutes ago   ·  4 min read
✓
✓
By Felicia Imohimi
The Federal Government is collaborating with stakeholders to validate a national action plan aimed at boosting local milk production and reducing the country’s annual 1.5 billion dollars dairy import bill.
The Minister of Livestock Development, Idi Maiha, said this at a validation workshop on the National Action Plan for the Promotion of Local Milk Production in Nigeria on Monday in Abuja.
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the workshop was organised by the Federal Ministry of Livestock Development (FMLD) in collaboration with the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS).
Maiha said reducing the import bill would require a practical and implementable action plan to build a modern, competitive and inclusive dairy sector.
He said the plan was anchored on the Nigeria Livestock Growth Acceleration Strategy (NLGAS 2025–2035), National Dairy Policy 2023–2028 and its implementation framework, as well as the Nigeria Livestock Master Plan and Livestock Sector Strategy 2026–2040.
Maiha said the era of holding conferences and workshops without tangible results in the dairy sector was over.
He urged stakeholders to move beyond discussions to implementing policies that would increase local milk production.
“Meaningful progress in the sector can only be achieved through direct engagement with farmers and other operators to identify challenges and develop practical solutions,” he said.
The minister expressed concern that Nigeria lacked reliable data on daily milk production, functional dairy cooperatives, their links with processors and challenges affecting milk collection and storage.
“How much have we done to reduce that $1.5 billion annual figure? How much milk are we making every day all over the country? That data is unavailable.
“So, whether import is going up or coming down, we do not know, because we have no evidence-based argument,” he said.
Maiha said the action plan must have clear priorities, designated implementing institutions, funded activities and measurable outcomes.
He outlined three priorities, including directing investment to commercially viable dairy-producing areas based on feed and water availability, farmers’ capacity, security, road access and demand from processors.
The second priority, he said, was addressing constraints to reliable local milk supply through year-round access to fodder and water, improved breeds, animal health services, extension support and quality control.
He identified the third priority as linking infrastructure to viable markets through milk collection and cooling centres managed by capable operators and supported by reliable off-take arrangements.
“We should invest in viable dairy businesses, not facilities that stand idle, because many dairy facilities built before independence are now moribund,” he said.
Maiha identified existing private-sector initiatives, including FrieslandCampina WAMCO’s farmer-centred programme, Nestlé Nigeria’s dairy development activities, and private farms operated by Arla, Integrated Dairies Ltd. and L&Z Integrated Dairy Farms, as foundations for expanding the sector.
He urged stakeholders to learn from Kenya, where cooperatives provide farmers with extension services on feeding, breeding, animal health and record-keeping, and Uganda, where private processors support milk collection, cooling and technical assistance for smallholder farmers.
“The lesson is straightforward: Connect farmers to advisory services, quality-based markets, and reliable buyers.
“Ensure the inclusion of women and youths in training, finance, technology and leadership,” he said.
Maiha assured stakeholders that the ministry would provide policy guidance, regulation and standardisation to support the sector.
He said the ministry would also work with investors and producers across the states, using quarterly dashboard reviews to monitor local milk procurement, quality, farmers’ incomes, private investment and the participation of women and youths.
“Let us create a plan that is ambitious in purpose and realistic in execution, one that strengthens livelihoods, expands safe milk supply, and makes Nigeria’s dairy sector more competitive and focused on national self-sufficiency,” he said.
He added that 21 states now had ministries of livestock, indicating readiness for coordinated action.
Earlier, the ministry’s Permanent Secretary, Dr Chinyere Akunjobi, said Nigeria spent more than 1.5 billion dollars annually on dairy imports in spite of its enormous livestock potential.
Akunjobi, represented by Dr Victor Egbon, Director of Ruminant and Monogastric Department, said the action plan would address major challenges affecting the industry.
She listed the challenges to include inadequate access to improved dairy breeds, quality feed, veterinary services, milk collection and processing facilities.
She called for increased private-sector investment and stronger capacity-building support for farmers.
Also, Dr Soule Goura, Coordinator, Milk Offensive Project, Agriculture and Rural Development, ECOWAS Commission, commended Nigeria’s efforts to develop the action plan.
He said Nigeria was a major dairy producer in West Africa, adding that the country played an important role in regional dairy development. (NAN)
FUA/TAK
Edited by Tosin Kolade

items.title: Nigeria trade chair urges Africa to harness economic integration for global trade power

original_payload.original_title: Nigeria trade chair urges Africa to harness economic integration for global trade power
original_payload.original_body:
Economy/Business  Nigeria trade chair urges Africa to harness economic integration for global trade power
By  Nefisetu Yakubu   ·   6 minutes ago   ·  3 min read
✓
✓
​‌‌​‍​​‍⁠⁠‍‍By Vivian Emoni
Prof. Ngozi Egbuna, World Trade Organisation (WTO) Chair for Nigeria, has urged African countries to translate the continent’s economic integration efforts into tangible prosperity through effective trade policies and implementation.
Egbuna, also Director, International Centre for Regional Integration and Trade Research (ICRITR), Nnamdi Azikiwe University, Awka, said this at a conference on Africa and Geoeconomics of African States, Integration, Power and Structural Transformation, on Monday in Abuja.
She said Africa must move beyond signing trade agreements to ensuring businesses trade successfully across borders, create jobs and retain economic value.
She called for stronger African trade cooperation to improve the continent’s influence in global economic affairs.
She described the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) as an unprecedented opportunity to change the continent’s position in the global economy.
Egbuna the host of the event, however, emphasised that signing agreements and establishing a continental market would not automatically translate into economic benefits without effective implementation.
According to her, the real test of AfCFTA lies in the ability of African businesses to trade successfully across borders, create jobs and retain economic value.
Egbuna urged Africa to move from supplying raw materials to shaping global trade rules, controlling value chains and influencing international economic decisions.
She described the African Trade Group of WTO Chairs as an important intellectual and policy platform for advancing African perspectives in global trade discussions.
She urged African scholars to ensure their research informed public policies, influenced trade negotiations and contributed to practical solutions rather than remaining confined to academic journals.
Egbuna challenged participants to examine how AfCFTA could become an instrument of economic power, strengthen Africa’s collective negotiating capacity and benefit manufacturers, farmers, entrepreneurs, women and young people.
She said the questions were not merely academic but directly concerned livelihoods and the economic future of African countries.
Prof. Pat Utomi, Founder/CEO, Centre for Values in Leadership (CVL), however, noted the paradox of Nigeria and the Democratic Republic of Congo possessing critical minerals while recording some of the world’s highest levels of poverty.
He described the fight against poverty as humanity’s greatest challenge, stressing the need to understand why some countries prosper while others remain poor.
Utomi said his longstanding academic interest had centred on understanding the factors responsible for economic inequality among nations.
He said quality education and healthcare were essential components of human capital development and critical to improving national productivity.
Utomi also identified entrepreneurship as an important driver of prosperity, noting that societies must encourage risk-taking, innovation and value creation.
He emphasised that culture and leadership played significant roles in shaping national development, adding that leaders were responsible for setting the tone of society.
He said he had come to appreciate trade as another critical factor in understanding the prosperity of nations. (NAN)
VOE/VIV

Economy/Business  NDIC insists on timely, transparent valuation of failed banks’ assets, engages stakeholders
By  Ndubisi Ijeoma   ·   9 minutes ago   ·  2 min read
✓
✓
By Ginika Okoye
The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) has engaged all stakeholders involved in the business of assets management to facilitate timely, credible valuation and transparent disposal of failed banks’ assets.
Mr Thompson Sunday, the Chief Executive Officer of NDIC, said at the Stakeholders Seminar and Public Relations Workshop, that delay in asset recovery could erode value.
Sunday, represented by Mr Oluyinka Ogungbemi, the Director, Asset Management Department of the Corporation, said the aim of the engagement was to broaden collaboration with stakeholders’ to improve failed banks’ assets recovery.
He said the workshop was aimed at ensuring higher loan and assets recovery and strengthening public confidence.
Sunday urged the stakeholders to uphold their professional conduct in the discharge of their duties, adding that the Corporation had zero tolerance for funds diversion in banks’ assets recovery.
”This seminar is not a routine gathering, it is a deliberate one.
”It is part of our strategic initiative of the Asset Management Department to improve asset realisation.
”’The first we aim to do is to strengthen our relationship with you (stakeholders).
”Secondly, we want to listen to you, to collate your feedback on the real challenges you face in the field while working for us.
”The ​‌‌‌⁠​​‍⁠⁠‍‍​‌‍‍‌‍‍‌​third reason is the fact that we hope that after the seminar, we will be able to onboard new stakeholders to this very important national assignment,” he said.
Sunday listed three classes of failed banks’ assets recovered by the Corporation to include risk assets, physical and investment assets.
He said that over and under valuation of some banks’ assets were challenges.
According to him, we have valuations that are like over the board and this makes it difficult for you to realise those assets when you test the market.
”So we need to agree on the valuation methods such that recovery is going to be much much easier,” he said.
Chukwuemeka Ani, the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Branch Chairman of the Nigerian Institute of Estate Surveyors and Valuers (NIESV), said the institute had a cordial working relationship with the NDIC.
Ani said the workshop would help facilitate better and more fruitful relationship between the Corporation and the institute.
The workshop was organised by the Asset Management Department (AMD) of the Corporation. (NAN)

items.title: Cotonou Comedy Festival 2026 : Le Bénin renforce son ambition de faire de l’humour une véritable industrie culturelle (Cotonou, Abomey-Calavi et Parakou accueille les activités du 1er au 6 décembre 20

original_payload.original_title: Cotonou Comedy Festival 2026 : Le Bénin renforce son ambition de faire de l’humour une véritable industrie culturelle (Cotonou, Abomey-Calavi et Parakou accueille les activités du 1er au 6 décembre 2026)
original_payload.original_body:
Après une première édition couronnée de succès, le Cotonou Comedy Festival revient en 2026 avec des ambitions renforcées. À l’occasion d’une conférence de presse organisée le lundi 9 novembre 2026 à Cotonou, le Gouvernement et son partenaire JokeNation ont présenté les grandes orientations de cette deuxième édition, qui entend contribuer à la détection des talents, à la professionnalisation des acteurs et au rayonnement de l’humour africain à l’international.
Promouvoir la création artistique, révéler les talents et renforcer la présence du Bénin sur les grandes scènes culturelles internationales. C’est l’une des ambitions portées par le Gouvernement à travers sa politique culturelle, dont le développement de la filière de l’humour constitue désormais un des axes d’intervention. Cette orientation a été réaffirmée lors de la conférence de presse consacrée à la deuxième édition du Cotonou Comedy Festival.
Représentant le Ministre de la Culture, des Arts et du Patrimoine, le Directeur de cabinet, Monsieur Bienvenu O. HOUNWANOU, a rappelé la genèse de ce festival, né d’une Convention signée entre le Bénin et le groupe JokeNation. Il s’inscrit dans la politique du Gouvernement en faveur des industries culturelles et créatives (ICC). « Ce partenariat est une école que nous co-construisons. Des talents sont détectés et des humoristes béninois sont formés. Des techniciens de l’image et du son travaillent aux côtés d’équipes internationales. Des professionnels de l’évènementiel et de la communication apprennent à produire et à promouvoir un festival de standard mondial. Notre objectif est simple : que, demain, une expertise locale soit capable de porter ce type d’événement. » a-t-il entendre le Directeur de cabinet. Il a également souligné la portée institutionnelle de ce partenariat, qui traduit la volonté du Gouvernement de donner davantage de perspectives aux acteurs de l’humour et de contribuer à la structuration de cette filière artistique.
Prenant la parole à sa suite, Monsieur Grégoire FURRER, président du groupe JokeNation, organisateur du Montreux Comedy Festival et partenaire du Gouvernement béninois, a présenté les ambitions de cette nouvelle édition. Fort du succès de la première expérience, le Cotonou Comedy Festival 2026 entend franchir un nouveau palier avec une programmation enrichie, des initiatives de détection de nouveaux talents et des rencontres professionnelles autour des enjeux de développement et de structuration de l’humour. Il a dévoilé la programmation générale des différentes activités prévues du 1er au 6 décembre prochain à Cotonou, Abomey-Calavi et à Parakou. De la formation des talents à la soirée Panaf Comedy Club en passant par les Rencontres de l’humour africain, le Spectacle du Tremplin du rire, le Gala Sacrées Amazones et le Gala à deux, le Village du rire et la Soirée de clôture. Tout a été bien concocté pour positionner le Bénin comme la capitale de l’humour africain.
Au-delà de la dimension festive et du divertissement, le festival ambitionne de créer un environnement favorable à l'émergence de nouveaux talents, au renforcement des compétences et à la professionnalisation des acteurs. Le partenariat avec JokeNation vise également à accompagner la production d’un humour africain de qualité, capable de conquérir les scènes internationales.
