items.title: Mauritanie: le député d’opposition Dah Abeid démissionne en fustigeant une «corruption généralisée dans le pays»

original_payload.original_title: Mauritanie: le député d’opposition Dah Abeid démissionne en fustigeant une «corruption généralisée dans le pays»
original_payload.original_body:
Mauritanie: le député d’opposition Dah Abeid démissionne en fustigeant une «corruption généralisée dans le pays»
En Mauritanie, coup de tonnerre à l'Assemblée nationale : le chef de l'opposition a démissionné de son poste de député. Dans une déclaration, Biram Dah Abeid estime que le Parlement est devenu inefficace. Ce dernier dénonce vivement la corruption du gouvernement actuel et l'absence de poursuites judiciaires, contrairement au précédent quinquennat. Il annonce désormais qu'il mènera son opposition sur le terrain et par les voies légales. Cette annonce a été faite lors de la séance plénière du vote de confiance de la déclaration de politique générale du Premier ministre.
Publié le :  10/11/2026 - 13:54
2 min     Temps de lecture
Biram Dah Abeid posant pour un portrait à Nouakchott, le 12 mai 2024.        AFP - MICHELE CATTANI
Par :
RFI
Publicité
En   Mauritanie  , c’est une décision politique qui fait du bruit. Le député de l’opposition Biram Dah Abeid a annoncé ce 9 novembre 2026 sa démission.
L’ex-candidat à la présidentielle est un fervent militant, une   figure locale de l'abolitionnisme   dans un pays où l'esclavage, officiellement aboli en 1981, persiste alors que les autorités nient son existence.
Biram Dah Abeid a justifié sa démission en affirmant que la Mauritanie était gangrenée par la corruption.
«  Une   généralisation de la gabegie entretenue par le gouvernement actuel  »
Invité à s’exprimer à la tribune dans le cadre du débat sur la déclaration de politique générale du gouvernement présentée par le Premier ministre Moctar Ould Djay, Biram Dah Abeid a immédiatement indiqué : «  J’annonce ma démission, ma présence au sein de cette assemblée s’arrête aujourd’hui. Je remercie le peuple mauritanien pour sa confiance.  »
L’ex-député a utilisé l’ensemble de son temps de parole, neuf minutes, pour argumenter sa décision en dénonçant notamment «  la corruption généralisée dans le pays  », en affirmant que «  les prisons ne comptent aucun détenu inculpé pour corruption  ».
Le leader de l’opposition, un temps en exil au Sénégal, élu député en 2018 alors qu’il était en prison, a fustigé les autorités et dénoncé la «  généralisation de la gabegie entretenue par le gouvernement actuel  ».
«  Je m'opposerai au régime actuel par la lutte, sur le terrain  »
Biram Dah Abeid, qui a obtenu 22% des suffrages à la présidentielle de 2024, compte néanmoins poursuivre son combat. Devant les députés et le gouvernement il a en effet déclaré : «  Les débats au sein de l'actuel Parlement n'ont plus d'utilité. Je m'opposerai au régime actuel par des moyens légaux, par la lutte, sur le terrain.  »

items.title: Le Botswana veut doubler sa participation dans le leader du diamant De Beers

original_payload.original_title: Le Botswana veut doubler sa participation dans le leader du diamant De Beers
original_payload.original_body:
Le Botswana veut doubler sa participation dans le leader du diamant De Beers
Le président du Botswana, Duma Boko, a annoncé lors d'un discours à la Nation que son pays veut doubler sa participation dans De Beers, géant du diamant, qui est à vendre depuis deux ans et demi. Une manière d'accroître la souveraineté de cet État d'Afrique australe sur une activité diamantifère en grande crise et qui n'est pas sans risque pour les finances botswanaises.
Publié le :  10/11/2026 - 16:16
2 min     Temps de lecture
Une enseigne du groupe De Beers sur la façade du siège social du producteur de diamants à Gaborone, au Botswana, le 19 octobre 2026.        Reuters - Stringer
Par :
RFI
Publicité
On savait que le   Botswana  , déjà actionnaire principal de De Beers, voulait augmenter sa part dans le leader du diamant, dont la maison-mère, Anglo American, se sépare pour se recentrer sur les métaux de base comme le cuivre, dans un contexte de dégringolade des prix de la pierre précieuse – concurrencée par le diamant synthétique – et moins prisée par les Chinois.
Le président Duma Boko a fait cesser le suspense en annonçant que son pays passerait de 15 à 30 % de l'entreprise diamantaire, au sein d'un consortium d'investisseurs mené par l'ancien patron de De Beers, Gareth Penny. Ce consortium inclut aussi deux autres pays producteurs de diamant, l'Angola et la Namibie, et un pays acheteur, Oman.
À lire aussi  Le Botswana veut prendre le contrôle majoritaire du De Beers
Une opération délicate pour ses finances publiques
Ce consortium pourrait être rejoint par des acteurs privés comme le groupe suisse Richemont, propriétaire de l’entreprise du secteur du luxe Cartier. Mais, globalement, les pays producteurs auraient la majorité dans De Beers.
Le Botswana reprochait à Anglo American d'avoir déprécié le diamant naturel en créant, de son propre chef, une filiale diamants synthétiques.
Même si De Beers a perdu plus de la moitié de sa valeur en moins d'un an, le Botswana va devoir investir plus et devenir encore plus dépendant du diamant, qui représente déjà 60 % de ses exportations et un tiers de ses recettes budgétaires, ce que le Fonds monétaire international lui avait déconseillé de faire, il y a moins d’un an, étant donné l’état de ses finances publiques.
À lire aussi  Chronique des matières premières - De Beers perd de la valeur en pleine crise du secteur du diamant

items.title: Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse: Au Sénégal, une sensibilisation à la question des règles pour les athlètes

original_payload.original_title: Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse: Au Sénégal, une sensibilisation à la question des règles pour les athlètes
original_payload.original_body:
Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse: Au Sénégal, une sensibilisation à la question des règles pour les athlètes
Les Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) battent leur plein à Dakar, avec de nombreuses jeunes sportives en compétition. Mais il est un sujet dont on parle peu dans le sport : les règles. Douleurs, saignements abondants, parfois même absence de cycle… Pour certaines athlètes, c’est un tabou, et un défi au quotidien. Au Sénégal, des femmes se mobilisent pour une meilleure prise en charge.
Publié le :  10/11/2026 - 13:06
3 min     Temps de lecture
Écouter - 01:25
Une triathlète disputant les Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse de Dakar 2026, sur la plage de Saly Ouest.        OIS/IOC/Handout via REUTERS - Joel Marklund
Par :
RFI
Publicité
Avec notre correspondante à Dakar,   Juliette Dubois
Des règles abondantes, douloureuses. Ou, parfois, pas de règles du tout. Dans son cabinet, le docteur Sokhna Dioum, cardiologue et médecin du sport, reçoit des sportives confrontées à ces problèmes. Elle travaille aussi avec la fédération de handball. Et sur l’absence de règles, elle tient à alerter. «  Il faut vraiment ne pas se dire que l'absence de règles est forcément en rapport avec un bon niveau d'entraînement , souligne-t-elle.  Malheureusement, c'est ce que beaucoup de jeunes filles pensent. L'absence de règles peut cacher autre chose, notamment le fait que l'énergie qu'on utilise s'épuise régulièrement parce qu'on est ultra entraînés. Ça peut avoir pour conséquence de l'anémie, (et/ou) des fractures parce qu'il y a une fragilité osseuse  ».
Ancienne nageuse de haut niveau, Aminata Diakhaté participe au projet « En-jeux », qui met en lumière quinze sportives en marge des   JOJ 2026  . Il prévoit une exposition pour sensibiliser au cycle menstruel et au sport, les 13 et 14 novembre à Yoff. Aminata témoigne au micro de Juliette Dubois de l’impact important de son cycle sur sa pratique sportive.
«  Franchement, quand mes règles sont là, je suis fatiguée, je suis épuisée , témoigne-t-elle.  C'est comme si on m'avait fait courir un marathon ou un semi-marathon. Je suis complètement vidée, j'ai des maux de ventre atroces. Après, ça me fait des crampes pas possible, à tel point que je ne peux même pas me lever. Parfois, je préfère rester juste couchée  ».
Elle soupire : «  Avoir ce cycle à une période où tu dois être dans l'eau, ça te fait une sensation bizarre, comme si ça allait sortir. En fait, c'est ce qui te trotte dans ta tête. Tu as constamment peur. Lorsqu’il n'y a pas de compétition en cours, une des choses les plus difficiles, c’est de faire avec. Parce que je sais que quand ça arrive, je ne pourrai pas augmenter mon volume d'entraînement.  »
«  Femmes et jeunes filles sont les moins nanties dans le sport  »
Pour les sportives, de bonnes conditions d’hygiène sont tout aussi essentielles. Yaye Hélène Ndiaye dirige Kitamba, une entreprise qui commercialise des serviettes et des culottes menstruelles lavables, pour l’autonomie des femmes. Elle milite pour une meilleure prise en charge : «  Les femmes et les jeunes filles sont les moins nanties dans les sports, en général. Donc, ce que nous aimerions, c'est qu'il y ait quand même des lignes budgétaires attribuées et que, par exemple, des toilettes soient accessibles aux jeunes filles, qu'elles soient propres, qu'il y ait des produits d'hygiène, etc.  »
Yaye Hélène Ndiaye demande aussi une meilleure formation des coaches à la santé menstruelle, et plus d’efforts pour distribuer des protections hygiéniques.
«  Je n'ai eu que des coaches hommes, alors ce n'est pas quelque chose qu'on a l'habitude d'aborder, qu'ils vont comprendre. Donc, j'essaie juste de m'adapter. Et si je peux m'absenter, je vais m'absenter  », nous explique Aminata Diakhaté.
Pendant les JOJ, ce sont les fédérations sportives qui gèrent la question des règles. Le docteur Sokhna Dioum, avec la fédération de handball a fait le nécessaire, mais ce n’est pas le cas dans toutes les disciplines.

items.title: NBTE, IOM partner to boost global job opportunities for Nigerian youths

original_payload.original_title: NBTE, IOM partner to boost global job opportunities for Nigerian youths
original_payload.original_body:
Education  NBTE, IOM partner to boost global job opportunities for Nigerian youths
By  Funmilayo Adeyemi   ·   6 hours ago   ·  4 min read
✓
✓
By Funmilayo Adeyemi
The National Board for Technical Education (NBTE) has partnered with the International Organisation for Migration (IOM) to equip Nigerian polytechnic graduates with skills for global employment opportunities.
The NBTE Executive Secretary, Prof. Idris Bugaje, disclosed this at the opening of a three-day capacity-building workshop for polytechnics lecturers on Tuesday in Abuja.
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the workshop is centred on Industry-Aligned Skills Development for the implementation of Reviewed National Diploma (ND) curriculum in Electrical and Electronics Engineering.
Bugaje said the aim of the training was to upgrade technical education and equip Nigerian graduates with industry-relevant skills for employment opportunities locally and internationally.
He said the initiative would also improve the quality of technical education, enhancing the employability of Nigerian graduates and creating safe pathways for skilled youths to access international labour markets.
He explained that the initiative was an extension of the Nigerian Youth Skills Empowerment Programme (NYSEP), introduced by the board to facilitate employment opportunities for Nigerian polytechnic graduates in selected European countries.
According to him, the programme initially targeted Germany but was later redirected to Denmark and Poland following challenges associated with migration concerns.
Bugaje said the first screening exercise involving 580 Nigerian diploma holders produced only 25 successful candidates, prompting the board to review the existing electrical engineering curriculum.
He said the outcome raised concerns about the relevance of the curriculum to contemporary industrial requirements and the ability of graduates to compete in the global labour market.
“The Danish Ambassador asked me whether we were producing 21st-century electrical technicians or still using the curriculum of the last century.
“That was what prompted the review of the ND electrical engineering curriculum to make it digital and align it with the demands of global industries,” he said.
Bugaje said experts from Denmark were subsequently engaged to support the review, while the IOM offered to sponsor the training of lecturers and technologists responsible for implementing the revised curriculum.
He urged participants to take the three-day training seriously; stressing that effective curriculum implementation depended on the capacity of lecturers to translate its contents into practical skills.
He added that the training would include hands-on sessions in laboratories and workshops, with support from relevant industry partners.
The NBTE executive secretary said the initiative could expand beyond the initial target of 1,000 beneficiaries, providing more Nigerian youths with opportunities to acquire internationally recognised skills and qualifications.
He expressed optimism that graduates who acquired relevant skills and work experience abroad would return to Nigeria with improved expertise, resources and knowledge to support local industrial development.
Bugaje urged polytechnics to reclaim their role in driving industrialisation, noting that practical and technical education remained critical to Nigeria’s economic transformation.
“Give these young people a sense of hope that even if the Nigerian system is not working as it should, there can be opportunities for them overseas.
“Let them acquire the skills and funds, and then come back home so that we can build a resilient economy,” he said.
In her remarks, the IOM Chief of Mission, Sharon Dimanche, said the partnership was aimed at strengthening the connection between skills development, employability and safe, orderly and regular labour migration.
Dimanche, represented by the Head of Suboffice, North-East Nigeria, Ali Abdi, said the revised curriculum and capacity-building workshop were designed to prepare Nigerian youths for changing labour market demands and improve the competitiveness of the country’s workforce.
According to her, skills development is not merely an educational issue but an economic development imperative, particularly as employers increasingly seek workers with practical and technical competencies.
She said the revised curriculum would help address skills gaps in engineering, manufacturing, construction, information technology, renewable energy and other emerging industries.
She noted that lecturers and technologists played a critical role in ensuring that graduates acquired practical competencies, adaptability and problem-solving skills rather than mere academic qualifications.
She said the partnership would promote workforce preparedness for employment opportunities within Nigeria, across the ECOWAS region and internationally.
The event witnessed the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the IOM and NBTE as a strategic commitment to strengthening technical and vocational education, employability and skills recognition.(NAN)

items.title: Wike’s Rainbow Coalition pledges N10m reward for each FCT ward on Tinubu’s victory

original_payload.original_title: Wike’s Rainbow Coalition pledges N10m reward for each FCT ward on Tinubu’s victory
original_payload.original_body:
Politics  Wike’s Rainbow Coalition pledges N10m reward for each FCT ward on Tinubu’s victory
By  Philip Daniel Yatai   ·   6 hours ago   ·  5 min read
✓
✓
By Philip Yatai
Minister of Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Mr Nyesom Wike, has reiterated the Rainbow Coalition’s N10 million reward to each political ward in Abaji Area Council and other area councils if President Bola Tinubu wins in the 2027 presidential election.
Wike stated this on Tuesday during a consultative meeting of the All Progressives Congress (APC) and Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) under the Rainbow Coalition, to mobilise support for Tinubu’s re-election.
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the meeting was also organised to galvanise support for Sen. Philip Aduda who is vying for the Senate seat to represent FCT and Mr Danladi Chiya gunning for Abuja South Federal Constituency seat.
He explained that if the president won in all the wards in the area council, each of the 10 wards would receive a N10 million reward, all amounting to N100 million.
The minister described it as an incentive to make the stakeholders work harder to ensure overwhelming victory for the president.
He likened the high-stakes and incentive-driven strategy to performance bonuses offered to national sports teams.
Comparing the bounty to football motivation, Wike stated: “When Nigeria plays a match, they tell them: ‘Score one goal, get $50,000; win the match, get $300,000.’ It is to motivate them to play well and win.
“I want to motivate my people. I want Abaji to beat every other area council in turnout and results.”
He challenged ward leaders, councillors and the area council chairman to demonstrate their political machinery rather than relying on empty promises.
The minister made it clear that political relevance and rewards under his leadership would be strictly tied to polling unit results, saying, “If you win your ward for Tinubu, come and get your reward.”
He, however, added that any leader who lost his immediate polling unit or ward would forfeit his standing in the coalition’s victory.
“If a chairman loses his unit and we manage to win his ward, did that chairman really win? No!. You cannot lose your own immediate constituency and expect to sit at the table.
“Everyone must go back home and work. We must win all 135 polling units in Abaji,” he charged.
Beyond the presidential mandate, the minister also urged Abaji residents to support Aduda for the FCT senate seat and Chiya for Abuja South federal constituency.
He cautioned voters against repeating past electoral choices, referencing the incumbent senator representing FCT, who he claimed abandoned the territory after getting elected.
“In 2023, you went to the market and bought something that yielded no profit. Have you seen the person you elected again?
“Has she come back to ask what your problems are? Anywhere you see her, tell her ‘Auntie, bye-bye.’ Time is up,” Wike told the cheering crowd.
Taking a swipe at opposition figures, Wike dismissed political rivals as “social media contenders” who lacked the stamina, political stability and track record to govern Nigeria.
The Executive Chairman of the area council, Mr Abubakar Abdullahi, pledged to deliver the 135 polling units to Tinubu, Aduda and Chiya.
Abdullahi declared that Abaji remains a solid stronghold for the ruling party, Abdullahi assuring that the council’s entire voting block would be mobilised for Tinubu and APC National Assembly candidates.
Recalling his past electoral success, Abdullahi reminded the audience that during his chairmanship election, his structure secured victory in 133 out of 135 polling units.
“I want to assure you, by the special grace of God, in January 2027, we are going to collectively re-elect Tinubu, our Senate and House of Representatives candidates.
“I assure you that all 135 polling units across Abaji Area Council will be delivered 100 per cent to Tinubu and other APC candidates,” he said.
The chairman linked the grassroots commitment to Tinubu’s administration and the unprecedented developmental interventions of the FCT minister within the area council.
“No sitting FCT minister in history had visited Abaji four consecutive times within a single tenure. This is proof of the administration’s deep commitment to rural development,” he said.
In his remarks, APC Chairman in the FCT, Mr Ishaku Yamawo, praised Wike for dismantling long-standing partisan animosities across the territory and setting a foundation of unity that transcends party lines, tribe and religion.
“You’ve laid a foundation of unity; you’ve raised a pillar of unity for us in the FCT. Rival factions are now sitting, working and eating together in support of Wike’s coordination,” he said.
Similarly, his PDP counterpart, Mr Mohammed Dogara, commended the minister for extinguishing election-related violence in the region, noting that historically-turbulent zones like Abaji now enjoyed peaceful coexistence.
“PDP as a party in Abaji Area Council flings with you. We have already keyed into the Rainbow Coalition. FCT is positioning itself to deliver the highest voting margin for President Tinubu in 2027,” he said.
Speaking on behalf of the youth, Mr Abdu Lukman said that Wike’s performance on infrastructure and governance served as the strongest campaign for Tinubu, Aduda and Chiya in Abaji.
Lukman announced the unveiling of a book entitled: “The Wike Strategy: A Guide to Mastering Nigerian Politics” on a date to be decided by the minister.
Representing female farmers, traders and mothers across the council, Mrs Asiya Suleiman applauded Wike for establishing the FCT Mandate Secretariat for Women Affairs, noting that women were now feeling seen and heard for the first time.
Suleiman said that women formed the majority of voters and were already organising into ward-level clusters to guarantee a decisive victory for Tinubu and allied candidates in 2027. (NAN)

items.title: FMC Abuja treats 11 snake-bite cases amid El Niño concerns

original_payload.original_title: FMC Abuja treats 11 snake-bite cases amid El Niño concerns
original_payload.original_body:
Health  FMC Abuja treats 11 snake-bite cases amid El Niño concerns
By  Folasade Akpan   ·   4 hours ago   ·  4 min read
✓
✓
By Folasade Akpan
Prof. Saad Ahmed, Medical Director of the Federal Medical Centre (FMC), Abuja, says the hospital treated 11 snake-bite cases in 2026, urging residents to remain vigilant as temperatures rise.
Ahmed told the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) in Abuja that rising temperatures could drive reptiles from natural habitats towards cooler environments, increasing encounters with people in residential areas.
He said changing environmental conditions associated with El Niño could influence reptile movements, potentially increasing contact between snakes and humans, particularly as temperatures rise across different parts of the country.
“El Niño is a situation whereby we have an increase in environmental temperature arising from the rise in temperature around the Pacific,” Ahmed explained, describing the phenomenon’s environmental implications.
“With that, you expect some reptiles to actually be affected. Certainly, they will come out of their hiding in order to get cooler environments where they can live.
“In doing so, they can come in contact with humans, and if one mistakenly comes in contact with them without knowing, it can lead to an encounter,” he warned.
NAN reports that El Niño is a climate phenomenon characterised by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, influencing weather patterns and temperatures worldwide.
Ahmed attributed human-reptile encounters partly to environmental conditions, particularly indiscriminate development, poor sanitation and the accumulation of materials around residential buildings, which could provide suitable hiding places for snakes.
He explained that properly planned development should reduce spaces available for reptiles, while poorly maintained surroundings could create hiding places, increasing the likelihood of encounters between snakes and residents.
“Where we keep things indiscriminately, you are leaving some spaces where these reptiles can actually go and hide,” Ahmed said, urging residents to maintain clean and organised surroundings.
“If everywhere is clean, the reptiles will have no chance of living in that place, which means they have to move away from those areas,” he added.
The medical director advised residents to seek immediate medical attention whenever someone sustained a snake bite, emphasising that early treatment remained critical to preventing potentially life-threatening complications.
He explained that venom types varied according to snake species, with some affecting the nervous system and potentially causing respiratory failure, while others damaged blood cells, causing bleeding and organ failure.
“The most important thing is to get the person to the nearest hospital as soon as possible,” Ahmed said, emphasising the importance of prompt medical intervention.
Ahmed said FMC Abuja maintained stocks of polyvalent anti-snake venom, dismissing claims that the hospital had previously lacked the treatment following a snake-bite incident that attracted attention on social media.
He explained that the hospital administered two doses of polyvalent anti-snake venom to the patient involved, but treatment was complicated because the patient arrived after a considerable delay.
According to him, polyvalent anti-snake venom covers different snake species, while monovalent anti-snake venom is administered when the particular snake responsible for the bite is known.
He said the Federal Government had commenced distributing anti-snake venom to health facilities through the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, from which FMC Abuja currently sourced supplies.
“The earlier you institute the modalities of treatment by giving anti-snake venom and all the other supportive treatment, the better the outcome.
“If you are able to transmit the person in less than 15 to 30 minutes, that’s a very good time within which intervention can be taken,” he added.
Ahmed called for increased public awareness and research into snake-bite management, noting that the Federal Government had upgraded a health facility in Ogun into a specialist research centre.
He said the facility was expected to conduct research and explore the production of locally manufactured anti-snake venom, potentially strengthening Nigeria’s capacity to manage snake-bite cases.
The medical director cautioned residents against delaying hospital treatment in favour of traditional remedies, while supporting scientific research into traditional practices to establish their safety and effectiveness.
He also advised residents to take precautions against heat-related illnesses during periods of high temperatures, recommending adequate hydration, appropriate clothing and reduced exposure to direct sunlight.
“Try to wear light clothing, drink lots of water and avoid sunny places. Always look for shelter so that you don’t have dehydration and heatstroke.
“While the heat is there, let’s see how we can take care of ourselves and also be mindful that reptiles could come out within this period.
“Let’s keep our environment clean and be very vigilant,” he urged residents, emphasising the importance of environmental sanitation and awareness in preventing snake encounters.(NAN)
Edited by Abiemwense Moru

items.title: Under-17 World Cup: Edo commissioner urges parents to support girl-child in sports

original_payload.original_title: Under-17 World Cup: Edo commissioner urges parents to support girl-child in sports
original_payload.original_body:
Sports  Under-17 World Cup: Edo commissioner urges parents to support girl-child in sports
By  Folasade Akpan   ·   4 hours ago   ·  3 min read
✓
✓
By Osayi Aghahowa
Eugenia Abdallah, Edo Commissioner for Women Affairs and Social Development, has urged parents to encourage and support their daughters to develop their talents in sports.
Abdallah made the call in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) in Benin while congratulating the Flamingos on their victory at the FIFA Under-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco.
She described the team’s triumph as a source of joy and a demonstration of what young girls could achieve when given the necessary support and encouragement.
The commissioner said she was particularly delighted to see girls succeed and gain recognition rather than being marginalised or relegated to the background.
“I feel happy whenever I see the girl-child winning and making progress, rather than being marginalised or pushed to the background.
“That is what this ministry stands for and continues to fight for: ensuring that they are given the necessary support and opportunities to realise their dreams,” she said.
She urged parents not to discourage their daughters from playing football or participating in other sporting activities but to identify their interests and encourage them to develop their abilities.
Abdallah said many talented girls remained undiscovered because they had not been given opportunities to demonstrate their capabilities.
“Parents should recognise the potential in their children, encourage them and allow them to develop their talents rather than discourage them because they are girls.
“There are many talented girls out there whose abilities are yet to be discovered. We should give them the opportunity to explore their interests and excel in whatever field they choose,” she said.
She described the Flamingos’ victory as an inspiration to young women, noting that the players had demonstrated that dedication, discipline and determination could lead to excellence.
Abdallah commended the players, coaching crew and management of the team for their commitment and hard work, while acknowledging the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) for its support.
She called for sustained support for female participation in sports and other areas of endeavour, stressing that no child should be denied the opportunity to pursue an interest because of societal expectations.
The commissioner reaffirmed the ministry’s commitment to promoting the protection, development and empowerment of women and children.
NAN reports that the Flamingos defeated Japan 2-1 in the final of the FIFA Under-17 Women’s World Cup played on Saturday, Nov. 7, at the Mohammed VI Football Complex in Rabat, Morocco.
Awawu Bashiru opened the scoring for Nigeria in the 39th minute, while Oluebube Umejiaku doubled the lead in the 47th minute.
Fuki Ito scored Japan’s only goal in the 80th minute.
The victory made Nigeria the first African country to win the FIFA Under-17 Women’s World Cup and the first African women’s national team to claim a FIFA World Cup title at any level. (NAN)

General News  Wema ​‌‍⁠‌⁠‍⁠⁠‍‍​‌‌​‍‍‌‌​Bank rewards 11 innovators with N300m at Hackaholics 7.0
By  Olawunmi Ashafa   ·   28 minutes ago   ·  2 min read
✓
✓
By Joy Oyerinde
Wema Bank Plc says it rewarded 11 young Nigerian innovators with a combined N300 million at the seventh edition of its Hackaholics innovation programme for developing technology-driven solutions to challenges across various sectors.
The bank said this in a statement on Sunday in Lagos.
The competition, with the theme:   “Festival of the Future”  , attracted 5,329 participants who generated 1,632 ideas across seven pitch centres in Uyo, Kano, Yaba College of Technology  , Benin, Ibadan, Enugu and Lagos.
The overall winner, Tony Nwose, founder of Niteon, received the N60 million grand prize for developing an agricultural technology platform connecting farmers with processors, financial services and market opportunities.
In the Startup/Ideathon category, Emmanuel Adeboje of Acceede, emerged first runner-up with N40 million, while David Lawani of All-Arbitrates came third with N20 million for his digital alternative dispute resolution platform.
In the Social Impact category, Kabir Olaosebikan of Craft Planet won N40 million for converting plastic waste into sustainable building materials.
Samuel Shonubi of SocialSign received N30 million for his sign language technology, while Oluwaseyi Akinlolu of Harthio won N20 million for his mental wellness solution.
Under the Women-Led category, Zainab Adeagbo of MamaAlert received N20 million for her digital healthcare innovation, while Precious Zino of URI won N10 million for her artificial intelligence-powered marketing solution.
In the Hackathon category, Kelvin Nnadi of Neural Forge received N30 million for his artificial intelligence-powered medical diagnostic innovation.
David Campbell of Nexa AI won N20 million for his customer intelligence solution, while Uti Henry of Vhorde received N10 million for IRIS, an artificial intelligence-powered smart glasses innovation designed to assist visually impaired people.
The Managing Director of Wema Bank Plc, Mr Moruf Oseni, urged banks, investors and corporate organisations to increase funding and institutional support for Nigerian startups.
Oseni said Nigeria had enormous entrepreneurial potential but required improved financial and institutional support to transform innovative ideas into viable businesses.
He identified inadequate access to funding as a major constraint confronting startups, noting that capital, mentorship, strategic partnerships and business networks were essential to their growth.
He challenged financial institutions, investors and corporate organisations to provide more resources and opportunities for young entrepreneurs to develop and commercialise their innovations.
Oseni also urged the finalists to remain persistent, emphasising that entrepreneurial success required continuous learning, adaptability and responsibility toward customers.  ( NAN )

items.title: Contempt: Court orders substituted service of Form 48 on EFCC chairman

original_payload.original_title: Contempt: Court orders substituted service of Form 48 on EFCC chairman
original_payload.original_body:
Judiciary  Contempt: Court orders substituted service of Form 48 on EFCC chairman
A Federal High Court in Ikoyi, Lagos State, has ordered substituted service of contempt  of court processes to the Chairman of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), Mr Ola Olukoyede.
By  Afonne Emmanuel   ·   38 minutes ago   ·  3 min read
Court logo
✓
✓
By Sandra Umeh
A Federal High Court in Ikoyi, Lagos State, has ordered substituted service of contempt  of court processes to the Chairman of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), Mr Ola Olukoyede.
Justice Dehinde Dipolu authorised substituted service of Form 48, Notice of Consequences of Disobedience to Order of Court, to the EFCC chairman, through the commission’s Legal Department in Abuja.
The order followed an application by the Founder/Managing Director of Chappal Energies, Mr Ufoma Immanuel.
The application was granted by Dipolu.
A copy of the order was made available to the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) in Lagos on Tuesday.
Immanuel’s application resulted from EFCC’s  alleged continued disobedience of a court order  and Immanuel’s failed attempts to effect service of the Form 48 personally on Olukoyede.
Immanuel’s counsel, Mr C.U. Wogu of Tunji Braithwaite Law Partners, had told the court that attempts to serve the notice to the EFCC chairman were frustrated.
The EFCC had, acting on a petition to it by Immanuel’s business partner,  Mr Adebisi Adebutu of R28 Ltd., declared Immanuel  wanted in a public notice on its social media platforms on Nov. 19, 2025.
The commission declared Immanuel wanted in a case of obtaining money by false pretences and forgery.
The case resulted from control of Chappal Energies and shareholder rights.
The commission made the publication in spite a subsisting order by Justice Josephine Obanor of the High Court of the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja, on  Sept. 11, 2025.
Obanor had restrained the EFCC and other respondents from taking any steps to arrest, detain, or prosecute Immanuel in respect of any issues emanating from the shareholding arrangements, cross-shareholding agreements, subscription rights, and performance of contractual obligations involving him (Immanuel) and Adebutu.
The judge also held that the case was civil in nature.
The EFCC, however,  began criminal proceedings against Immanuel in another court of coordinate jurisdiction.
Immanuel , through his counsel, had challenged the publication by the EFCC at the Federal High Court, Lagos.
On Feb. 10, 2026,  Dipolu, ruled that the publication  amounted to infringement of Immanuel’s constitutional rights to personal liberty and freedom of movement.
The judge also held that the commission lacked the power to restrain Immanuel’s fundamental rights on the matter in spite of  a subsisting court order.
The judge ordered the EFCC to withdraw all publications declaring Immanuel wanted and replace them with a public notice retracting the declaration.
Dipolu also directed the EFCC to pay Immanuel five million Naira as compensation for infringing on his rights to personal liberty, freedom of movement and dignity.
In the latest order, Dipolu granted Immanuel’s prayer for substituted service, but declined to deem the service automatically sufficient.
The EFCC, on March 11, 2026, arraigned Immanuel alongside his company, Intermediate Investment Holdings Ltd., before Justice Mojisola Dada of the High Court of  Lagos State, Ikeja Division, on a two-count charge of forgery and obtaining  $1.5 million by false pretences.
However, in October 2026, Obanor issued a restrictive injunction, reaffirming her earlier order and restraining the commission from continuing with the criminal proceedings at the High Court of Lagos State.
The judge held that the Sept. 11, 2025 court order remained binding on the EFCC and other respondents since it had neither been set aside nor lawfully discharged. (NAN) www.nannews.ng

original_payload.original_body:
Culture & Tourism  CBAAC urges revival of African languages, traditions
By  Folashade Adeniran   ·   45 minutes ago   ·  3 min read
✓
✓
By Vivian Ihechu
The Centre for Black and African Arts and Civilisation (CBAAC) has called for the revival of endangered African languages, indigenous traditions and cultural practices, to preserve the continent’s identity and heritage.
Director-General of CBAAC, Aisha Adamu-Augie, made the call in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) on the sidelines of the CANEX WKND2026 in Lagos.
NAN reports that the CANEX 2026 was hosted by the Federal Government and organised by the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) from Nov. 5 to Nov. 8.
The event has the theme: “One People, United in Culture, Creating for the World”.
She expressed concern over the gradual loss of indigenous knowledge and traditional systems of communication.
According to her, many African languages are endangered, with some surviving through only a handful of speakers, while traditional cultural expressions are increasingly disappearing.
Adamu-Augie noted that even the symbolic meanings embedded in indigenous fabrics and traditional communication systems were gradually being forgotten.
She stressed the need for Africans to remember, revive and document their cultural heritage, in a bid to ensure that younger generations understood and benefited from its value.
“We have a lot that we have to lose, that we have lost. And now where we are, is to remember, revive, document and ensure that our younger generation can utilise that power,” she said.
The director-general said the renewed global interest in African fashion and indigenous fabrics was helping to revive traditional production communities and create economic opportunities.
She cited the historic dye pits in Kano, where families had passed down traditional knowledge across generations, noting that the growing demand for authentic African fabrics was restoring livelihoods and cultural practices.
Speaking further, she said the revival of indigenous crafts and textiles would create jobs, while enabling communities to preserve their stories, rituals and traditions.
Adamu-Augie also emphasised the importance of teaching children indigenous languages, describing language as a powerful tool for cultural identity, unity and mutual understanding.
The CBAAC boss then encouraged parents to expose children to different languages and cultures, stressing that cultural diversity should be appreciated, rather than viewed as a basis for superiority.
The director-general further noted that learning another person’s language could foster kinship and strengthen relationships across cultural boundaries.
She urged Africans to embrace their cultural identity and recognise the value of their heritage without depending on external validation.
“Our hope is to remind Nigerians and Africans that what they have is enough. You don’t need external validation to realise that you are just as powerful as any other continent in the world,” she said.
Adamu-Augie said CBAAC was also working toward promoting African history and culture, through international exchanges and activities planned around the 50th anniversary of the 1977 Festival of Arts and Culture (FESTAC 77).
She said the initiative would involve existing festivals, cultural institutions, diaspora communities and international partners, to strengthen the global visibility of African heritage. ( NAN )www.nanews.ng
Edited by Chinyere Nwachukwu

items.title: Noma ​‌‍‌‌⁠‍⁠⁠‍‍​‍‍⁠​⁠​‌​Centre performs 457 free reconstructive surgeries on children – Coordinator

original_payload.original_title: Noma ​‌‍‌‌⁠‍⁠⁠‍‍​‍‍⁠​⁠​‌​Centre performs 457 free reconstructive surgeries on children – Coordinator
original_payload.original_body:
Health  Noma ​‌‍‌‌⁠‍⁠⁠‍‍​‍‍⁠​⁠​‌​Centre performs 457 free reconstructive surgeries on children – Coordinator
By  Folashade Adeniran   ·   56 minutes ago   ·  4 min read
✓
✓
By Angela Atabo
The Noma Centre at the National Hospital, Abuja, says it has carried out 457 complex reconstructive surgeries on children affected by noma since its establishment, with all treatments provided free of charge.
A statement by the centre on Tuesday in Abuja, quoted Dr Charles Ononiwu, National Coordinator of the Noma Aid Nigeria Initiative (NANI), as saying this during the 2026 Oral Health Week, Noma Day and Scientific Conference.
Ononiwu said the centre had managed 321 patients and currently had more than 80 children receiving treatment, adding that 208 surgeries were performed this year alone.
He said the facility maintained an average of 82 patients monthly, providing comprehensive care through a multidisciplinary team of plastic surgeons, ear, nose and throat specialists, paediatricians, clinical psychologists and other healthcare professionals.
The coordinator warned that noma could cause severe facial destruction within a week if left untreated, urging parents to seek immediate medical attention when children, particularly those aged between two and six years, complained of mouth pain.
“Make sure you maintain good oral hygiene for your children. If your child complains of pain in the mouth, please look for a hospital immediately,” he advised.
He identified poor oral hygiene, severe malnutrition and weakened immunity as factors that predisposed children to the disease, stressing that early detection and treatment could prevent extensive tissue damage.
According to him, early treatment involves basic antibiotics and adequate feeding, while reconstructive surgery for advanced cases can cost between N7 million and N10 million.
He urged families, healthcare workers and the public to report suspected cases through NANI’s toll-free line, assuring that the initiative would facilitate treatment, transportation and hospital bills for affected children.
Ononiwu said the centre also provided basic education, psychological support and vocational training for children and their parents during treatment, which could last several months.
He added that the facility received patients from other African countries, including Mozambique and Burundi.
He said the initiative also supported families with business equipment and resources to establish small businesses, as part of efforts to address poverty and reduce the risk of noma.
“The centre provided direct social assistance to 57 severe cases, enrolled 132 pupils in educational programmes, and empowered 143 participants through specialised skill acquisition classes during 2026,” he said.
Meanwhile, the Federal Government has unveiled a N70 billion five-year National Strategic Plan for Oral Health (2026–2030), aimed at strengthening oral healthcare delivery in the country.
The Minister of State for Health, Dr Adekunle Salako, said state and local governments would provide 49 per cent of the funding, the Federal Government 30 per cent, while development partners would contribute the remaining 21 per cent.
The World Health Organisation (WHO) called for the integration of noma prevention, early detection and referral into primary healthcare services to reduce avoidable deaths and permanent facial disfigurement among children.
Also, the Director of Hospital Services at the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, Dr Adebimpe Adebiyi, called for stronger community-based prevention and early detection to reduce noma cases in Nigeria.
Adebiyi, who delivered a memorial lecture titled: “A Legacy of Healing and Hope: Celebrating a Life of Dedication to Children Affected by Noma”, urged the integration of noma awareness into school curricula.
She also called on Nigerians to end discrimination against survivors of the disease.
Similarly, the President of the Nigerian Dental Association, Dr Tope Adeyemi, acknowledged the association’s contributions to efforts to improve oral healthcare in the country.
The conference, organised by the Noma Centre Abuja in partnership with the Federal Ministry of Health, brought together key stakeholders to discuss progress in patient care, surgical interventions and public health advocacy.
The memorial lecture honoured the late Mama Ute Winkler Stumpf (1943–2020), founder of Hilfsaktion NOMA E.V., whose work supported the treatment and rehabilitation of children affected by the disease.
WHO defines noma as a severe infection that primarily affects malnourished children and can rapidly destroy facial tissues, noting that early detection and treatment can prevent its devastating consequences. ( NAN )

items.title: NICOLD urges private investment, innovation to strengthen dam safety

original_payload.original_title: NICOLD urges private investment, innovation to strengthen dam safety
original_payload.original_body:
Environment  NICOLD urges private investment, innovation to strengthen dam safety
By  Tosin Kolade   ·   2 hours ago   ·  Updated  20 minutes ago   ·  4 min read
✓
✓
By Angela Atabo
The Nigerian Committee on Large Dams (NICOLD) has called for increased private-sector investment and sustained training of young engineers to strengthen dam safety and management in Nigeria.
The committee’s President, Dr Johnson Adewumi, made the call at its 2026 National Conference and Annual General Meeting (AGM) in Abuja on Tuesday.
The conference was themed “Sustainable Dams for Water, Energy and Climate Resilience”.
Adewumi said the conference provided a platform for engineers, policymakers, researchers and other stakeholders to exchange knowledge and develop solutions to challenges in dam engineering.
He said while the public sector was responsible for policy development, private organisations had a critical role in translating policies into practical programmes and projects.
He urged more companies to partner with NICOLD, noting that the committee brought together professionals involved in dam engineering and technology.
Adewumi said NICOLD had organised seven training sessions on dam operations and maintenance with sponsorship from partners, including Mainstream Energy Solutions and DeCrown West Africa Company, whose contributions he acknowledged.
The president stressed the need to equip younger engineers with skills in dam design, construction, operation and management to sustain professional expertise and prevent infrastructure failures.
He said NICOLD was promoting knowledge transfer from experienced professionals to younger engineers, adding that continuous training was necessary to prepare them for future responsibilities.
Adewumi, who said he was 75, noted that experienced professionals had a duty to mentor younger engineers and ensure the transfer of technical knowledge.
He said dams remained vital to water security, food production, hydropower generation and flood control, adding that reservoirs also supported irrigation, livestock production, industrial activities and public water supply.
He called for the adoption of modern technologies, research and innovation to improve dam monitoring, structural assessments and maintenance.
Earlier, the Minister of Water Resources and Sanitation, Prof. Joseph Utsev, called for stronger collaboration and investment to improve dam safety, hydropower generation and water resources management.
Utsev, represented by the Acting Permanent Secretary of the ministry, Ali Dallah, said sustainable dam development was essential to water security, agricultural production, energy generation and flood management.
He identified the Sustainable Power and Irrigation for Nigeria (SPIN) Project, implemented with Federal Ministry of Power and World Bank support, as a key initiative to strengthen dam safety, modernise irrigation and promote hydropower.
The minister said effective dam management required regular inspections, structural assessments, preventive maintenance and timely rehabilitation to identify risks and protect infrastructure.
He also warned that changing hydrological conditions and extreme weather events posed challenges to dam design and operations, making climate resilience necessary throughout the development and management of dams.
Utsev said the ministry, through the Nigeria Hydrological Services Agency, was strengthening hydrological data collection, flood forecasting and early warning systems.
He said the Annual Flood Outlook provided information to support flood preparedness, reservoir management and decisions by relevant stakeholders.
Also speaking, Irrigation and Drainage expert, Mr Matthew Offie, called for the reassessment of existing dams using current climate data to ensure their safety and functionality.
Offie said many dams were designed using historical hydrological data that might no longer reflect prevailing climate conditions.
He cited changing rainfall patterns, erratic flooding and prolonged droughts in parts of the country as reasons for updating hydrological assessments.
He recommended retaining the original engineering principles of existing dams while incorporating current climate data into their operation and management.
Offie said satellite information and emerging technologies could make such assessments more affordable and accessible.
He said his conference paper examined cost-effective approaches to hydrological assessment, drawing on lessons from more than 40 years of professional experience to recommend solutions and avoid repeating past project failures.
The   News Agency of Nigeria (NAN)   reports that dams support water supply, irrigation, electricity generation and flood control, making their safety critical to communities and economic activities.
The National Emergency Management Agency reported that floods affected 315,762 people, displaced 113,367 and killed 231 across 25 states and 86 local government areas as of September 2025.
The floods also damaged 46,304 farmlands.
The Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission reported that hydropower plants generated 3,081.88 gigawatt-hours of electricity in the first quarter of 2025, compared with 3,029.07 gigawatt-hours in the preceding quarter.
Changing rainfall patterns and extreme weather events also highlight the need to incorporate current climate data into dam planning, operation and maintenance to reduce risks and sustain water and energy supplies. (  NAN  )

items.title: SPLM warns caretaker officials against interfering in primaries

original_payload.original_title: SPLM warns caretaker officials against interfering in primaries
original_payload.original_body:
The ruling SPLM has warned members serving in the caretaker government against interfering in its ongoing congresses and primaries, threatening disciplinary action against officials found intimidating candidates or influencing members’ voting decisions.
SPLM Secretary-General Akol Paul Kordit said in Juba on Tuesday that the party had received reports of caretaker government officials attempting to influence internal elections and taking action against fellow members over their voting preferences.
He said the party is documenting the alleged violations and would hold those responsible accountable once sufficient evidence had been gathered.
“We are recording all the violations, all the actions, and once sufficient evidence has been put together, anybody who infringes or obstructs people’s will will also be held accountable,” Kordit told journalists at a news conference.
He said officials serving in the caretaker administration must remain neutral and allow party members to choose their leaders freely, without intimidation or interference.
Kordit said the directive also apply to other political parties, arguing that the caretaker government has a responsibility to provide an enabling environment for all political groups to organise and prepare for the general elections.
He also warned against inflammatory statements and actions that could deepen divisions within the party, urging candidates and their supporters to exercise discipline and respect the outcome of the internal elections.
The secretary-general further cautioned active-duty military personnel against participating in party political activities, including the ongoing primaries, unless they had formally left active service and obtained clearance from their respective military units.
He said some military officers seeking to participate in the internal elections had been referred to their units for clearance. Some generals, he added, had been decommissioned to allow them to take part in the political process.
Electoral boundaries
On electoral preparations, Kordit warned party members against attempts to alter existing electoral constituencies, insisting that the December 22 general elections should be conducted using boundaries based on the 2008 population census.
He said attempts by individuals in some counties and states to introduce new administrative arrangements are unacceptable, urging party members to respect existing electoral and administrative structures.
Kordit also condemned alleged threats against SPLM candidates in Tambura County, Western Equatoria State, saying the party had received audio recordings containing threats against aspirants.
He called on the government to guarantee the safety of candidates, voters and members of other political parties.
“We don’t want violence in this process. We don’t want a war in South Sudan. We want peace,” he said.
Primaries face hurdles
The warning comes as the SPLM’s internal electoral process faces challenges in several parts of the country, raising concerns about the party’s ability to complete its candidate selection and organisational exercises ahead of the December elections.
In Unity State, the party’s national leadership warned caretaker governors and party officials against interfering in the primaries after a high-level committee overseeing the process encountered difficulties. The committee subsequently returned to Juba to brief the party leadership.
In the Greater Pibor Administrative Area (GPAA), the SPLM suspended its ongoing congresses and primaries on November 6, citing unspecified technical challenges. The suspension came after more than a week of internal electoral activities.
The process has also been marred by allegations of bias. Some SPLM cadres in Greater Pibor accused the committee overseeing the primaries of favouring particular candidates and working with local authorities to influence the outcome. They called for the committee to be replaced by a neutral team. The allegations had not been independently verified, and the officials accused were not immediately available for comment.
Despite the challenges, Kordit said the internal congresses and primaries are progressing across the country, with Upper Nile State having completed its process. He expressed confidence that the remaining exercises in the nine states and three administrative areas would be concluded in time for the December 22 elections.

items.title: RSF accused of abuses, market closure in West Kordofan

original_payload.original_title: RSF accused of abuses, market closure in West Kordofan
original_payload.original_body:
The Dar Hamar Emergency Response Room has accused the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of committing abuses against civilians in the Foga and Wad Banda areas of Sudan’s West Kordofan State.
According to sources, the abuses include beatings, humiliation, the imposition of exorbitant levies on mining mill operators, and the confiscation of Starlink satellite internet equipment.
The group also accused the RSF of shutting down the market in Wad Banda.
“RSF personnel have subjected civilians to beatings and degrading treatment at the mining mills market in Foga, near the town of En Nahud,” Azzam Hamid, spokesperson for the Dar Hamar Emergency Response Room, told Radio Tamazuj. “The RSF also imposed levies on mill operators, requiring each mill to surrender a barrel of diesel fuel. The RSF looted the entire market.”
“Such conduct has become part of their daily practices in the northern localities of West Kordofan State, particularly En Nahud, Wad Banda, Foga and the surrounding areas,” Hamid added.
He further accused RSF personnel of confiscating Starlink satellite internet terminals, restricting residents’ ability to communicate and access telecommunications services amid the deteriorating security situation in the area.
Meanwhile, the vicinity of Foga has witnessed fierce fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF over the past two days, amid an escalation of military operations in the area.

items.title: Former MPs left waiting for 924 promised vehicles

original_payload.original_title: Former MPs left waiting for 924 promised vehicles
original_payload.original_body:
Former members of South Sudan’s Transitional National Legislative Assembly (TNLA) say they have yet to receive 924 vehicles and other financial benefits promised by the former parliamentary leadership, nearly two months after the legislature was dissolved on September 22.
On September 22, former parliament spokesperson Oliver Mori announced that the government  planned to provide vehicles to lawmakers  under a proposed car-loan scheme. He said President Salva Kiir had approved the purchase and that the then finance minister had issued a non-objection certificate for the process.
In a separate announcement shortly before the dissolution, former Speaker Joseph Ngere Paciko said Kiir would provide 924 vehicles to lawmakers. The announcement came as parliament prepared to pass amendments to the election law that paved the way for the dissolution of the transitional government and allowed Kiir to remain in office with full executive powers until an elected president takes office.
The proposed fleet was  estimated  to cost about $85 million, although the government has not publicly confirmed the overall cost.
However, several former lawmakers told Radio Tamazuj on Tuesday that they had received none of the promised vehicles and remained owed medical allowances, recess payments and salary arrears.
Bol Joseph Agau, a former lawmaker and senior member of the National Democratic Movement (NDM), said parliamentarians had accumulated years of unpaid entitlements, including annual medical allowances of $30,000 per member.
He said the allowances had not been paid for three years, while payments in the fourth year were made in irregular instalments.
“Every year you pass a budget, there is a budget item called medical funds for the MP, and it is $30,000 each. That had never been paid for three years. And the fourth year was being paid in bits, $2,000, $3,000, $5,000. We don’t even know where it is now, whether it is exhausted or not,” Agau said.
He also cited four years of unpaid floating allowances and outstanding recess allowances, saying lawmakers had sometimes sacrificed their parliamentary breaks to clear a legislative backlog.
Agau added that some former MPs were owed up to 19 months of salary arrears. He said promises made by Paciko in his final address before parliament’s dissolution had not materialised.
“There is no car. I am here speaking to you. I’m using my personal car,” he said.
Peter Lomude Francis, another former lawmaker, said he had received none of the promised vehicles, arrears or other benefits since the dissolution.
“Since the dissolution of the government on the 22nd of September, I’m one of the former MPs who did not see even a penny,” Francis said, adding that the outstanding payments included emoluments and other parliamentary privileges.
He accused parliamentary leaders of making promises they had failed to fulfil and called for greater integrity and accountability in public institutions.
Francis said the Emoluments Act of 2022 provided for parliamentary benefits, including vehicles and sitting allowances, and argued that former lawmakers should receive their legally recognised entitlements.
He also called for stronger parliamentary oversight of public finances and executive officials, saying lawmakers should scrutinise government spending and hold institutions accountable.
Francis blamed corruption and the mismanagement of public funds for the country’s economic difficulties and urged voters to elect representatives committed to oversight and public service rather than political loyalty.
The new finance minister could not immediately be reached for comment on the outstanding payments or the proposed vehicle scheme.
The complaints come as South Sudan prepares for general elections scheduled for December 2026. The ruling Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM) has been conducting party primaries and other political activities, while other parties have shown less visible mobilisation ahead of the polls.

items.title: Opinion| Decentralization in South Sudan: Between local empowerment and tribal fragmentation

original_payload.original_title: Opinion| Decentralization in South Sudan: Between local empowerment and tribal fragmentation
original_payload.original_body:
Decentralization in South Sudan was intended to bring government closer to the people, promote equitable development, distribute political power, and strengthen local participation in governance. It was also expected to accommodate the country’s ethnic and cultural diversity while consolidating national unity.
However, more than a decade after independence, the implementation of decentralization has raised serious questions about whether it has achieved these objectives or instead contributed to ethnic fragmentation, political patronage, and the weakening of professional public administration.
The problem is not decentralization itself, but how it has been interpreted and implemented. Rather than consistently empowering citizens, administrative restructuring has, in some instances, encouraged competition over territorial boundaries, political appointments, and public resources along tribal lines.
From national unity to administrative fragmentation
One of the fundamental objectives of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement/Army (SPLM/A), established in 1983, was to resist political arrangements that divided Southern Sudan along regional and ethnic lines. The redivision of Southern Sudan under the Nimeiri regime was widely perceived as an attempt to weaken the collective political identity and political aspirations of its people.
It is therefore a historical irony that the movement that fought for the unity and liberation of South Sudan later presided over administrative restructuring that, at certain stages, reinforced internal divisions.
Historically, the demand for federalism among Southern Sudanese leaders was primarily intended to protect the political, cultural, and religious identities of the predominantly African South against forced Arabization and Islamization by the central government in Khartoum. It was not a demand for tribal federalism within Southern Sudan.
Following independence in 2011, however, federalism and decentralization increasingly became associated with demands for administrative units shaped by ethnic and tribal considerations. Consequently, some communities began perceiving counties and other administrative territories as belonging exclusively to particular tribes rather than serving all citizens within their jurisdictions.
This development has undermined the principle of equal citizenship and transformed administrative boundaries into potential sources of political competition and intercommunal conflict.
The cost of tribal-based decentralization
South Sudan initially adopted a ten-state administrative structure after independence. However, the establishment of 28 states in 2015, followed by 32 states in 2017, significantly expanded the country’s administrative and political structures.
Although these changes were presented as measures to bring government closer to the people, they increased administrative expenditure, multiplied political appointments, and intensified competition over territory and public resources.
The return to ten states and three administrative areas in 2020, under the political arrangements associated with the Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan, did not automatically resolve the underlying weaknesses of local governance.
The consequences of excessive administrative fragmentation are evident in several areas.
First, tribal interpretations of administrative boundaries have contributed to disputes over land, grazing areas, water resources, county headquarters, and political representation. Where historical grievances and weak conflict-resolution mechanisms exist, such disputes can escalate into intercommunal violence.
Second, the expansion of administrative units has increased government expenditure without necessarily improving public services. Resources that could otherwise support education, health care, roads, clean water, and agricultural development are consumed by salaries, offices, vehicles, allowances, and administrative operations.
Third, weak oversight and politically motivated appointments have created opportunities for corruption, financial mismanagement, and patronage. Public positions are sometimes perceived as rewards for political allegiance or tribal loyalty rather than responsibilities requiring professional qualifications and competence.
Most importantly, tribal-based administrative arrangements weaken national identity by encouraging citizens to prioritize ethnic affiliations over their common South Sudanese citizenship.
Politicization of the civil service
Another serious weakness in South Sudan’s decentralization system is the politicization of public administration.
Under the former unified Sudan, administrative officers were generally appointed, transferred, and supervised through centralized bureaucratic institutions. Although the system had shortcomings, including political interference and regional inequalities, it provided a recognizable framework for managing the civil service.
In South Sudan, administrative appointments, particularly at state and county levels, have frequently been influenced by political loyalty, personal relationships, and tribal considerations.
Although the Local Government Act of 2009 established a framework for accountable local administration, the appointment and management of local-government officials have not always reflected the principles of professional independence and merit-based administration.
County commissioners and other senior administrators should be accountable to the law and the citizens they serve, rather than primarily to political patrons or particular ethnic constituencies.
A further concern is the institutional imbalance between the attention given to military and security appointments and the development of civilian administrative institutions. While military and security personnel are frequently subject to national appointment, promotion, and transfer arrangements, the civil service lacks an equally effective and consistently implemented national mechanism for managing administrative personnel.
South Sudan cannot build a stable and functional state through security institutions alone. It equally needs a professional, politically neutral, and nationally integrated civil service.
The need for a unified national civil service
The government should undertake a comprehensive review of the decentralization system, particularly the management of administrative personnel.
The recruitment, appointment, promotion, transfer, and redeployment of senior administrative officers should be guided by a unified national framework based on professional qualifications, competence, integrity, and national administrative requirements.
A qualified administrator from one state should be eligible to serve in another state or county without discrimination based on ethnicity, clan, geographical origin, or political affiliation.
Such a system would promote national integration, reduce local political patronage, and strengthen the professional identity of the civil service.
This does not mean abolishing decentralization or returning to rigid centralized government. Rather, it means distinguishing between the decentralization of political and administrative responsibilities and the national coordination of professional civil-service management.
Reactivating local government boards
One practical institutional reform would be to reactivate and strengthen Local Government Boards as professional institutions responsible for coordinating and supervising local administration.
The government should consider placing these boards within a nationally coordinated framework under the Office of the President or the Presidency, subject to appropriate constitutional and legislative provisions.
Their responsibilities should include coordinating the recruitment and deployment of administrative officers, monitoring performance, promoting professional training, enforcing administrative standards, and advising on local-government reforms.
This arrangement would help protect civil servants from inappropriate local political interference while maintaining the ability of state and county governments to deliver services and respond to community needs.
The objective should be to combine local administrative autonomy with national professional standards and accountability.
Recommendations for reform
To make decentralization an instrument of national development rather than tribal fragmentation, the following reforms are necessary:
Review administrative boundaries:  States, counties, payams, and bomas should be established or adjusted according to population, geography, economic viability, and service-delivery requirements rather than exclusively tribal claims.
Establish a unified national civil service:  Recruitment, appointment, promotion, transfer, and redeployment should be guided by merit, professional competence, and national needs.
Reactivate Local Government Boards:  Strengthen their institutional mandate and consider their attachment to the Presidency within a legally defined national administrative framework.
Strengthen fiscal decentralization:  Provide local governments with predictable and adequate financial allocations corresponding to their responsibilities.
Promote accountability and local democracy:  Strengthen public participation, transparent appointments, regular elections, independent audits, and legislative oversight.
Promote national integration:  Government institutions, educational establishments, civil society, and the media should promote equal citizenship, peaceful coexistence, and respect for cultural diversity.
Conclusion: decentralization must unite, not divide
South Sudan’s experience demonstrates that creating more administrative units does not automatically produce better governance. A country may have numerous states, counties, and local-government structures and still suffer from insecurity, corruption, underdevelopment, and institutional weakness.
The historical irony is that a liberation movement that fought against the division of Southern Sudan has, at certain stages, presided over administrative arrangements that contributed to internal fragmentation.
South Sudan must therefore move beyond tribal-based political competition and build institutions founded on equal citizenship, national unity, professional competence, and accountability.
Decentralization should empower communities, not tribal political elites; strengthen public institutions, not multiply administrative offices; and promote equitable development, not expand political patronage.
The challenge is not whether South Sudan should decentralize, but how to ensure that decentralization serves the national interest.
South Sudan needs fewer political divisions, stronger local institutions, and one professional national civil service committed to serving all citizens without discrimination.
The writer is a South Sudanese author, journalist, and university lecturer at Starford International University, Juba. He specializes in Security Studies, International Development, and Development Studies, with professional experience in public administration, anti-corruption, and governance. His writings focus on politics, peace, security, and national development. He can be reached via williamtor2011@gmail.com /+211 922 402 262.

items.title: W. Bahr el Ghazal women fault parties for high nomination fees

original_payload.original_title: W. Bahr el Ghazal women fault parties for high nomination fees
original_payload.original_body:
Women leaders in Western Bahr el Ghazal State have raised concerns over political parties charging exorbitant nomination fees to contest in elections, saying they will frustrate women from participating in the upcoming elections.
They said many of them cannot afford the fees and that it will affect women’s political representation.
Julet Luka Mudiria, a peace mediator, said the money required by parties from candidates is blocking women from contesting. She urged the political parties to reduce the amount.
“There are many women who are proficient and well equipped with knowledge, willing to lead the country, but their limited resources will not enable them to participate in the coming polls,” she stated. “Women normally save their money for their children. The huge fees demanded by parties will lead to limited participation of women in the election.”
For her part, Carmela Augustino, Acting State Women Union chairperson, revealed that women have not received any funds to help them mobilize fellow women to understand their rights in the upcoming election.
“We have been talking about election preparedness with our mouths; there are no funds to help us move around to sensitize women,” she said. “If any well-wishers are willing to fund women to push for the 35 percent affirmative action and beyond, we will be happy.”
Meanwhile, Regina Edward Dimo, Director General at the State Ministry of Gender, Child and Social Welfare, said they are trying to educate women about the upcoming election, but they have no funding to run the activities.
“There are no donors supporting women with civic education, and the high fees for candidates are affecting women’s participation in the state,” she said.
