items.title: Maintenance routière : les entreprises bientôt jugées sur la qualité des routes

original_payload.original_title: Maintenance routière : les entreprises bientôt jugées sur la qualité des routes
original_payload.original_body:
Le Bénin s’apprête à expérimenter un nouveau mécanisme de gestion de l’entretien de son réseau routier. Baptisée Gestion de l’entretien routier par niveaux de service (Genis), cette approche entend faire évoluer les contrats de maintenance en liant davantage la rémunération des entreprises à la qualité des infrastructures mises à la disposition des usagers. Une formation consacrée à son appropriation a été lancée le lundi 9 novembre dernier à Cotonou, avec l’appui du Mca-Bénin Régional.
L’entretien des routes pourrait bientôt obéir à de nouvelles règles au Bénin. Plutôt que de payer les entreprises principalement pour les travaux réalisés et les quantités exécutées, le pays envisage de privilégier un système fondé sur les performances des infrastructures. C’est le principe de la Gestion de l’entretien routier par niveaux de service (Genis), dont les modalités d’application sont actuellement en préparation.
Pour permettre aux acteurs du secteur de maîtriser ce dispositif, le Millennium challenge account-Bénin Régional (Mca-Bénin Régional) a initié une formation de cinq jours à l’hôtel Azalaï de Cotonou. Des cadres de l’administration routière, des responsables de la Société des infrastructures routières et de l’aménagement du territoire (Sirat), des entreprises de travaux et des bureaux d’études et de contrôle y prennent part. La particularité du Genis réside dans le mode d’évaluation des prestations. Les entreprises retenues ne seront plus seulement appréciées sur la base des travaux effectués, mais également sur leur capacité à garantir, pendant toute la durée du contrat, un niveau de qualité défini pour les routes concernées. L’état de la chaussée, le drainage, la signalisation, la sécurité et la disponibilité des infrastructures feront notamment partie des critères de performance. Les résultats constatés sur le terrain serviront ainsi à apprécier le respect des engagements contractuels et à déterminer les rémunérations. « L’attention se porte particulièrement sur le niveau des services effectivement rendus aux usagers de la route », a expliqué Afiss Bileoma, coordonnateur national du Mca-Bénin Régional.
Un marché pilote attendu en 2027
La Sirat entend jouer un rôle central dans l’expérimentation de ce mécanisme. Son directeur général, Ranti Akindès a indiqué que sa structure prépare un dossier d’appel d’offres type destiné à encadrer les futurs contrats. Le Mca-Bénin Régional accompagne ce travail pour garantir la conformité du document aux exigences techniques et contractuelles du Genis. Selon le calendrier annoncé, la Sirat prévoit de lancer, au cours du deuxième semestre 2027, la procédure d’acquisition des prestations devant aboutir à la conclusion des premiers contrats. Cette phase expérimentale permettra de tester les outils de contrôle, les modalités de suivi et les mécanismes de gestion avant d’envisager une extension du dispositif. Pour Ranti Akindès, cette réforme représente également une occasion de combler les insuffisances constatées dans l’entretien du réseau et de préserver plus efficacement les investissements routiers.
Au-delà de ce nouveau mode de contractualisation, le programme de modernisation soutenu par le Mca-Bénin Régional prévoit plusieurs autres équipements et instruments techniques. Des véhicules intelligents, des véhicules multifonctions et des déflectographes seront notamment acquis pour faciliter l’inspection des routes et améliorer la collecte des données relatives à leur état. Le dispositif comprend aussi le développement du système de gestion du patrimoine routier (Sgpr), la mise en place d’une unité de gestion et d’évaluation routière (Ugr) et l’acquisition du logiciel Hdm-4, destiné à améliorer la programmation des interventions.
Des compétences à renforcer
Pour Joseph Ahissou, représentant du ministre du Cadre de vie et des Transports chargé du Développement durable, la réussite de cette réforme dépendra aussi de la capacité des acteurs à s’approprier les nouveaux outils. Il attend du dispositif une meilleure préservation des infrastructures, une gestion plus efficace des ressources affectées à leur entretien et une responsabilisation accrue des entreprises prestataires. Il a, par ailleurs, invité les participants à transmettre les connaissances acquises à leurs collègues afin d’élargir le cercle des professionnels maîtrisant cette nouvelle approche.
Conduite par Akli Ourad, spécialiste international de la gestion des réseaux routiers, la formation alterne exposés techniques, partages d’expériences, études de cas et exercices pratiques. Elle doit permettre aux participants de mieux comprendre les exigences du Genis et les changements qu’il introduira dans la préparation, l’exécution et le contrôle des contrats d’entretien. Cette réforme s’inscrit dans le cadre du Compact régional conclu entre le Bénin et les États-Unis, par l’intermédiaire du Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC). Le programme mobilise une enveloppe globale de 291 millions de dollars, à raison de 202 millions de dollars de contribution américaine et 89 millions de dollars apportés par le gouvernement béninois.

items.title: Regards croisés Québec-Bénin : les enfants de Houinta au cœur d’une création collective

original_payload.original_title: Regards croisés Québec-Bénin : les enfants de Houinta au cœur d’une création collective
original_payload.original_body:
Les élèves de l’École primaire publique (EPP) de Houinta ont découvert les arts plastiques à travers une expérience participative, le samedi 7 novembre 2026 à l’Escale Zêvougnon à Porto-Novo. Initiée par les artistes de la résidence « Regards Croisés Québec-Bénin #MinoNexus 2026 », cette activité leur a permis de s’initier au dessin et à la peinture, tout en contribuant à la réalisation d’une fresque murale.
Des couleurs, des formes et beaucoup d’imagination. À l’Escale Zêvougnon, les enfants de l’École primaire publique (EPP)Houinta ont vécu une immersion dans l’univers de la création artistique. Encadrés par des artistes béninois et québécois, ils ont découvert les bases du dessin et de la peinture avant de prendre part à une œuvre collective. Une expérience qui leur a offert l’occasion d’exprimer leur créativité dans un cadre différent de celui de la salle de classe.L’atelier d’initiation a été conduit par Natoutchika Saint-Pierre, connue sous le nom de Na2 Toutis, artiste multidisciplinaire basée à Montréal. À travers une approche ludique et interactive, elle a familiarisé les apprenants avec les couleurs, les formes, les ombres et les dégradés. Des notions simples leur ont permis de comprendre comment la lumière et les nuances donnent du relief à un dessin. Privilégiant la liberté d’expression, elle les a invités à représenter ce qui nourrit leur imagination, sans leur imposer de modèles. Elle s’est réjouie de leur enthousiasme et de leur facilité à assimiler les enseignements.
Une fresque aux couleurs de la rencontre
La séance s’est poursuivie par la mise en couleurs d’une fresque représentant une jeune femme entourée de fleurs, sur un arrière-plan abstrait. Cette composition est l’œuvre de Mekudi Pamela Chablis, artiste peintre et illustratrice béninoise, et de Maliciouz, artiste peintre et muraliste d’origine haïtienne installée à Montréal. Les deux créatrices ont associé leurs univers pour donner naissance à une œuvre ouverte à plusieurs sensibilités artistiques. Les enfants ont été initiés au choix des couleurs et à leurs différentes nuances avant d’apporter leur contribution à la fresque. Maliciouz s’est dite agréablement surprise par leur engagement et leur rapidité à comprendre les consignes. D’autres artistes béninois et québécois sont également appelés à intervenir sur l’arrière-plan afin d’enrichir cette réalisation collective.Au-delà de l’apprentissage technique, cette initiative traduit une volonté de faire de l’art un moyen d’expression, de transmission et d’inclusion. Elle s’inscrit dans la résidence « Regards Croisés Québec-Bénin #MinoNexus 2026 », initiée par l’Afromusée de Montréal, en collaboration avec Femme & Pouvoir, et accueillie au Bénin par Le Monde de Sica, autour du thème « Traversées, identités & éco-matériaux ».À travers cette rencontre, les élèves de Houinta ne se sont pas contentés de découvrir la peinture. Ils ont apporté leur propre sensibilité à une œuvre appelée à porter les empreintes de plusieurs cultures. Une belle manière de leur faire comprendre que l’art se découvre, s’apprend et se construit aussi ensemble.

items.title: « Adjah, Adjah » : Queena chante la désillusion amoureuse et les promesses trahies

original_payload.original_title: « Adjah, Adjah » : Queena chante la désillusion amoureuse et les promesses trahies
original_payload.original_body:
CULTURE
« Adjah, Adjah » : Queena chante la désillusion amoureuse et les promesses trahies
À travers son nouveau titre « Adjah, Adjah », l'artiste Queena dresse le portrait poignant d'une femme brisée par les mensonges et le silence d'un amour déçu.
Alwihda Info
10 nov. 2026
© DR
Par Nguessitta Djimtengaye William
Derrière les promesses d'un partenaire et une confiance aveugle se cachent parfois la déception, les blessures et le chagrin. C'est cette réalité douloureuse que met en scène l'artiste Queena dans sa nouvelle œuvre, « Adjah, Adjah ».
À travers ce projet, elle dresse le portrait d'Adjah, une jeune femme éperdument amoureuse qui mesure aujourd'hui les conséquences de sa naïveté. Malgré un cœur brisé, le personnage fait le choix de la souffrance en silence, dissimulant sa peine au quotidien.
Avec « Adjah, Adjah », Queena signe une interpellation sensible sur les illusions amoureuses, livrant une fresque intimiste de la désillusion dans laquelle nombre d'auditeurs pourrons se reconnaître.

Former Iraqi lawmaker Ahmed al-Alwani has been found dead in an apartment in the Lebanese capital, Beirut, according to a security source, prompting a “murder” investigation.
The source, who spoke to Al Jazeera on Tuesday, did not disclose how al-Alwani had died.

The official National News Agency described al-Awani’s death as a “murder” and said authorities in Lebanon have launched an investigation.
It said al-Alwani’s body was found in an apartment in the Tariq Al-Jadeeda neighbourhood of Beirut on Monday.
According to NNA, Judge Ahmed Rami al-Hajj will oversee the investigation by Lebanon’s Internal Security Forces.
In a statement on X, al-Alwani’s office called the former lawmaker’s death an “assassination” and a “treacherous crime”.
It called for an investigation and accountability for the perpetrators.
“This is not a passing incident to be brushed aside with condolences and condemnation,” it said. “It is a crime that demands a firm official response and a transparent investigation that reveals who planned it, who carried it out and who else was involved. Whoever is behind it, no one is above accountability.”
A Lebanese judicial source, meanwhile, told the AFP news agency that preliminary findings indicate al-Alwani was strangled to death and that a Lebanese national suspected of involvement has been arrested.
The official said authorities are looking for two Syrian suspects still at large. He added that the suspects had taken al-Alwani from the airport to his hotel when he arrived in Beirut last week.

items.title: US charges 3 ‘Iranian-backed’ men over alleged plot at UK Fairford air base

original_payload.original_title: US charges 3 ‘Iranian-backed’ men over alleged plot at UK Fairford air base
original_payload.original_body:
Prosecutors in the United States have charged three men they describe as Iranian-backed operatives over their alleged role in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across the US and Europe, including a plot targeting the United Kingdom’s  Fairford air base .
The Department of Justice said on Tuesday that the three men acted in support of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Iraq’s Kataib Hezbollah.

It identified the men as Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, who face what it called “terrorism-related offenses”.
Al-Saadi is already in jail in New York. Prosecutors did not disclose the whereabouts of Mohajeri and al-Hassani.
The charges announced on Tuesday centre on RAF Fairford in southwest England, where US forces and bombers had been stationed. The US had used the base to deploy bombers in its war against Iran.
Police were called to the Fairford site in September after a local farmer reported seeing a group of men with several white vans engaged in “suspicious” activity.
Six men were arrested in connection with the episode, and all were released on bail. Two were subsequently re-arrested on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence service and charged under the National Security Act.
Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the incident.

items.title: ‘Everything and everyone we love is at stake’: Thunberg slams COP31 talks

original_payload.original_title: ‘Everything and everyone we love is at stake’: Thunberg slams COP31 talks
original_payload.original_body:
Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg has condemned the United Nations climate talks as hypocritical and urged world leaders to put people and planet ahead of profits and power.
Thunberg made the comments on Tuesday as she arrived at the  COP31 conference in the Turkish resort city of Antalya .

“It’s a hypocrisy every year that the host countries are given an opportunity to whitewash themselves and we know that these negotiations are filled with lobbyists, paid by the very destructive industries which are benefiting from our extremely violent status quo,” Thunberg said.
“Our political and economic systems that have become incompatible with human nature.”
The talks follow a year of deadly climate-related disasters, including heatwaves and floods, and another energy shock caused by the US-Israel war on Iran.
COP31 co-hosts Turkiye and Australia are promoting renewable energy and rooftop solar installations, but both still rely heavily on fossil fuels, especially coal, to generate electricity. Previous hosts, including Brazil, the United Arab Emirates and Azerbaijan, are major oil producers.
Climate change is “threatening everything”, Thunberg said, warning that “everything and everyone we love is at stake”.
“We should act to protect and benefit people rather than constantly sacrificing the global majority and the very planet we are all living on, for a fortunate few to keep making unimaginable profits and maintaining geopolitical power,” she said.
Thunberg rose to  prominence in 2018  as a 15-year-old, when she began a solitary “School Strike for Climate” outside the Swedish parliament.

items.title: Fire contained on platform in Iran’s South Pars gas field

original_payload.original_title: Fire contained on platform in Iran’s South Pars gas field
original_payload.original_body:
Iranian authorities have contained a fire that broke out on a platform in South Pars gas field, the world’s largest offshore natural gas field.
The Pars Oil and Gas Company said the fire broke out on Tuesday on a gas platform in Phase 14 of the South Pars field and was extinguished immediately, Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency reported.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items    list 1 of 3  ‘Another round of war less likely’: Momentum builds for peace in Iran
list 2 of 3  Qatari PM’s Washington visit comes amid renewed US–Iran diplomacy
list 3 of 3  Iran backs nuclear treaty even as hardliners raise prospect of bomb
end of list
“During the incident, 17 workers jumped into the sea to save their lives; rescue operations for them are currently underway,” Kourosh Dehghan, Bushehr Province’s director general of crisis management, told Fars.
“Further details regarding the scale of the incident and the condition of the workers will be announced later,” Dehghan added.
Bushehr’s crisis management office later said all 17 workers were in good condition after boarding lifeboats and rescue craft, and that three heavy rescue vessels had been sent to the platform to bring them back.
Officials are considering a gas leak or an operational mishap as possible causes for the fire, Fars said.
The news agency added that the platform accounts for only 14.5 million cubic metres of South Pars’s total daily production of more than 700 million cubic metres of gas.
Iran shares the reservoir with major gas exporter Qatar, which calls its portion the North Dome.
The reservoir contains an estimated 1,800 trillion cubic feet (51 trillion cubic metres) of usable gas, enough to supply the world’s needs for 13 years.

items.title: Poland defeat inspired World Cup win – Flamingos captain

original_payload.original_title: Poland defeat inspired World Cup win – Flamingos captain
original_payload.original_body:
Flamingos  captain, Harmony Chidi, has attributed Nigeria’s historic triumph at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup to faith, hard work and team unity, revealing how the players rallied together after their opening defeat to Poland to win the title, PUNCH Sports Extra reports.
Nigeria defeated Japan 2-1 in Saturday’s final at the Mohammed VI Football Academy in Rabat, Morocco, becoming the first African country to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup and the first to claim a FIFA women’s world title at any level.
The Flamingos recovered from their opening loss to Poland to win their remaining six matches, including a group-stage victory over defending champions DPR Korea, on their way to the historic triumph.
In the final, Nigeria scored through Awawu Bashiru and Oluebube Umejiaku, whose goal two minutes into the second half proved decisive.

items.title: BII backs Okra with $7m to accelerate clean energy

original_payload.original_title: BII backs Okra with $7m to accelerate clean energy
original_payload.original_body:
British International Investment, the UK’s development finance institution and impact investor, on Tuesday announced a $7m debt facility to Okra, a provider of mesh-grid technology for off-grid communities.
The investment is expected to accelerate access to reliable and clean electricity, primarily in Nigeria. Nigeria has one of the world’s largest electricity access deficits, with an estimated 90 million people lacking reliable and affordable power.
BII’s financing will enable Okra to procure equipment for approximately 150,000 new connections, with the potential to provide electricity to 750,000 people in rural Nigeria for the first time. With Okra’s current installed base at more than 13,000 households and over 2.3MW of installed capacity, the facility is expected to enable the company to achieve more than 10x its connections.
The investment addresses a key barrier to scaling distributed renewable energy: access to flexible working capital to procure equipment. By enabling Okra to purchase manufacturing inputs upfront and in greater volumes, the facility will help reduce equipment costs and shorten delivery times to Nigeria from four months to approximately two months.
The British Deputy High Commissioner in Lagos, Mr Jonny Baxter, said: “Reliable electricity is fundamental to economic growth, job creation and improved livelihoods. Yet millions of Nigerians still lack access to dependable power. Through British International Investment, the UK is supporting innovative Nigerian solutions that can help close this gap. Not only is this about expanding access to power, but it is also about clean power. More reliable power creates opportunities for businesses and entrepreneurs, which generates jobs and drives inclusive economic growth. And clean power means less pollution. This investment reflects the strength of the UK-Nigeria partnership and our shared commitment to sustainable development, energy security and long-term prosperity.”

items.title: GDIZ au Bénin : AGOOJIYÉ, le bus électrique conçu et assemblé localement bientôt à l’essai

original_payload.original_title: GDIZ au Bénin : AGOOJIYÉ, le bus électrique conçu et assemblé localement bientôt à l’essai
original_payload.original_body:
GDIZ au Bénin :  AGOOJIYÉ, le bus électrique conçu et assemblé localement bientôt à l’essai
10/11/2026    par    Armel Tognon
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Un prototype de bus électrique, baptisé AGOOJIYÉ, prend forme dans la Zone industrielle de Glo-Djigbé (GDIZ). Initié par Exportunity Machinery avec l’accompagnement de la Société d’investissement et de promotion de l’industrie du Bénin (SIPI-Bénin), le projet associe étudiants, ingénieurs, techniciens et entreprises locales. Le véhicule devrait effectuer ses premiers essais de conduite le 23 novembre 2026 dans l’enceinte de la zone industrielle.
Présenté à la presse le lundi 9 novembre, au cours d’une conférence suivie d’une visite de l’atelier de fabrication, AGOOJIYÉ est destiné, dans un premier temps, à répondre aux besoins de mobilité des travailleurs de la GDIZ. Cette zone compte plus de 25 000 employés, dont les déplacements quotidiens entre leurs domiciles et leur lieu de travail, ainsi qu’entre les différentes unités de production, posent des défis logistiques.
Pour Létondji Béhéton, directeur général de la SIPI-Bénin, ce projet ouvre des perspectives pour l’industrie locale.  « La GDIZ, c’est un endroit où nous innovons » , a-t-il déclaré. Il a également évoqué la recherche de solutions de transport moins polluantes et adaptées aux besoins des entreprises installées sur le site.  « Nous pensons qu’en travaillant avec Exportunity Machinery, nous allons pouvoir trouver des solutions aux problèmes de mobilité auxquels nous sommes confrontés dans la zone » , a-t-il ajouté.
Des étudiants et des entreprises béninoises associés
À l’origine du projet, Vital Sounouvou, responsable d’Exportunity Machinery, défend l’ambition de développer des solutions industrielles à partir des compétences disponibles au Bénin. Le chantier a débuté le 10 juin 2026 par un challenge auquel ont pris part 85 étudiants issus de plusieurs établissements et écoles techniques. Ils ont travaillé sur le design du véhicule ainsi que sur ses schémas techniques et électriques.
Plusieurs structures ont contribué à cette première phase. Africa Design School a participé à la conception du design, tandis qu’Epitech intervient sur le tableau de bord. Future Studio a accompagné l’organisation du challenge et la mobilisation des établissements participants.
La réalisation du châssis et les premiers travaux de métallurgie ont ensuite été menés avec la SIAB. Des ingénieurs, des étudiants de l’École polytechnique d’Abomey-Calavi (EPAC) et des soudeurs ont travaillé pendant douze jours à l’assemblage des premières structures. L’EPAC a également accueilli, durant dix-sept jours, des travaux consacrés à la carrosserie et à la vérification des schémas, avec la participation d’étudiants et d’enseignants.
« Pendant 17 jours, nous avons prouvé que les étudiants béninois font plus que de la théorie. Il y a des ressources incroyables dans notre pays et des compétences incroyables dans nos écoles » , a souligné Vital Sounouvou. Les opérations se poursuivent actuellement dans un hangar mis à disposition par la GDIZ. Mécaniciens, soudeurs et électriciens y travaillent à l’assemblage et aux finitions du prototype.
Premiers essais annoncés pour le 23 novembre
Au 9 novembre, le taux d’exécution de la carrosserie était estimé à 98 %, contre 96 % pour la mécanique. Les travaux restants portent notamment sur l’intégration du moteur électrique, des batteries et du circuit électrique, ainsi que sur l’aménagement intérieur. Le véhicule pourra transporter huit personnes, conducteur compris. Une place à l’avant est prévue pour un passager à mobilité réduite, tandis que l’espace arrière comprend deux rangées de trois sièges.
Selon le calendrier présenté par Exportunity Machinery, les premiers essais de conduite sont prévus pour le 23 novembre dans la GDIZ. Vital Sounouvou assure que le prototype est destiné à circuler après sa mise au point et non à rester un simple modèle d’exposition.  « Ce n’est pas un projet académique. Ce n’est pas un prototype qu’on va exposer une fois. Non, c’est un bus qui va rouler dès qu’il sera fini. Il va rouler ici dans la zone industrielle de Glo-Djigbé » , a-t-il affirmé.
À terme, Exportunity Machinery envisage de produire environ 680 véhicules pour répondre aux besoins de transport de la zone. Des circuits touristiques figurent également parmi les pistes d’utilisation évoquées, notamment à l’occasion des Vodun Days ou sur la Route des Pêches. Pour le promoteur, AGOOJIYÉ représente une expérience de collaboration entre acteurs industriels, établissements de formation et compétences locales. Il entend ainsi démontrer la capacité des équipes béninoises à concevoir et à assembler un véhicule électrique.

items.title: Espionnage au profit de la Russie : un militaire américain de 41 ans arrêté en Angleterre

original_payload.original_title: Espionnage au profit de la Russie : un militaire américain de 41 ans arrêté en Angleterre
original_payload.original_body:
PHOTO : rawpixel
Espionnage au profit de la Russie : un militaire américain de 41 ans arrêté en Angleterre
10/11/2026    par    Francis Noude
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Un militaire de l’armée américaine a été arrêté mardi 10 novembre 2026 près de Gloucester, dans le sud-ouest de  l’Angleterre , pour des soupçons d’espionnage liés à la  Russie , selon un  communiqué de la police antiterroriste britannique . Toutefois l’homme, âgé de 41 ans, n’a pas été identifié, mais son arrestation est le résultat d’une enquête menée avec les autorités américaines.
En effet, le suspect est visé par les articles 1 et 3 du  National Security Act  de 2023, un texte qui encadre la lutte contre l’espionnage et les ingérences étrangères, et il reste en garde à vue dans un commissariat de Londres. Le premier article porte sur l’obtention ou la divulgation d’informations protégées, tandis que le second concerne l’aide apportée à un service de renseignement étranger.
La police antiterroriste a mené l’opération en coopération étroite avec le FBI et les forces militaires américaines. Toutefois, le directeur du FBI,  Kash Patel,  a souligné la gravité de l’affaire dans le communiqué :  « Il s’agit d’une arrestation importante qui concerne des accusations d’espionnage. Cela constitue une préoccupation majeure pour les États-Unis et leurs alliés » . Un responsable de l’armée américaine a ensuite insisté sur la position du suspect au sein de l’institution, en déclarant :  « Le comportement présumé d’un soldat haut gradé, à qui des informations sensibles avaient été confiées, rappelle de manière saisissante que les menaces internes sont réelles et persistantes » .
Aucun lien avec l’affaire de Fairford
Cependant la police a indiqué que cette arrestation n’est pas liée aux autres enquêtes antiterroristes en cours, et elle écarte ainsi tout rapport avec le complot présumé associé à  l’Iran , évoqué en septembre autour de la base de  RAF Fairford , dans le Gloucestershire. Cette installation britannique abrite en effet la 501e escadre de soutien au combat de l’ US Air Force , une unité administrative américaine, et cinq hommes avaient été arrêtés près du site pour préparation d’un acte terroriste.

items.title: Troupes algériennes au Niger : l'UE s'explique après la polémique

original_payload.original_title: Troupes algériennes au Niger : l'UE s'explique après la polémique
original_payload.original_body:
Photo © CNSP
Troupes algériennes au Niger : l'UE s'explique après la polémique
10/11/2026    par    Gildas Amoussou
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Mardi 10 novembre 2026, l’ Union européenne  a tenté de dissiper le malaise provoqué par ses propos sur l’envoi de soldats algériens au  Niger . Interrogé à nouveau, son porte-parole,  Anouar El Anouni , a repris le dossier point par point.
Pour rappel, le 30 octobre, lors du point de presse quotidien de la Commission à Bruxelles, le porte-parole avait indiqué que l’UE suivait la situation de près et souhaitait connaître la portée, les objectifs et le fondement juridique de ce déploiement. Quelques jours plus tard, Alger a réagi. L’agence officielle  APS  a qualifié ces propos d’«  affabulation pure et simple  » et a affirmé qu’aucune démarche de ce type n’avait été faite auprès des autorités algériennes. Le lundi 9 novembre,  Niamey a reçu le chargé d’affaires de la délégation européenne,  Olaï Voionmaa, pour dénoncer des déclarations « condescendantes et inacceptables ».
Les précisions de Bruxelles
Anouar El Anouni  a d’abord indiqué : «  Notre ambassadeur en Algérie ainsi que notre chargé d’affaires au Niger ont été convoqués par les autorités locales.  » Il a ajouté «  qu’il s’agit de pratiques établies par la Convention de Vienne sur les relations diplomatiques.  »
Sur le fond, il a affirmé : «  L’Union européenne respecte pleinement la souveraineté des deux nations et n’a pas de volonté d’ingérence.  » Il a précisé que «  La décision algérienne de déployer des troupes au Niger relève de la relation bilatérale entre l’Algérie et le Niger . »
Ensuite, il a déclaré : «  L’Union européenne précise qu’elle n’a, et ce, à aucun moment, eu l’intention de demander à l’un ou à l’autre de ses deux partenaires des clarifications sur leur engagement bilatéral.  » Cette formulation contraste avec les termes utilisés le 30 octobre, qui évoquaient précisément une demande d’éclaircissements.
Il a conclu : «  L’Union européenne est attachée à entretenir de bonnes relations bilatérales tant avec l’Algérie que le Niger, et ce, à travers un dialogue respectueux à tous les niveaux, en vue de promouvoir la sécurité, la stabilité ainsi que la prospérité au Sahel.  » Interrogé dans la foulée sur d’éventuels retours concernant les entretiens entre diplomates européens, il a répondu :  « Nous ne commentons pas sur les échanges diplomatiques qui sont confidentiels. »

original_payload.original_body:
Brahim Ghali (Photo : facebook)
Maroc - Algérie : la mobilisation générale du Polisario fait craindre une escalade au Sahara occidental
10/11/2026    par    Francis Noude
Facebook  Twitter  WhatsApp
Le  Front Polisario  a décrété mardi 10 novembre 2026 l’état de mobilisation générale au Sahara occidental, à l’issue d’une réunion d’urgence présidée par son secrétaire général,  Brahim Ghali . Le mouvement indépendantiste, dont les dirigeants sont installés à Tindouf, en  Algérie , justifie sa décision dans un communiqué de son agence de presse, où il affirme avoir décidé  « de décréter l’état de mobilisation générale face à l’escalade militaire marocaine, en dénonçant une concentration de troupes, d’armements et d’équipements militaires le long du mur d’occupation » .
Il appelle ainsi tous les Sahraouis à se préparer, et accuse le  Maroc  de déployer ses forces en grand nombre à plusieurs endroits du mur de sable qui divise le territoire. Ces accusations n’ont pas été confirmées de manière indépendante, et Rabat n’a pas réagi publiquement à ce stade. L’annonce relance toutefois les craintes d’une confrontation plus large avec Alger, car les deux capitales s’opposent depuis des décennies sur ce dossier.
Une décision prise dix jours après la fin de la mission de l’ONU
Le  Polisario  annonce cette mobilisation dix jours après l’expiration du mandat de la  MINURSO , la mission des Nations unies présente dans le territoire depuis 1991. Les projets de résolution présentés par les États-Unis et par la  Russie  au Conseil de sécurité n’ont pas abouti, ce qui a mis fin à la mission. Le Palais royal marocain a pourtant affirmé le 4 novembre que le Royaume continuerait de respecter le cessez-le-feu, même sans les casques bleus. Le jour même de l’annonce du Polisario, Washington a demandé au mouvement, à la tribune de l’ONU, de respecter la trêve, alors que les  États-Unis  et la  France  ont réaffirmé leur soutien au plan d’autonomie proposé par le Maroc. Le   Polisario  rejette ce plan  et réclame un référendum d’autodétermination.
Un cessez-le-feu fragile depuis 2020
Le  Maroc  contrôle environ les trois quarts du Sahara occidental, côte atlantique comprise, tandis que le Polisario tient le reste du territoire à l’est du mur. En novembre 2020, le Front avait en effet déclaré la fin du cessez-le-feu en vigueur depuis 1991, après un incident au poste d’El Guerguerat, ce qui avait ouvert une période d’affrontements de faible intensité. Depuis, le  Polisario  revendique régulièrement des tirs contre des positions marocaines, mais Rabat minimise ces attaques.
L’Algérie  accueille sur son sol les camps de réfugiés sahraouis de Tindouf et soutient politiquement le Polisario, et le Maroc l’accuse de lui fournir un appui militaire et financier, ce qu’Alger conteste. Les relations diplomatiques entre les deux pays sont rompues et leur frontière terrestre est fermée depuis les années 1990, si bien que chaque annonce du Polisario est suivie de près dans les deux capitales.

items.title: Real Madrid's Vinícius Jr sends surprise message to boy who lost his legs in Sudan's war

original_payload.original_title: Real Madrid's Vinícius Jr sends surprise message to boy who lost his legs in Sudan's war
original_payload.original_body:
Real Madrid's Vinícius Jr sends surprise message to boy who lost his legs in Sudan's war
Image source,  Joe McNally/BBC
Image caption,    Zaher is one of millions of children whose lives have been devastated by Sudan's civil war
By  Nawal Al-Maghafi   Senior international investigations correspondent   ,   Reporting from Cairo
Published
2 hours ago
In a dark room in Cairo, a 13-year-old boy looks up at a television screen, barely blinking.
The screen flickers and Real Madrid's superstar winger Vinícius Júnior appears addressing the young boy directly, in Arabic: "Zaher, mahaba" - Hello Zaher.
Zaher barely moves, his eyes wide, locked on his favourite footballer.
We first met Zaher a year ago in the ruins of Sudan's capital, Khartoum. He was a small quiet child, scarred by war - one of millions of children whose lives have been upended since the country's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) started fighting in 2023.
More than 17 million children are now in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan, according to the UN children's charity, Unicef. It says it has been able to verify that at least 4,300 have been killed or maimed, although it believes the true figure is far higher.
Zaher had lost both his legs in a drone strike. With little access to specialist treatment, he dreamed of the day he might walk and play football again.
More than a year later, as we walk into an apartment in the Egyptian capital, Zaher greets us with an enormous hug. His mother, Habibah, embraces us too.
Image source,  Vinícius Júnior
Image caption,    In his video message, Real Madrid star Vinícius Jr invited Zaher to watch a Real Madrid match together
The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs.
For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball again.
When we met in 2025, he had told us his favourite footballer was Vinícius Júnior. We were able to pass this on to the Real Madrid star, who said he wanted to send a personal video message of support. Reunited in Cairo, we gather round to watch it together.
"I was made aware of your story. I know how difficult the last few months must have been for you," the Brazilian footballer begins.
Vinícius has become a leading voice challenging racism in football and supporting black people, and a smile spreads across Zaher's face as the player tells him: "You are a hard-working black man. I really hope you will make good use of your new prosthetic legs, that you return to playing football and that you find happiness. You deserve it."
Then comes an invitation: "I would like to invite you to attend a Madrid match. We can spend the day together."
Overwhelmed, Zaher gets up and leaves the room. A few moments later, he returns wearing his new Vinícius Jr football shirt. He hopes that one day he will be able to get a visa and accept the offer.
"Tell Vinícius, I love him," he says. "His message has really uplifted me." His mother Habibah says she feels "like the whole world is cheering Zaher on, wanting him to succeed".
Image source,  Liam Weir/BBC
Image caption,    Zaher in 2025 - his legs were amputated after he was hit in a drone strike
Zaher lost his legs in 2024, when he and his mother had been trapped in Khartoum. Much of the city had become a battleground as it was torn apart by fighting between Sudan's army and the RSF.
Food and basic supplies were running short and the family did not have enough money to flee. To survive, they sold lentils on the streets.
Then one morning, as Zaher and his mother worked side by side, a drone struck.
"I looked at him and he was bleeding. There was blood everywhere," Habibah explained last year.
She was devastated. "He would wake up and ask: 'Why did you let them cut off my legs?' I couldn't answer."
Back then, Zaher was wheeling himself through the rubble of his neighbourhood in a wheelchair, past burnt-out cars, abandoned tanks and shattered homes.
Before the war, Zaher had loved football. After the drone strike, he could only play on his knees, a painful process that put him at risk of serious infection.
"I wish I could have prosthetic legs so I can play football with my friends like I used to,"  he said at the time .
There seemed little prospect of that happening, but his story resonated far beyond Sudan, prompting an outpouring of support from people around the world.
Among them was Dena Latif, a UK-based lawyer of Sudanese origin. After seeing the BBC report, she helped spearhead an online campaign raising £45,000 ($60,000) for his medical care.
Unable to get the treatment he needed in Sudan, Zaher had to leave the country, which was far from straightforward. He and his mother had no passports and their birth certificates had been destroyed during the war.
Image source,  Joe McNally/BBC
Image caption,    Zaher has learned to use his new legs with months of support from doctors and physiotherapists in Cairo
After months of planning, he and his mother were able to fly to Cairo where an apartment had been prepared for them, with food in the fridge and medical appointments arranged.
For the first time in years, their immediate concern was no longer simply how to survive.
'I can't afford to save both twins': Sudan's war left one mother with an impossible choice
Published
16 October 2025
A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan
Published
13 November 2025
Zaher underwent further surgery, followed by months of physiotherapy and training to learn to use his prosthetic legs. He also received psychological support to help him process the trauma he had been through.
"He was shy, a little bit depressed, sad," says Dr Bintelmuna Eltayeb , one of the doctors involved in his care. "To get a smile out of him was almost impossible, but now you can see he's laughing. He has great confidence in himself."
His transformation has been as much psychological as physical, say those close to him, and Dena says Zaher now approaches life with a determination that has surprised them.
As we spend time with Zaher, he laughs and jokes, making up for some of the childhood that war has taken from him.
He is eager to try new things, from horse riding to cycling, and wants to become an airline pilot. He hasn't had a game of football yet but is looking forward to playing with his friends back home.
For Habibah, watching her son regain his confidence has brought enormous relief. But she worries about his future, his education and how he will be received in Sudan, a country still locked in civil war.
Image source,  Anadolu via Getty Images
Image caption,    Khartoum has suffered extensive damage, with many buildings damaged and their contents stolen
The state of emergency has been lifted in their home city, Khartoum, with the Sudanese army back in control there. But throughout the capital, buildings have been left destroyed - burned, blackened and looted.
Concerns over security remain and 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of food insecurity, according to a recent statement released by the US and 30 other Western states.  The group also warned of "potential famine" .
"I hope that Zaher's story doesn't end with him," says Dena. She hopes his recovery will attract more attention and funds for the thousands of other Sudanese children who have suffered life-altering injuries.
Zaher and his mother are now back in Khartoum. They hope that as the city is more stable at the moment, he will be able to get his prosthetic legs checked and adjusted there as he grows.
Despite the safety they found in Cairo, they missed their home, family and friends. And while Zaher has been given a chance to reclaim his childhood, millions of other Sudanese children are still waiting for theirs.
Additional reporting by Scarlett Barter and Abdelrahman Abutaleb

items.title: 'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted

original_payload.original_title: 'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted
original_payload.original_body:
'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted
Image caption,    Agnes Shikoli says she fears either drowning, or being crushed by her house
Published
2 hours ago
"It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the six-foot [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, one of the largest informal settlements in Kenya.
Her tiny house lies just a couple of metres from the Ngong river, which runs through this densely populated area in the capital, Nairobi.
The scars of floods in the long rainy season earlier this year   can still be seen - including a broken TV in the corner which was immersed in water.
Tucked out of sight is a photo of her sister Beatrice Khalayi, 58, who died when intense rains caused widespread destruction in Kibera. She was among more than 60 people across the country who lost their lives.
"Someone called me to tell me that she had died of electrocution after her house flooded," Shikoli recalls. "When I see a picture of her, I feel uneasy, that's why I keep it far from me, so I don't see it."
With Kenya's short rainy season now starting, Shikoli tells the BBC she is afraid – especially following warnings that the El Niño weather phenomenon could bring a new round of flooding.
"I feel like it can kill us. These houses aren't made of stone," says the 62-year-old. "They can fall on us, or the water can drown us."
Kibera - and Kenya more widely - are on the frontline of preparations for the potential impact of El Niño.
Forecasters have warned that this year could see one of the strongest on record, bringing extreme weather to many parts of the world.
In southern Kenya, that means the threat of rains even more intense than usual.
Outside Shikoli's house, groups of men and women wearing high-visibility vests are shovelling and raking garbage out of the riverbed and disposing it far from the water.
This programme called Climate Worx, under the office of President William Ruto, is meant to rehabilitate Nairobi's rivers. Such exercises have intensified since August  when warnings increased about the possible scale of this year's El Niño .
Image caption,    Rubbish clogging Nairobi's drains and sewers was seen as a major factor in the deadly floods earlier this year
Similar work to unclog drainage systems is ongoing across Nairobi, a sprawling city built on hilly ground crossed by three major rivers.
But the workers have a huge task on their hands.
Blocked drains and inadequate sewage systems were widely blamed for the high number of deaths after the floods earlier in the year, as the excess rainfall had nowhere to escape.
The Nairobi County disaster management chief, Bramwell Simiyu tells the BBC that drainage systems have been "untouched for many years" and that removing the rubbish from them will save lives.
Floods disproportionately affect informal settlements in Nairobi, especially those near rivers, like Kibera and Mathare.
In most of these settlements, houses sit just a few metres from rivers. Some people, including Shikoli, live on the slopes of the river itself due to the constant expansion of the settlements. When flash floods occur, these houses are swept away, endangering the lives of their occupants.
Nairobi's drainage system hasn't been upgraded to deal with the rapid growth in the population and infrastructure over the decades
"The existing drainage system was developed 30 years ago to cater for a population of about 2.5 million residents but we're dealing with about 7 million in the daytime and 5.5 million night-time," Simiyu says.
He adds that investment of up to $192m (£143m) is needed to upgrade the sewerage and drainage system entirely.
But there is little sign that either the cash-strapped national or city council will able to raise this kind of money.
The Nairobi River Basin Regeneration programme, a government programme aimed at restoring the city's rivers, found that settlements near rivers, and where there is weak enforcement of regulations, have increased flooding risks. It recommended a "buffer" to protect rivers and "humane relocation" of communities where necessary.
However, rising poverty has driven many people to live close to rivers.
"Our worst case scenario looking at low-income settlements is that up to about 100,000 people are at risk," Simiyu says. "Moderate projections is about 5,000 households or about 20,000 people may be at risk."
Anyone forced to leave their homes will be relocated to 167 designated holding grounds where a stockpile of relief food and supplies will be distributed, Simiyu says.
Nobody knows exactly when the rains will come – or how much rain there will be.
But Kenya's meteorological department warns that November is usually the peak rainfall month of the short rainy season, which normally lasts from October to December.
A regional forecast from the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (Igad) warned in September that there was "an 81% probability of a very strong El Niño during October–December 2026".
So far, the heavy rains predicted have not occurred but experts remain concerned.
In East Africa, this El Niño is being widely compared to a similar weather event in 1997-1998 which caused widespread flooding and destruction in Somalia and Kenya.
Weather forecaster Jemima Gacheru tells the BBC that's because temperature conditions in the Indian Ocean in the 1997 El Niño and those recorded now are similar. This interaction, she says, has been seen to result in very strong rainfall.
"For this season we have a very strong El Niño already in play in the Pacific and then we have a positive Indian Ocean dipole," Gacheru said. This is often called the "Indian Niño" because of its similarity to its Pacific equivalent and  refers to the difference in sea-surface temperatures in opposite parts of the Indian Ocean .
"We expect to have some enhanced rainfall over several parts of the country."
The UN's migration body the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has warned that almost 900,000 people could be forced to leave their homes in Kenya this year, mostly because of the predicted floods.
Image source,  Anadolu via Getty Images
Image caption,    Dozens of people died in floods in Kenya earlier this year
Kenya is not the only African country worried about the potential impact of El Niño.
In neighbouring Somalia, the country's disaster management agency has warned that 1.2 million people are at risk of displacement caused by extreme weather – including the risk of both floods and drought.
The 1998 floods killed 2,000 people in Somalia and forced a further 250,000 to flee their homes, according to the Food and Agriculture Organisation. Up to 80% of crops were destroyed in some parts of the country.
The United Nation's famine warning system IPC has warned of the increased risk of food insecurity in Somalia due to supply chain issues exacerbated by the impact of El Niño.
Elsewhere on the continent forecasters fear El Niño could bring extreme heat and prolonged periods without rain.
It could cause a crisis for farmers across parts of West Africa, including the semi-arid Sahel region south of the Sahara, as well as in southern parts of the continent, where the risk of crop failure is high.
There are fears El Niño's impact will worsen existing issues.
Communities like Kibera are already grappling with poor housing and rampant poverty, while parts of Somalia are already in the middle of a devastating drought.
National governments in many countries are doing what they can to prepare but the extent of El Niño's impact is impossible to predict.
Back in Kibera, Shikoli and her family are preparing for the worst.
Council officials have told them they should leave their home on the riverbank until the rainy season has passed but Shikoli makes just $2 (£1.5) a day selling groundnuts and fruit from a small stall next to the river.
"I want to move," she says. "But I don't have the means.
"We just have to persevere and leave it to God."

items.title:
Reexamining Ethiopia’s Ethnic Federal Model to Advance Peace and Security
  Reforming Ethiopia’s ethnic federal model provides an opportunity to pivot away from the persistent instability generated by

original_payload.original_title:
Reexamining Ethiopia’s Ethnic Federal Model to Advance Peace and Security
  Reforming Ethiopia’s ethnic federal model provides an opportunity to pivot away from the persistent instability generated by ethnic militias, though this will require opening political space as well as disarmament.
original_payload.original_body:
By  Joseph Siegle  and  Hany Wahila
November 10, 2026
Reforming Ethiopia’s ethnic federal model provides an opportunity to pivot away from the persistent instability generated by ethnic militias, though this will require opening political space as well as disarmament.
A man walking at the Bakelo Camp housing thousands of internally displaced Amharas resulting from militia conflict in Ethiopia’s Oromia region. (Photo: AFP/Marco Simoncelli)
Attacks launched by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allies against the federal government in September 2026 raised fears of a return to the destructive conflict of 2020-2022, in which an estimated 600,000 people perished. While the federal government subsequently regained control over virtually all of the  territories taken during the offensive, concerns persist that instability in northern Ethiopia could trigger a wider regional war—potentially colliding with the catastrophic conflict in Sudan and drawing in rival, well-resourced Gulf States.
Overshadowed by these regional tensions are Ethiopia’s ongoing domestic security challenges. The TPLF attacks were launched under the rubric of the so-called “Alliance for Survival”—comprised of a disparate coalition of seven Ethiopian armed groups:
Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF)
Oromo Liberation Army (OLA)
Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM)
Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF)
Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (ARDUF)
Benishangul People’s Liberation Movement (BPLM)
Gumuz People’s Democratic Movement  (GPDM)
Representing dissident factions from their respective regions, the stated objective of the Alliance is to overthrow the government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. While loosely organized (the alliance was declared just weeks before the September attacks), each of the seven groups had taken up arms against the government over the preceding years (and in some cases decades). Some were part of a  precursor alliance formed in 2006 .
The Ethiopian federal government’s 2023 decision to integrate all regional militias under the federal army or police following the destructive Tigray conflict has met armed resistance from these and other militias, propelling an escalation in violent clashes in recent years.
Fighting involving these groups and federal forces has resulted in an average of 1,500 clashes and 4,900 battle-related fatalities annually since 2024. Roughly 90 percent of these fatalities are linked to two groups: the Amhara Fano National Movement (60 percent) and the Oromo Liberation Army (30 percent). Left to fester, the threat from regional militias poses a deeper source of instability for the country.
Ethiopia’s ethnic federal model represents a source of structural instability.
The militias’ unwillingness to disarm and accept a unitary chain of command under the federal government exposes a  structural defect in Ethiopia’s ethnic federal model.  Established by the TPLF-led federal government in 1995, the model created ethnically based jurisdictions and gave regions the right to secede. The constitution also authorized regional police forces, which have evolved into  militarized special forces .
Experience from other federal systems shows that ethnically based political jurisdictions and autonomous regional security forces  contribute to fragmentation and increase the likelihood of conflict .
Understanding the political, economic, and security drivers of Ethiopia’s regional militias, therefore, can provide context for how the country addresses these persistent domestic security challenges and how it builds a federal governance structure that can be resilient and responsive to the diverse needs of Ethiopia’s 135 million citizens.
Tigray Region
The political-security equation in Tigray is unique given the dominant role the TPLF held in national politics for nearly three decades. When the ruling Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Defense Forces (EPRDF) dissolved in 2019, the TPLF retained considerable political influence, experienced military commanders, and military assets. The unwillingness of the TPLF leadership to accede to federal authority set the stage for the 2020-2022 conflict.
Even following the TPLF’s 2022 defeat and the signing of the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement (COHA, also referred to as the Pretoria Agreement), hardliners in the TPLF, led by Debretsion Gebremichael, have attempted to undermine federal authority in Tigray. Debretsion was the former Minister of Communications and Information Technology and the Deputy Prime Minister in Ethiopia during EPRDF rule.
Established under the COHA, the Tigray Interim Administration (TIA) was intended to facilitate the reintegration of Tigray into Ethiopia’s federal structure. The TIA’s authority, however, has been consistently challenged by the Debretsion-led faction of the TPLF, including the  failure to give up heavy weapons  as stipulated under COHA. This resistance grew more brazen over time, ultimately resulting in the TPLF unilaterally asserting the reinstatement of the pre-2022 regional council in April 2026.
The majority of Tigray’s citizens did not support the TPLF reigniting the conflict with the federal government.
This  power grab was rejected by many Tigrayans . A statement by the Salsay Weyane Tigray party in May 2026 captured these concerns: “For over three decades, this organization [the TPLF] has monopolized the politics of Tigray. It has now devolved into a tool for competing factions to seize power by force, making the gun the primary rule of the political game.” This view was a recurring theme of a coalition of Tigrayan opposition parties that formed the  Covenant for Radical Change  in 2023, calling for political reforms in the region.
TPLF hardliners were emboldened by an undeclared alliance with Eritrea that is believed to include  access to weapons  and deployment of Eritrean military forces in Tigray. This deepening belligerence culminated in a declaration of war and seizure of federal government assets in Tigray on September 23, 2026. Subsequent fighting with federal forces resulted in at least 277 battle-related fatalities.
What becomes of the TPLF hardliners will be a central issue for the region moving forward. Given that the party has twice launched violent attacks on the federal government—at great cost in lives, economic loss, and regional stability—it has limited credibility as a democratic political actor.
Members of the Ethiopian Federal Police on patrol after federal forces pushed back the TPLF in Mekelle, October 2026. (Photo: AFP)
Rebuilding Tigray as part of Ethiopia’s federal structure involves far more than the TPLF, however. Still recovering from the previous conflict, the majority of Tigray’s 7.5 million citizens did not support the TPLF hardliners reigniting the conflict with the federal government. This limited support, underscored by the widespread evasion of the TPLF’s forced conscription, is a key factor in the rapid collapse of the TPLF offensive in September and October 2026.
The TPLF’s short-lived territorial gains were also due to the creation of the Tigray Peace Force (TPF) in 2025. The TPF was formed by disaffected TPLF fighters who saw no future for themselves under the TPLF leadership and believed they should be defending Tigray rather than “ preserving the same old elite .” The TPF contends that the Tigrayan military should be apolitical rather than aligned with one party. When fighting broke out in 2026, the TPF fought with the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) to repulse the TPLF offensive.
Western Tigray
A flashpoint in tensions between the Tigray and Amhara Regions is the status of Western Tigray (also known as Wolkayit). The jurisdiction was the focus of some of the most vicious violence during the 2020-2022 conflict, after which many Tigrayan residents were forced to flee the area and the land subsequently settled by Amhara communities. The region is the focus of competing territorial claims linked to iterative episodes of forced displacement and resettlement from previous eras.
The COHA does not explicitly address the status of the area, and the federal government has called for a referendum by the territory’s residents to resolve the matter. Tigrayans contend this solution would not account for the estimated 800,000 Tigrayans who have been displaced since 2020. The ongoing uncertainty and polarization around this issue have been a justification for militias in both Tigray and Amhara to retain their arms.
After reclaiming the regional capital of Mekelle and other parts of Tigray, the federal authorities appointed a new TIA leadership, comprised of ethnic Tigrayans, in October. Their mandate is to oversee elections by April 2027, restore basic public services and infrastructure, and facilitate the return of displaced communities.
Given the security challenges in the region, Tigrayans were unable to go to the polls during Ethiopia’s general elections in June 2026. A participatory electoral process has the potential to redirect Tigrayan interests into institutionalized political channels—and undercut the rationale for violence.
Some of the emerging political parties in Tigray include:
Salsay Weyane Tigray
Arena Tigray for Democracy and Sovereignty
Tigray Democratic Solidarity
National Congress of Great Tigray
The varied political affiliations within Tigray underscore that the instability in the region has been largely driven by political rivalries. As in other  political jurisdictions defined along ethnic boundaries , such structures  provide a ready means to politicize ethnicity.
Central issues will be how best to rebuild Tigray, provide basic services, facilitate the return of displaced populations, generate investment, and clarify the authorities of the regional administration. Given Tigray’s location on the border with Sudan and Eritrea, security arrangements will be particularly critical. One of the sensitivities of the implementation of the COHA was that Eritrean forces never fully withdrew from some of Tigray’s border districts.
The extent to which this transition is perceived by Tigrayans as representative of their interests will have far-reaching implications for the stabilization of this turbulent region. Political stability, in turn, will contribute to economic reconstruction and foster  stronger integration between Tigray and the much larger Ethiopian economy.
Amhara Region
With an estimated 33 million people, the Amhara Region is Ethiopia’s second most populous and historically the most influential. Massive youth protests in the region facilitated the dissolution of the EPRDF in 2019. Animosities built up over the 30 years of TPLF control fueled Amhara’s regional militias to fight alongside the ENDF during the 2020-2022 conflict.
Some of these trained and experienced Amhara militias subsequently resisted the federal government’s decision to dismantle all regional forces starting in April 2023. The leader of the Amhara Prosperity Party, Girma Yeshitila, was  assassinated soon after the announcement . This sequence of events triggered a spike in violence between the decentralized Fano (“freedom fighter” in Amharic) militias and the regional and federal forces that has persisted across the Amhara Region ever since. Whereas the Amhara Region had been among the most stable in Ethiopia before the 2020-2022 conflict, it subsequently has faced some of the highest levels of violence, including approximately 3,500 battle-related fatalities annually since 2024.
Fano’s lack of a cohesive political structure has impeded a clear articulation of the militias’ agenda or negotiation positions.
Composed of former youth protesters, vigilantes, and special police forces, the Fano militias claim a mandate to  protect the interests of ethnic Amharas . Some make more zealous demands of Amhara ethnic nationalism and territorial claims in neighboring regions, including Tigray. Still others advocate for a greater Ethiopian identity. Collectively, the Fano militias are estimated to have 15,000-20,000 fighters.
Fano’s lack of a cohesive political structure has impeded a clear articulation of the militias’ agenda or negotiation positions. The merger of five Fano militias under the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM) in January 2026 was viewed as a step toward a more formalized Fano structure. The AFNM’s subsequent decision to sign onto the “Alliance for Survival,” however, may undercut the group’s ability to speak for the wider spectrum of Fano militias, most of which do not fall under the AFNM.
The degree of popular support for the Fano militias is unclear. Some Fano militias have attempted to undermine the electoral process by intimidating citizens who sought to participate in the electoral process. As a result, voting did not take place in 8 of Amhara Region’s 130 electoral districts.
The ruling  Prosperity Party claimed 117 seats  in the House of People’s Representatives 2026 election. In 2021, the Prosperity Party garnered 114 seats. The National Movement of Amhara (NaMA) secured six seats, and the Amhara Democratic Force Movement (ADFM) took three. The remaining seats were distributed among other parties, including the Ethiopians Citizens for Social Justice (EZEMA) party. Ethno-nationalist parties like the Argoba Unity Jeberti party are also active, though did not gain any seats.
Roughly 90 percent of the fatalities linked to ethnic militias are tied to the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army.
NaMA alleges it has faced intimidation from federal authorities and several of the Party’s  elected members of parliament have been detained . In 2023, the Party’s most vocal critic of the government,  Christian Tadele , was charged with terrorism and possession of firearms. Despite Tadele’s immunity, he was held in prison for over 3 years before being released in 2026 following a pardon.
Between 80 and 90 percent of the population in Amhara rely on agriculture for their livelihoods. Incentivizing and scaling up investments to improve productivity and diversify the economy will  depend on greater security in the region .
Oromia Region
Oromia is Ethiopia’s most populous region with an estimated 43 million people. It is also one of the poorest and has not historically had significant representation at the federal level despite its relative proximity to the national capital Addis Ababa. Comprising roughly equal numbers of Muslims and Christians, Oromia has also been a focal point of  periodic religious tensions .
The Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) was established in the 1970s as the armed wing of the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF) to advance Oromo self-determination. OLF leaders were forced into exile following a falling out with the TPLF-led transitional government in 1992, and the group was subsequently banned in 2008. Upon coming to power in 2018, Abiy signed a peace agreement with the OLF enabling its leadership to return.  A faction of the OLA, however, refused to disarm , leading to a split from the OLF.
While never commanding a large following, the OLA has been resilient.
While never commanding a large following (the OLA is currently estimated to have 3,000 fighters), the OLA has been resilient. Following the federal government’s 2023 decision to ban all armed militias,  some splinter elements of the OLA did reach agreement with the regional authorities  and gave up their arms. However, violence between the main OLA faction and the federal government has escalated. This has resulted in an average of roughly 1,200 annual battle-related fatalities since 2024, destabilizing parts of western Oromia where the OLA is most active. Even though it signed onto the Alliance for Survival, the OLA has yet to coordinate military operations with its alliance partners.
The Oromo Prosperity Party dominates Oromia’s representation in the House of People’s Representatives, controlling 167 of the 178 available seats in the 2026 general elections. The remaining nine seats were won by unaffiliated opposition candidates. The two most prominent opposition parties in the region, the OLF and the Oromo Federalist Congress (OFC) party, did not gain any representation. As in 2021, the OFC did not contest the elections, lacking confidence in the fairness of the process. The OLF did campaign in the 2026 elections (after boycotting in 2021) yet failed to win a seat.
The limited opposition representation has been used as a justification for the OLA’s continued attacks.
The OLF has faced  detention, harassment, and other restrictions  that have impeded its ability to campaign. In April 2024, Bate Urgessa, an OLF spokesperson, was killed by an unknown attacker in Oromia 2 months after being detained for “conspiring to incite unrest” after speaking to a foreign journalist.
The limited opposition representation has been used as a justification for the OLA’s continued attacks. This includes blocking key roads and raids on foreign mining operations, demanding that extractive companies ensure local community beneficiation. An attack on the $340 million  Tulu Kapi gold mine  operated by UK-based KEFI Gold and Copper resulted in several fatalities and the suspension of mining operations.
The OLF has called for  negotiated settlements to end the clashes . They have called for proposals to establish a  transitional national unity government in the Region to ensure representation  and constructive engagement among opposition political parties and armed groups that have gone unrecognized by the ruling party.
Ogaden, Benishangul, and Afar Regions
Elements of the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF) have fought for greater autonomy of the Somali Region of Ethiopia since the 1977-1978 Ogaden War between Ethiopia and Somalia. Following the signing of a peace agreement with the federal government in 2018 as part of Abiy’s reconciliation process, the majority of the ONLF  disavowed armed struggle  and has sought to represent the Somali Region’s 13 million residents through political channels.
Since signing the peace accords, the main Jijiga-faction of the ONLF has had its terrorist designation removed, re-registered as a political organization, disarmed and reintegrated most of its forces, and secured representation of 20 seats in the Regional Council during the last election cycle. The ONLF, accordingly, has been among the most successful parties to return from exile and engage in the political process.
However, an old guard of the ONLF led by Abdirahman Mahadi has continued to mount guerrilla attacks against the federal government and is the faction that signed onto the Alliance for Survival. Comprised of an estimated several thousand fighters, the ONLF is linked to 111 reported fatalities in 2024, but less than 20 deaths since that time.
The ONLF has been among the most successful parties to return from exile and engage in the political process.
Comprising an estimated 1 million inhabitants, the Benishangul Region in northwest Ethiopia on the borders of Sudan and South Sudan is among the smallest in Ethiopia. The region is noteworthy for hosting the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD). The Region has had armed groups intermittently fighting the federal government since the 1990s, claiming to represent indigenous ethnic groups. Despite various signed political settlements in 2005, 2012, and 2022, the Benishangul Peoples’ Liberation Movement (BPLM) and Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movement (GPDM) persist in their armed struggle largely from bases in Sudan’s Blue Nile State, where they are reported to be  supported by the Sudanese Armed Forces . Battle-related fatalities linked to these groups have increased in recent years from 10 in 2024 to 80 in 2026. The BPLM is one of the signatories to the Alliance for Survival.
Members of an Afar militia stand at a checkpoint in the town off Abala. (Photo: AFP/Eduardo Soteras)
The Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (ARDUF), also known as Ugugumo, has engaged in armed struggle against the federal government since 1993 with the stated aim of self-determination for the 2.5 million ethnic Afar in Ethiopia. Under the leadership of Ibrahim Osman Aliyu, a former mayor of Berhale, the ARDUF has collaborated closely with the TPLF and Eritrea, from which Aliyu has been operating since 2025. This proximity enabled the TPLF to establish a front in Afar during its offensive in September 2026, even though the ARDUF is reported to field only 300 fighters. This territory has subsequently been retaken by the federal government. Like the Fano militias in Amhara, the ARDUF was previously aligned with the federal government during the 2020–2022 conflict against the TPLF. They were not parties to the COHA, however. This perceived exclusion and ongoing marginalization were justifications for joining the TPLF coalition in 2026.
State Building as Stabilization
The current moment provides an opening to reexamine the lingering challenge of regional militias lest these fester and become sources of worsening destabilization.
Ethiopia’s ethnic federal model represents a source of structural instability by incentivizing ethno-nationalist militias to amplify ethnically based grievances as a means of mobilizing local recruitment and rationalizing violence. In most regions where these ethnic militias operate, they command relatively small forces and limited popular support. These ethnic militias, moreover, are by and large not pursuing democratic solutions to their grievances, as evidenced by their threats to or attacks on electoral processes. Rather, these militias are often splinters from a larger political party that has disavowed violence and is willing to pursue political channels to advance the interests of their regions.
While small in size, many of these ethno-nationalist militias have persisted for decades, underscoring their resilience. Moreover, several are in regions that border Ethiopia’s neighbors and are easily instrumentalized by foreign actors. This has had tangible consequences, with roughly 4,900 annual battle-related fatalities linked to these groups in recent years. This insecurity, in turn, is a significant handicap for investment, infrastructural development, and job creation—which would enhance the quality of livelihoods in marginalized parts of these regions.
The repelling of the TPLF’s 2026 offensive—supported to varying degrees by its Alliance for Survival partners—provides an opening to reexamine the lingering challenge of regional militias lest these fester and become sources of worsening destabilization. The TPLF is the largest, most capable, and most regionally connected of these militias. Their military setbacks and loss of popular support create an opportunity to turn the page on this era of regional militias challenging the federal government. The disarming of nonstate militias, moreover, is a prerequisite for realizing a unitary chain of command and state building.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed addresses the National Dialogue in June 2024. (Photo: screengrab)
This is a political as much as security process. There are parties across Ethiopia’s diverse spectrum of communities willing to engage in such a political dialogue. The degree to which these parties gain official representation in legislative assemblies is a barometer for citizens as to whether there are genuine avenues for political participation. The 2026 general elections did not yield such representation at either the national or regional level, with the Prosperity Party controlling roughly 90 percent of seats in the House of People’s Representatives and, collectively, the Regional Councils. Similarly, the high-profile National Dialogue held in July 2026 was widely seen as  lacking significant independent perspectives .
Aside from elections, building a more stable federal model will require ensuring adequate space for politicians from opposition parties to contribute to the regional and national agenda, independent media to fulfill their role in informing the public, civic education on Ethiopia’s federal system, and strengthening institutional checks and balances to uphold the rule of law.
Building a more stable federal model will require ensuring adequate space for politicians from opposition parties to contribute to the regional and national agenda.
Facilitating such exchanges will provide the opportunity to reorient Ethiopia’s federal system away from the ethnic characteristics that currently define it. As in successful federal systems, this will require clarifying the authorities, responsibilities, and revenues available for each layer of government. Doing so can contribute to making government more responsive and adaptable to the unique priorities, services, and customs of local communities across Ethiopia’s diverse population while simultaneously reinforcing the economic, cultural, security, and national identity benefits of being part of a larger federal system.

items.title: Nigeria: CJID Announces Finalists for the 2026 Alfred Opubor Next-Gen Awards for Campus Journalism

original_payload.original_title: Nigeria: CJID Announces Finalists for the 2026 Alfred Opubor Next-Gen Awards for Campus Journalism
original_payload.original_body:
The Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID) has announced the finalists for the 2026 Alfred Opubor Next-Gen Awards for Campus Journalism, recognising outstanding student journalists whose work demonstrates a commitment to public-interest reporting, accountability and amplifying underrepresented voices.
Organised through CJID's Next Gen Campus Reporter Project, the annual awards celebrate emerging journalists who use evidence-based storytelling to investigate issues, spotlight challenges affecting their communities and institutions, and contribute to public discourse.
Named in honour of Nigeria's first Professor of Mass Communication, Alfred Opubor, the awards recognise his pioneering contributions to communication scholarship and journalism education.
Since its  inception in 2018 , the Alfred Opubor Awards has served as a platform to identify, mentor, and celebrate outstanding student journalists across Nigerian universities.
Over the years,  the prize  has recognised 40 winners across multiple categories, including Investigative Reporting, Gender, Environment, Health, and Accountability Journalism. These categories have amplified the voices of young journalists working to deepen democratic accountability and promote human rights through storytelling.
The  2025  edition only rewarded the best three stories overall without the usual categorisation.
2026 Finalists
The 2026 edition recognises excellence across six categories: Investigative Journalism, Community Reporting, Data Journalism, Campus Affairs, Health Reporting, and Reporting on Inclusion.
Following the evaluation process, 12 campus journalists -a winner and runner-up across the six categories- and one overall winner have emerged as finalists.
The finalists were selected from entries submitted by undergraduate student journalists across Nigerian tertiary institutions. Their stories address a range of public-interest issues, reflecting the role of campus journalism in documenting institutional challenges, examining community concerns and holding decision-makers accountable.
